memory_size (line 30) and num_filters (line 26) are unconstrained int32 model inputs; the product at line 50 is computed in 32-bit int and overflows (e.g. 65536 * 65536 = 2^32 wraps to 0). The wrapped value is consumed by this equality comparison that gates state-shape validation, so a state tensor with dim[1] == 0 passes Prepare although the shown arithmetic requires 2^32 elements, defeating the validation gate (CWE-190); the undersized state is then used by the (unshown) Eval writes.

assumptions: `params->rank`, `node->builtin_data`, and all `dims->data[]` values are derived from attacker-controllable model/delegate metadata and are treated as entry-point inputs (no shown statement proves trust).
`context->ResizeTensor(context, tensor, dims_array)` consumes the dims values as tensor sizes/dimensions per the standard, name-implied semantics of tensor resize.

`TfLiteIntArray`/`TfLiteIntArrayCreate(2)` yields an int array of declared capacity 2 (visible at lines 53, 74, 171), so the writes at lines 54-55, 75-76, 172-173 are in-bounds; the defect is the value domain, not the write itself.
int overflow is evaluated on the shown 32-bit `int` type (wrap behavior used for the 65536x65536 witness).
limitations: The concrete memory-corruption consequences of the negative dims (allocation size wrap and resulting out-of-bounds access in Eval / resize internals) are not visible inside this fragment; the confirmed in-fragment mechanism is the unvalidated negative-size flow at the ResizeTensor call sites.
A potential OOB read of `input->dims->data[1]` (lines 31-32) when the input tensor has fewer than 2 dims is not reported because the `dims` array capacity is not visible in the fragment.

Dereferences of `input/weights/state/output->quantization.params` and `scale->data[0]` (lines 184-199) have no visible NULL/length check; whether the TFLite runtime always populates them for int8 tensors is a framework invariant not shown in the fragment, so it is recorded as unconfirmable rather than a finding.
`rank != 0` (line 27) correctly guards the divisions at lines 28-29 (it executes before them), so divide-by-zero is not a finding; the residual defect is that the guard admits negative ranks.

The int-overflow finding (CWE-190) is secondary: the corrupted value's immediate consumer is the validation comparison at lines 49-50; the resulting undersized-state OOB would occur in the unshown Eval.
Single-shot parameter leaks or unchecked-but-constant framework allocations (TfLiteIntArrayCreate results) are treated as robustness concerns, not findings.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The fragment is the guarded/fixed form of the QuantizeV2 kernel: every input-derived size or index is validated by shown OP_REQUIRES checks before use. min/max tensors are required to be 1-D of size num_slices (lines 15-40) or to hold exactly one element (lines 42, 47), which bounds the scalar flat<float>()(0) reads (lines 64-65) and all i < num_slices loop accesses (lines 92-97). axis_ is bounded to [0, dims-1] (lines 7, 9), and the derived reshape argument axis_ - 1 (line 80) is in [-1, dims-2], which the fragment's own chip<1>(i) slice loop requires to be valid (middle dim = dims[axis_]); the suspected negative-axis OOB depends on an unshown callee convention and is not confirmable from the shown code. The int64->int narrowing of num_slices (line 14) has no confirmed security consequence.

assumptions: axis_ is bounded by the shown guards: axis_ > -1 (line 7) and input.dims() > axis_ (line 9), so axis_ in [0, dims-1].
min/max residual ranges are fixed by the shown equality checks: 1-D with dim_size(0) == num_slices (lines 15-40) or NumElements() == 1 (lines 42, 47).
output tensors 1 and 2 are allocated with minmax_shape = input(1).shape() (lines 54, 74-77), whose size was checked equal to num_slices, so flat<float>()(i) with i < num_slices is in bounds.
pre_dim * num_slices * post_dim equals input.NumElements() exactly because the dims partitions the shape (lines 81-89, allocation at line 56).

The 3-D input view at line 80 must have middle dim dims[axis_], otherwise the chip<1>(i) loop over i in [0, num_slices) would be inconsistent; this is the only shown-code-consistent reading of the axis_ - 1 argument.
limitations: The lone suspicious flow is flat_inner_outer_dims(axis_ - 1) with axis_ = 0 (line 80) reaching argument -1. Whether -1 is an OOB/abort depends entirely on the unshown callee convention for the axis parameter; the fragment's own slice loop implies -1 must be valid, so a positive CWE-125/CWE-617 verdict is not demonstrable from the shown code and is demoted.

int64 -> int narrowing of num_slices (line 14) is not a confirmed finding: negative truncations are rejected by the dim_size(0) == num_slices checks (non-negative int64 vs negative int), and positive small truncations would require a tensor with >= 2^32 elements and produce only partial output initialization, with no shown memory-safety impact.

int64 multiplication of pre_dim/post_dim (lines 82-87) has no confirmed overflow path: each is a sub-product of an already-allocated tensor's total element count, and the fragment shows no security-relevant consumer of a wrapped value.
Dtype/registration invariants (input must be float) are not shown and were not used to justify any conclusion.

verdict.summary: The RTCP XR parser dereferences its common header before validating the buffer capacity: `rtcp_xr->common.pt` (line 14) and `rtcp_xr->common.length` (line 17) are read while `size` is still unconstrained (the only size guard, `(pkt_len + 1) > (size / 4)`, executes after, at line 19). For a 2-byte packet whose byte 1 equals RTCP_XR, the 16-bit `common.length` read at byte offset 2 reads 2 bytes out of bounds; sizes 0-3 similarly make the line-14/17 header reads OOB (CWE-125). The out-of-bounds value only feeds the early-return guard, so impact is a small over-read rather than corruption.

evidence.reason: CWE-125 OOB read: `size` (parameter, line 3) retains its full unsigned domain at this sink because the only size check, `if ((pkt_len + 1) > (size / 4))` at line 19, executes after this line (order 17 < 19) and line 14's `pt` comparison admits equality, so the read is reachable. Witness: `size = 2`, byte 1 of `pkt` = RTCP_XR; the 16-bit read of bytes 2-3 exceeds the 2-byte buffer by 2 bytes (byte index 3 > size 2). No protective statement precedes this read.

CWE-125 OOB read at the same missing-bound defect: `rtcp_xr->common.pt` is at byte offset 1 of the packet and is dereferenced before any statement constrains `size` (line 3) to be >= 2; for `size` in {0,1} this byte read is itself out of bounds. This is the same missing minimum-size validation as the line-17 sink, listed as a distinct sink statement.

assumptions: `size` is the caller-provided capacity of the buffer pointed to by `pkt`; no statement in the fragment establishes a minimum value for `size`.

The RTCP common header fields `pt` and `length` occupy the first 4 bytes (bitfield byte 0, `pt` byte 1, `length` bytes 2-3), so reading both requires `size >= 4`; the fragment contains no statement enforcing this.
limitations: NULL `sess` dereference demoted: caller-contract robustness, no attacker-directed NULL source shown in the fragment (CWE-476 not confirmed).

DLRR unsigned arithmetic (`now - lrr - dlrr`, line 99) can wrap, but line 120 routes wrapped cases to the else log branch and line 126 caps `eedelay` before `pj_math_stat_update`; no security-relevant state is corrupted.
Format-specifier mismatches in log calls (lines 112-115, 144-149) use constant format strings with numeric arguments; no injection is possible.
Division by `sess->rtcp_session->ts_freq.u64` inside TRACE_ (line 77) is evaluated only when logging is enabled and depends on framework state, not on attacker-controlled packet data.
Unaligned-access concerns from casting `pkt` to struct pointers are platform-dependent and not substantiated by any statement in the fragment.

The loop (lines 23-64) and the per-type `<= (char*)pkt + size` checks (lines 31-32, 38-39, 45-46, 52-53) were verified safe: the `+1` in line 19 keeps every in-loop header read within `size - 4` bytes.

verdict.summary: The PORT command handler formats attacker-controlled integers into a 16-byte stack buffer with sprintf at line 15, allowing a stack buffer overflow (e.g., 123456789.123456789.123456789.123456789 writes 40 bytes into addr[16]); additionally, sscanf's return value is discarded at line 14, so uninitialized a..f are used in the sprintf and in the data-port computation (line 25) when fewer than six fields are matched.

evidence.reason: Taint: a,b,c,d hold the full int residual range from sscanf(str, "%d,%d,%d,%d,%d,%d", ...) at line 14, which imposes no magnitude cap and whose return count is discarded. Sink: sprintf writes up to 48 bytes (worst case 4 * 11-char ints + 3 dots + NUL) into addr[16], whose capacity is declared at line 4 (char addr[INET_ADDRSTRLEN]; = 16 bytes). Witness: str = "123456789,123456789,123456789,123456789,0,0" passes line 14 (all conversions valid, 123456789 <= INT_MAX) with no intervening check; line 15 then writes 39 chars + NUL = 40 bytes, a 24-byte stack OOB write. The only later guard, !inet_aton(...) at line 18, executes after the write and cannot protect it. Primary CWE-787 stack buffer overflow via input-derived size/format output.

Taint: e and f are uninitialized unless sscanf at line 14 matched all six fields; the sscanf return count is discarded, and the declaration at line 3 (int a, b, c, d, e, f;) provides no initializer and no shown statement guarantees six matches. Reachability: on admitted input str = "1", line 14 matches one field, leaving e and f uninitialized; line 25 then reads them and stores the result into the security-relevant data-connection port value. Secondary CWE-457 uninitialized use; the corrupted port value feeds the later data connection (consumer outside the fragment, noted in limitations).

assumptions: INET_ADDRSTRLEN is the standard POSIX constant with value 16, used at line 4 as the declared capacity of addr.
str is the attacker-controlled argument of the FTP PORT command (entry-point network input) consumed at line 14.
ctrl is a framework/session pointer; its lifetime invariant is not derivable from the fragment.
limitations: Null dereference of ctrl (lines 7-10, 18, 24, 25, 27, 28) is not a confirmed finding: no shown statement can produce a NULL value for it.

Integer overflow in e * 256 at line 25 for |e| >= 2^23, and missing 0..65535 port-range validation: the type of ctrl->data_port and the consumer of the port value are not shown, so the corrupted-value impact cannot be anchored in the fragment.
Info-leak/log-injection via ERR at line 19 and DBG at line 27: the log backend is not shown, and addr contains only %d-formatted digits/dots when all conversions succeed.

Confidence for CWE-457 is 0.62 because part of its impact depends on a downstream consumer of ctrl->data_port that is outside the fragment; the uninitialized read itself is fully demonstrated by the discarded sscanf return at line 14.

verdict.summary: recalc_intercepts dereferences the svm parameter and its fields svm->vmcb and svm->vmcb01.ptr (lines 6, 11, 12, 13) with no NULL validation anywhere in the function; a NULL value admitted by the unconstrained parameter/field domain reaches the unconditional dereferences (e.g., svm->vmcb01.ptr->control at line 12), causing a kernel NULL-pointer oops / host DoS (CWE-476).

evidence.reason: svm->vmcb01.ptr is a pointer extracted from the function parameter svm with no NULL check on any path; its residual range (Phase 1) is the full pointer domain, including NULL. The dereference at the ->control member is unconditional and no guard (L8 tests is_guest_mode, not NULL) excludes the NULL witness svm != NULL, svm->vmcb != NULL, svm->vmcb01.ptr == NULL. A NULL vmcb01.ptr yields a kernel page fault/oops, a host-availability impact; primary mechanism CWE-476 (NULL pointer dereference).

svm is a pointer-typed parameter whose residual range is the full pointer domain (no NULL check appears before this first use); evaluating svm->vmcb in the call argument unconditionally dereferences it. The witness svm == NULL passes every guard in the fragment (there is no NULL test) and faults at this statement, before the L8-9 guest-mode guard is even meaningful for the resulting state; same mechanism CWE-476 (kernel oops).

assumptions: MAX_INTERCEPT is a compile-time constant bounding both loops at L15-16 and L33-34; the capacity of c->intercepts[]/h->intercepts[]/g->intercepts[] is not declared in the fragment, so array sizing is taken as the same constant.
svm->nested.ctl is L1-guest-controlled (nested VMCB content) with no constraint shown in the fragment; its intercept words can carry any bit pattern.
vmcb_mark_dirty, vmcb_clr_intercept, vmcb_set_intercept are void helpers with no return status to mishandle in this fragment.
limitations: Out-of-bounds access on the intercept arrays is not confirmable: the array capacity is not visible in the fragment, and the loop index is a constant, not an input-derived size.

The VMMCALL/CR8/VINTR clears at L20/21/27/31 execute before the OR loop at L33-34, so L1-controlled g->intercepts bits can reappear in c->intercepts; this ordering flaw is mechanically demonstrated but its failure consequence depends on L0's exit-handling semantics outside the fragment, so it carries no CWE here.

The NULL production for svm/svm->vmcb/svm->vmcb01.ptr is caller-side state not exhibited in the fragment; per the analysis rules a missing NULL check on an unconstrained parameter/field is still the finding, but reachability of an actual NULL in the kernel's normal call paths is not shown.
intercept_smi (L37) is an unconstrained global; it only gates a clear operation and has no separately confirmed security-relevant consumer.

verdict.summary: nbFields is read directly from the bitstream (lines 19-20) and is never capped; its residual range [0, 2^31-1] flows unvalidated into the allocation-size sink gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc (line 29), the length sink gf_bifs_dec_qp14_set_length (line 25), both loop bounds (lines 32 and 43), and the index argument of gf_sg_vrml_mf_get_item (line 33), letting a crafted BIFS stream drive unbounded allocation and up to 2^31-1 decoder iterations (missing bound / resource exhaustion).

evidence.reason: nbFields is derived from the attacker-controlled bitstream via lines 19-20 (gf_bs_read_int(bs,5) <= 31 then a 31-bit read), leaving residual range [0, 2^31-1] with no shown cap; this value is passed as the element-count/size argument of gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc, and the fragment shows no bound on the target capacity. This is a confirmed missing-bound (unvalidated-size) flow: witness NbBits=31, nbFields=0x7FFFFFFF admitted by the reads and by guard line 28 (non-MFNODE type). An allocation request of 2^31-1 elements is an unbounded resource request, primary CWE-770.

Same attacker-derived nbFields (residual [0, 2^31-1] from lines 19-20, no cap) is passed as a length argument to gf_bifs_dec_qp14_set_length on the path admitted by line 22 (codec->ActiveQP true); the guard only tests the flag and does not constrain nbFields, so a length of 0x7FFFFFFF is admitted with no visible bound on the receiver (missing-bound length flow).

Loop bound is the unvalidated bitstream value nbFields in [0, 2^31-1] (lines 19-20); the admitted set admits i=0x7FFFFFFE and the loop can execute up to 2^31-1 times in the non-MFNODE branch (guard line 28 admits non-MFNODE types without capping nbFields). No shown statement bounds nbFields, so the iteration count is attacker-chosen (CWE-770); each iteration also issues sf-field decode calls (line 35).

MFNODE-branch loop bound is the same unvalidated nbFields (residual [0, 2^31-1] from lines 19-20); guard line 28 admits fieldType == GF_SG_VRML_MFNODE on this path without capping nbFields. Termination shortens only on callee errors (lines 47/59/64/71/78/82), so an admitted nbFields=0x7FFFFFFF drives up to 2^31-1 node decodes and list mutations (lines 44, 63/70/77) — unbounded resource consumption (CWE-770).

Index i is generated by the loop over unvalidated nbFields (lines 20, 32), admitted range [0, nbFields-1] up to 0x7FFFFFFE. The fragment shows no capacity for the MF array backing field->far_ptr (the allocator at line 29 is the only sizing statement and its element-count argument is the same unvalidated value), so this is a missing-bound index flow on an attacker-derived count; a large admitted i is passed to gf_sg_vrml_mf_get_item with no visible bound protecting the access.

assumptions: gf_bs_read_int(bs, n) returns an unsigned 32-bit value in [0, 2^n - 1] (0 on read failure); NbBits and nbFields are both declared u32 (line 4), so nbFields fits in u32 with maximum 2^31-1.
gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc(far_ptr, type, nbItems) consumes nbItems as the element count for the internal MF array (name- and call-site-implied semantics).

The bitstream bs carries attacker-controlled data; the branch at line 28 admits all non-MFNODE field types, and the fieldType parameter's declared domain includes non-MFNODE values, so a witness in that admitted set is valid.
No capacity for the QP14 length buffer or the MF item array is declared anywhere in the fragment, so the flows are analyzed as missing-bound (unvalidated-size/index) per the analysis standard.
limitations: The exact memory-corruption consequence (e.g., integer wrap in count x element_size, or OOB writes in gf_sg_vrml_mf_get_item / gf_bifs_dec_sf_field / gf_bifs_dec_qp14_set_length) occurs inside callees not shown; the confirmed in-fragment defect is the missing bound on the attacker-derived count feeding size/length/index/loop sinks.

The practical iteration count of loop 2 (lines 43-84) can be shortened when gf_bifs_dec_node returns NULL on stream exhaustion (lines 80-83); the CPU-amplification aspect depends partly on unshown callee behavior, while the loop bound itself is confirmed as 2^31-1.
NULL dereferences of the codec/bs/node/field parameters are not reported because no shown path can produce NULL for them.
The QP force_keep_qp=false path (lines 66-67) re-registers/unregisters new_node after the line 46 registration; any refcount/use-after-free consequence cannot be confirmed from the shown code.
No integer overflow occurs in the fragment itself: maximum nbFields = 2^31-1 fits u32; a wrap would only be possible in unshown callee arithmetic.

verdict.summary: params->rank is only validated with 'rank != 0' (line 27), so a negative rank (e.g., -1) is admitted. With num_filters = 4, line 29 computes num_units = -4, which is stored into output_size_array->data[1] (line 55) and passed as a tensor dimension to context->ResizeTensor (line 57) without any non-negative bound; the negative dimension corrupts the tensor-size computation (signed-to-unsigned conversion to a huge size or wrapped allocation), leading to heap corruption / OOB writes. The same negative num_units reaches ResizeTensor on the full-integer path (lines 172, 180-181).

evidence.reason: Sink consumes output_size_array whose data[1] was set to num_units (line 55). num_units = num_filters / rank (line 29); rank originates from params->rank (line 24), whose residual range after the only guard 'TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, rank != 0)' (line 27) is all int32 except 0, including negatives. Witness: rank=-1, num_filters=4 (both entry-point int32 inputs, unconstrained further by lines 28, 31-33, 47-50) yields num_units=-4, admitted by every guard on the path (lines 19-20, 27, 28, 31-33, 47-50). No statement bounds rank/num_units/dims to non-negative, so a negative tensor dimension is forwarded to a size-consuming resize operation; TFLite computes tensor size from these int32 dims, converting the negative element count to a huge unsigned size (or wrapped allocation), producing heap corruption / OOB write when the tensor is filled (CWE-787).

Second sink for the same root cause on the is_full_integer path (input type kTfLiteInt8, line 169): output_temp_size_array->data[0] = num_units (line 172) carries the same negative value derived from an admitted negative rank (lines 24, 27, 29). With rank=-1 and num_filters=4, num_units=-4 is resized as a tensor dimension with no visible non-negative bound, corrupting the allocation size computation (CWE-787).

assumptions: params->rank and tensor dims are model-supplied int32 entry-point inputs; the shown code imposes only the equality checks at lines 27-33, 37, 47-50 and the type check at lines 19-20.
TfLiteIntArray data entries are int32_t, so tensor dimensions admitted by the fragment span the full int32 range.
TfLiteIntArrayCreate(2) (lines 53, 74, 171) yields 2-element arrays, so the stores at lines 54-55, 75-76, 172-173 are in-bounds writes of out-of-domain values.
TF_LITE_ENSURE / TF_LITE_ENSURE_EQ / TF_LITE_ENSURE_OK abort Prepare on failure, so passing a guard is required to reach the sinks.
context->ResizeTensor consumes the supplied dims array as tensor sizes (standard TFLite semantics).
limitations: Demoted: int32 overflow in 'memory_size * num_filters' (line 50) is reachable with large dims but its only in-fragment consumer is the SizeOfDimension(state,1) equality check; concrete memory impact would require unshown Eval code, so it is not reported as a confirmed CWE.

Demoted: 'scale->data[0]' reads (lines 201-206) have no check that the scale array has size >= 1 or that quantization.params is non-NULL; a model with affine quantization and an empty scale vector could trigger an OOB read, but the tensor-level invariant is established outside the fragment, so confidence is too low for a confirmed finding.
Demoted: unchecked TfLiteIntArrayCreate returns (fixed small allocations) and NULL node->user_data are framework/OOM robustness concerns, not attacker-directed findings.

Demoted: negative batch_size/num_filters dims could further corrupt scratch_size_array (lines 75-76) and row_sums dims (line 161), but that requires assumptions about model dim validation outside the fragment.

The eventual OOB write materializes in the framework resize and kernel write path, which is not part of the fragment; the confirmed portion here is the unvalidated negative-size flow into ResizeTensor (call-site out-of-domain argument).

verdict.summary: Integer overflow in the oversize screening at lines 28-30 defeats the constant-folding size gate: num_elements() * DataTypeSize(...) is computed in unsigned 64-bit arithmetic, and a fully-defined shape can make the product reach 2^64 and wrap to 0 (e.g., num_elements() = 2^61 with a DT_DOUBLE output), so '0 > max_constant_size_in_bytes' is false and an unboundably large output is admitted to constant folding (returns true at line 70), enabling resource exhaustion/OOM on crafted graph shapes (CWE-190; the resource-exhaustion consequence is not an independent root cause).

evidence.reason: Confirmed CWE-190: line 29 computes out_shape.num_elements() * DataTypeSize(n->output_type(i)) with num_elements() (int64_t, residual range [0, 2^63-1] — no magnitude cap is imposed by any shown guard, and the shape_map entry at lines 24-26 is input-derived) converted to unsigned size_t; uint64 modulo-2^64 arithmetic wraps num_elements()=2^61 with DataTypeSize=8 (DT_DOUBLE) to 0. Line 30 then evaluates 0 > max_constant_size_in_bytes as false for every non-negative int64 threshold (negative thresholds also never exclude due to unsigned conversion), so the guard fails to return false and the function proceeds to return true at line 70, admitting an oversized constant to folding. The corruption targets a security-gating comparison (the size check protecting the folding pipeline), so the primary mechanism is CWE-190; the resource-exhaustion impact is a consequence, not a second root cause.

assumptions: DataTypeSize() returns size_t (unsigned 64-bit), making the product at line 29 well-defined modulo 2^64; even under an int-typed alternative the overflow still occurs (as UB), so the finding does not depend on this detail.
PartialTensorShape::num_elements() returns int64_t; IsFullyDefined() (line 28) only requires all dims known/non-negative and imposes no upper magnitude bound on the returned product.
max_constant_size_in_bytes (line 6) is treated as a non-negative size threshold; the witness holds for every value in [0, 2^63-1].
limitations: The witness magnitude (num_elements() = 2^61) is a member of the Phase 1 residual range but is not synthesized by a shown statement; the finding is therefore a range-anchored claim, calibrated to confidence 0.62 instead of a fully demonstrated witness.

Potential OOB read of n->output_type(i) (line 29) if shape_it->second.size() (line 26) exceeded the node's output count: the target capacity is not visible in the fragment, so no excess can be demonstrated; demoted, no CWE.

NULL dereference of n (line 9) and unchecked shape_replacement_map passed to MaybeReplaceShapeOp (line 13): no NULL producer is shown and the callee body is not shown; treated as caller-convention robustness, not findings.
Log write VLOG(2) << n->DebugString() (lines 66-67) uses fixed << formatting on an internal node string; no format-string vulnerability.
No other memory, injection, crypto, file, or authz sinks exist in the fragment; no additional sinks were confirmed.

verdict.summary: TensorFlow-style matmul kernel narrows int64 tensor dimensions into int at lines 9-12 with no magnitude check; true dims in [2^32, 2^32+2^31-1] wrap to non-negative ints that pass the m>=0 && n>=0 && k>=0 guard at line 18, so the output is allocated from the truncated shape (line 23) while the sparse-path DoMatMul calls (lines 106-109, 111-114) compute the full m_real x n_real product into the undersized buffer, causing a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), with the narrowing store as the independent root cause (CWE-681).

evidence.snippet:
DoMatMul<TL, TR>::Compute(&this->cache_nt_, left->matrix<TL>(),
                                right->matrix<TR>(), transpose_a,
                                ctx->device()->tensorflow_cpu_worker_threads(),
                                transpose_output, &out);
evidence.reason: Heap OOB write (CWE-787): dims of a (entry-point tensor, unconstrained magnitude after the rank-only IsMatrix checks at lines 4-7) are truncated to int at line 9 (a.dim_size(0) = 2^32+2 -> m = 2); the guard m>=0 && n>=0 && k>=0 at line 18 tests the truncated value and admits m=2; output is allocated with TensorShape({m,n}) = {2,2} at line 23 (4-float capacity); the DoMatMul at lines 111-114 then writes the full (2^32+2) x 2 product (2^33+4 elements) into out (line 38), exceeding the line-23 capacity by 2^33 elements. No shown statement bounds the true dimension magnitude before the narrowing stores at lines 9-12.

evidence.snippet:
DoMatMul<TR, TL>::Compute(&this->cache_tr_, left->matrix<TR>(),
                                right->matrix<TL>(), transpose_a,
                                ctx->device()->tensorflow_cpu_worker_threads(),
                                transpose_output, &out);
evidence.reason: Same CWE-787 mechanism on the transpose_output branch: reached when a_is_sparse_ is false and b_is_sparse_ is true (lines 72-80 swap and set transpose_output), with out still sized by the truncated m/n from line 23 while the operand matrices carry real dims from lines 9-12; the full-size product is written past the 4-float buffer for dims in the admitted wrap band [2^32, 2^32+2^31-1].

evidence.snippet: const int m = transpose_a_ ? a.dim_size(1) : a.dim_size(0);
evidence.reason: Narrowing store (CWE-681, secondary root cause): dim_size result (64-bit, unconstrained by the shown IsMatrix rank checks at lines 4-7) is truncated to 32-bit int with no magnitude check; for true dim 2^32+2 the admitted value is 2 (2^32+2 mod 2^32), which passes line 18 and corrupts the allocation size at line 23 and the write volume at lines 106-109/111-114. The destination int range is the visible bound that the admitted source range exceeds.

assumptions: int is 32-bit two's complement for the wrap arithmetic at lines 9-12; this is the standard width and the fragment's own non-negative guard at line 18 only makes sense if the conversion can produce negative values.
TensorShape dimensions are non-negative, so negative m/k/n can only arise from conversion wrap; the dangerous positive wrap band [2^32, 2^32+2^31-1] is not excluded by any shown statement.
a_is_sparse_/b_is_sparse_/transpose_* are kernel attributes; the analysis uses the branch structure they select as shown.
DoMatMul::Compute(&out) is a matmul that writes its full m x n product into the passed destination, per its name and its use with the destination argument &out.
limitations: The literal return type of TensorShape::dim_size is not declared inside the fragment; the finding relies on the standard 64-bit dims / 32-bit int width, which the fragment neither states nor contradicts and which its negative-value guard implies.

The dense-path contract assignment at lines 62-63 is treated as destination-driven (Eigen tensor assignment iterates over the destination index space), so the truncation there produces a silently wrong result rather than a confirmed memory violation; it is demoted and carries no CWE.

A practical witness requires an input tensor with at least 2^32+2 elements in one dimension (roughly 34 GB for float32), which the fragment neither permits nor forbids; no memory-size cap is visible in the shown code.
Wrong-result behavior in the dense path and matched-size copies (BFloat16ToFloat lines 48-49/54-55, SetZeroFunctor line 34, shuffle lines 96-100) were reviewed and are not reported as findings.

Non-termination and error/status-handling flaws were not found: the fragment has no loops, and allocated-buffer failures (allocate_output line 23) are handled by OP_REQUIRES_OK before any security-relevant use.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read: pj_scan_get_char advances scanner->curptr past an admitted non-zero byte and dereferences the next byte (line 6) with no visible in-bounds/capacity/terminator check; a scanner pointing to a buffer whose last byte is non-zero (e.g., one-byte buffer 'A') yields a read one byte past the allocation. Secondary: NULL/arbitrary scanner pointer is dereferenced at line 5 with no NULL check.

evidence.reason: scanner is an entry-point parameter with the full declared pointer domain; the fragment imposes no end, capacity, or terminator bound on it. On an admitted input (final byte != 0 passes the if (!chr) guard at line 5), ++scanner->curptr (line 5) advances to one past the last allocated byte, and this line dereferences that byte. With a one-byte non-zero buffer, the read is exactly one byte beyond the allocation; for longer unterminated buffers any length is admitted. This is a confirmed missing-bound OOB read (CWE-125) at the dereference on line 6: the capacity of the scanned buffer is not shown, and no protective statement between line 3 and line 7 excludes a non-zero final byte with no allocated successor.

Unconditional dereference of the pointer-typed parameter scanner->curptr (and thereby scanner) with no NULL check and no preceding validation; the only test, if (!chr), executes after this dereference and tests the fetched byte, not the pointer. A NULL scanner or NULL curptr value is within the parameter's unconstrained residual range and faults at this line: NULL-pointer dereference (CWE-476).

assumptions: PJ_SCAN_IS_PROBABLY_SPACE evaluates its argument (a dereference of the advanced curptr) — the potential out-of-bounds byte read is performed at line 6.

The buffer backing scanner->curptr is assumed by callers to be NUL-terminated and to contain a legitimate byte sequence, but no such invariant is stated in the shown fragment and cannot be used as the missing bound.
limitations: The precise allocation behind scanner->curptr is not shown; the OOB claim is a confirmed missing-bound/range finding (unvalidated advance + dereference), calibrated at 0.62 rather than as an exact one-byte witness with a visible capacity.
An unterminated all-space buffer would also make pj_scan_skip_whitespace (line 7) read past the allocation; this is the same missing-bound class and is not reported as a separate finding.
pj_scan_syntax_err's return value is discarded, but the path returns 0 immediately, so no security-relevant operation runs on the failure state.

A NULL scanner/curptr in real use may be prevented by a caller contract, but the shown code neither validates it nor establishes such a contract; the NULL-deref is confirmed only at the fragment's own standard and is secondary to the OOB read.
Severity is rated medium for a memory read in a parsing primitive; actual impact depends on the untested caller context (e.g., network parsing), which is not shown.

verdict.summary: Integer overflow (wraparound) in the constant-size guard: at lines 28-29, out_shape.num_elements() (int64) is promoted to 64-bit unsigned size_t and multiplied by DataTypeSize(...). A fully-defined shape of 2^60 elements (e.g. dims [2^30, 2^30]) with a 16-byte output type (DT_COMPLEX128) yields 2^60 * 16 = 2^64 ≡ 0 mod 2^64, so the comparison 0 > max_constant_size_in_bytes is false for every positive limit and the line-30 oversized rejection is skipped. The node is then treated as constant-foldable and the folder materializes a tensor far larger than the configured limit, causing memory exhaustion (DoS).

evidence.reason: The shape is taken from shape_map's per-node vector (lines 23-26); its residual range is constrained only by IsFullyDefined() (line 27), which admits arbitrarily large dims such as [2^30, 2^30] (num_elements() = 2^60). C++ usual arithmetic conversions promote the int64_t operand to size_t (64-bit unsigned), so the product 2^60 * 16 (DataTypeSize of a 16-byte output type) wraps to 0 mod 2^64. Guard line 25 admits i=0 and guard line 27 admits the fully-defined shape; the wrapped 0 is compared against the positive int64_t max_constant_size_in_bytes (line 29, converted to size_t), the comparison is false, and line 30's rejection of oversized outputs is bypassed. The corrupted comparison gates a security-relevant size-limit decision (CWE-190), and the downstream constant folder materializes the oversized tensor, leading to memory-exhaustion DoS.

assumptions: out_shape.num_elements() returns int64_t and DataTypeSize(...) returns size_t; on this platform size_t is 64-bit, so the int64_t operand is converted to size_t before the multiply (standard C++ usual arithmetic conversions).
IsFullyDefined() (line 27) guarantees all dimensions are known and non-negative; it imposes no magnitude cap.
The loop at line 25 admits i=0 for any shape vector of size >= 1, which is the natural precondition for executing the arithmetic.
limitations: Secondary candidate (not a confirmed CWE): n->output_type(i) (line 28) is indexed only by i < shape_it->second.size() (line 25) with no visible bound against the node's real output count; the capacity of the node's output-types container is not visible in this fragment and the per-output alignment of shape_map is an implicit invariant of that data structure, so the missing-bound OOB-read candidate is recorded, not confirmed.
n (line 2) is dereferenced at line 9 with no NULL check, but no shown statement produces NULL and the graph walker never supplies it; treated as robustness, not a confirmed vulnerability.
The NULL-safety of the call at line 12 depends on MaybeReplaceShapeOp's unshown internal checks.
The actual OOM materialization occurs in the constant folder that consumes the return value, outside this fragment; impact is inferred from the name-implied semantics of IsConstantFoldable.
max_constant_size_in_bytes is assumed positive per normal configuration; a negative value would fail safe, so the bypass is demonstrated against every positive limit.

verdict.summary: The fragment is the patched form of njs_function_frame_save: before the argument-move loop, the cursor is re-initialized with `p = native->arguments;` (line 39), so `njs_is_valid(p)`, `njs_set_undefined(p)`, and `*local++ = p++` (lines 43-47) operate on the first slots of the copied value area rather than the uninitialized tail left by the copy loop (lines 32-35). No out-of-bounds, injection, or logic defect can be demonstrated from the shown statements alone; the remaining capacity relationships (args_count/args_offset vs the value_count + temp frame capacity at lines 19-20) are engine-internal invariants not visible in the fragment.

assumptions: The new frame's pointer-array and value-area capacity is `value_count + function->u.lambda->temp` slots, derived from the only visible allocation math at lines 19-20 (`value = (njs_value_t *) (new + value_count + function->u.lambda->temp);`).

`njs_function_frame_values(active, &end)` (line 29) and `njs_function_frame_value_count(active)` (line 14) are expected to describe the same active-frame value range (`end - start == value_count`); this consistency is not itself visible in the fragment.
`function->args_count` and `function->args_offset` are non-negative compile-time metadata; their magnitude relative to `value_count` and `temp` is not constrained by any shown statement.
limitations: An OOB claim against the argument-move loop cannot be demonstrated: the pointer-write span `njs_function_frame_args_count(active) + function->args_offset + function->args_count` versus the `value_count + temp` capacity is not derivable from the shown code in either direction (no shown bound or counter-capacity).
The argument-move loop's value reads (first `args_count` slots) are in-bounds only if `args_count <= value_count + temp`, an invariant not visible in the fragment.
A copy-loop overflow would require `end - start > value_count + temp`, which cannot be derived from the two helper calls shown (lines 14 and 29).
NULL-dereference concerns for `vm->active_frame` (lines 8, 13) and `active->function` (line 16) have no NULL producer or check in the fragment and are treated as engine-invariant robustness concerns.

If the line-39 reset (`p = native->arguments;`) were absent, the argument-move loop would consume the uninitialized tail of the copied value area and could write pointers into it — that defect is the one fixed by the statement at line 39, which is present in this fragment.

verdict.summary: Gather indices from the `positions` tensor are validated only for non-negativity (lines 5-13); no statement bounds them against the input dimension along `axis`. Every index in [dim, max(PositionsT)] passes the guard and flows into `optimized_ops::Gather` (lines 18-21), which reads `input` at those values, causing an out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125) with attacker-controlled magnitude.

evidence.snippet:
optimized_ops::Gather(op_params, GetTensorShape(input),
                        GetTensorData<InputT>(input), GetTensorShape(positions),
                        GetTensorData<PositionsT>(positions),
                        GetTensorShape(output), GetTensorData<InputT>(output));
evidence.reason: The model-supplied `positions` tensor is read into `indexes` at line 4; the only constraint applied (lines 5-13) leaves residual range [0, max(PositionsT)]. The gather call at lines 18-21 indexes `input` with those values and requires each index < dim(input, axis); no shown statement ties any `indexes[i]` to that dimension, so no capacity/bound on the target is visible, and every index in [dim, max(PositionsT)] is admitted by the only guard (line 8) and the ensure (line 13) yet is outside the gather's in-domain set. This is a confirmed missing-bound out-of-bounds read (CWE-125): the negative-only guard does not exclude positive over-large indices, and the call is not provably in-domain for the whole admitted set.

assumptions: `PositionsT` is a signed integer type, implied by `indexes[i] < 0` at line 8, with a finite maximum (e.g., int32 -> 2^31-1).
`positions`, `input`, and `output` are TFLite model tensors; tensor contents (including `positions`) are externally supplied with the model, so `positions` values are attacker-controlled.
`optimized_ops::Gather` name-implied semantics: it reads `input` at the `positions` values, whose required domain is [0, dim(input, axis)).
limitations: The concrete input dimension along `axis` is not shown, so the demonstrated witness is a range (any index in [dim, max(PositionsT)]) rather than a single exact value; the byte-level excess depends on that unshown dimension.

`params.axis` / `params.batch_dims` are forwarded unvalidated (lines 16-17); an out-of-range axis is a related gather-misbehavior concern, but no input rank or capacity is visible to pin an independent mechanism, so it is not separately evidenced.
Negative indices are fully excluded by lines 5-13, so no negative-index OOB is claimed.

A mismatch between `positions->bytes` and the declared shape (line 6) could make the validation loop cover fewer elements than the gather consumes; this depends on a malformed tensor size and is not separately confirmed.

verdict.summary: rsi_send_beacon calls skb_pull(skb, 64 - dword_align_bytes) on a freshly allocated, empty skb (skb->len == 0) whenever the data pointer is not 64-byte aligned (dword_align_bytes in 1..63, admitted by the L13 guard). The pull length (1..63) always exceeds skb->len, so skb_pull underflows skb->len and invokes skb_under_panic()/BUG(), a reachable kernel abort (CWE-617, local DoS). Guards on the path only check NULL (L7) and nonzero alignment (L13); nothing bounds the pull against skb->len.

evidence.reason: The sink's length argument, 64 - dword_align_bytes, is in {1..63} for every value admitted by the L13 guard (dword_align_bytes in {1..63}, derived at L12 as ((unsigned long)skb->data & 0x3f)), while skb->len is 0: the skb from dev_alloc_skb (L6) is empty and no shown statement (L10 memset does not modify length) ever increases it. skb_pull requires len <= skb->len; for every admitted value, skb->len decreases below 0, triggering skb_under_panic()/BUG() — a confirmed reachable kernel abort (CWE-617). The L13 guard tests only dword_align_bytes != 0 and never compares the pull length against skb->len; the missing check is skb->len >= (64 - dword_align_bytes).

assumptions: Standard kernel sk_buff semantics: dev_alloc_skb(size) returns an empty skb with skb->len == 0 and size bytes available at skb->data; skb_pull removes len bytes from the front and calls skb_under_panic()/BUG() when len exceeds skb->len.
MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE is the data capacity of the L6 allocation; its numeric value is not shown and is irrelevant to the L14 skb_pull failure.
limitations: The exact trigger value dword_align_bytes in {1..63} is determined by the allocator-returned data pointer, not by a shown constant, so the confirmation is a full residual-range claim rather than a single literal witness; all 63 admitted values fail deterministically.

The L15 rsi_prepare_beacon(common, skb) call is a potential post-pull destination-capacity concern, but the callee's write size is not shown, so no OOB write arithmetic is confirmable in the fragment.

The panic trigger is not directly attacker-chosen (it requires a non-64-byte-aligned allocation), so the confirmed impact is kernel crash / denial of service; no memory-corruption or privilege mechanism is demonstrated.

verdict.summary: Matrix dimensions read as int64 (a.dim_size/b.dim_size at lines 9-12) are narrowed into int32 with no magnitude constraint in the shown code, then immediately used to size the output allocation at line 19 (TensorShape({m, n})); any admitted dimension >= 2^31 truncates (e.g., m = 2^31 becomes -2^31), yielding an out-of-domain output shape and a reachable abort or corrupted allocation size (CWE-681).

evidence.reason: a.dim_size(0) returns int64 from the entry-point tensor and is narrowed to int32 at line 9 (`const int m`); the fragment imposes no magnitude cap (IsMatrix at lines 4-7 only enforces rank 2, and `k == k2` at line 14 compares only the already-narrowed ints), so every dim in the residual range [0, 2^63-1] that is >= 2^31 truncates. Concrete member of the admitted set: a = [2^31, 1] with transpose_a_=false passes the guards at lines 4, 6 and 14 (k = k2 = 1) and is not stopped by the zero-inner-dim branch at line 21 (k=1); m becomes -2^31 before reaching this sink. TensorShape({-2^31, 2}) is an out-of-domain shape argument, so the input-derived dim is consumed as an allocation-size value with no visible bound — the missing bound is confirmed by the shown arithmetic (CWE-681 narrowing; reachable CHECK/abort, i.e., a corrupted output allocation).

assumptions: Tensor::dim_size returns int64 per the standard TensorFlow API (not shown in the fragment); a 32-bit return would remove the narrowing, which is not the case here.
int is 32-bit, so the destination type bound is [-2^31, 2^31-1]; admitted int64 dims above 2^31-1 exceed it.
limitations: The zero-dimension transpose path is protected by OP_REQUIRES guards at lines 77-80 (admit only right->dim_size(0) != 0 and dim_size(1) != 0) and the zero inner-dimension path by the k==0 early return at lines 21-27; those classes are not findings in this fragment.
The confirmed narrowing witness is a residual-range claim (any dim >= 2^31) requiring a tensor on the order of 2 GB+ of element storage; confidence is capped at 0.6 accordingly.

A masked k==k2 variant (true inner dims differing by multiples of 2^32 truncating to equal ints) could desynchronize the Eigen contraction at lines 53-54 / DoMatMul, but the callee behavior is not shown and the required magnitudes are extreme; not confirmed.
new Tensor allocations (lines 38, 44, 81-83) may fail on OOM, but their sizes are not attacker-scaled beyond the already-existing input tensors, so this is a robustness concern only.

verdict.summary: wci/wcf/wco are rank-checked only (dims()==1 at lines 130/134/138) and their dim_size(0) is never validated against cell_size before being passed as vec<T>() to LSTMBlockCellFprop (lines 173-182). With use_peephole_ true and, e.g., cell_size=1 (line 28) while wci has dims {0}, the functor's peephole consumption spans index 0 of a 0-length vector: an out-of-bounds read resulting from a missing length bound (unvalidated-size flow, CWE-125).

functor::LSTMBlockCellFprop<Device, T, USE_CUBLAS, gate_layout>(
        batch_size, input_size, cell_size)(
        ctx, device, forget_bias_, cell_clip_, use_peephole_,
        x_tensor->matrix<T>(), cs_prev_tensor->matrix<T>(),

The sink passes each as vec<T>() (lines 177-178) into the LSTM peephole consumption, which spans cell_size=1 elements elementwise with cs_prev; for a witness of wci dims {0} (admitted by line 130) and use_peephole_=true (unconstrained member, line 175), index 0 reads one element past the 0-length wci backing storage. The absent length check is the defect: no statement on any path admits only dim_size(0)==cell_size, so the undersized vector reaches the sink (CWE-125 OOB read).

assumptions: cell_size, batch_size, input_size are derived solely from tensor dim_size reads at lines 26-28; the equality guards at lines 31-61 bound nothing absolutely, so cell_size may take any nonnegative int64 value the tensor system can hold.
wci/wcf/wco are entry-point (graph/feed-controlled) tensor inputs; the fragment shows no producer guaranteeing a minimum element count for them.
use_peephole_, forget_bias_, cell_clip_ are member values with no shown constraints; use_peephole_ == true is a valid witness member value.

limitations: The functor body is not shown; if Eigen raises a size-mismatch assertion rather than performing a raw out-of-bounds read, the same missing length validation yields a reachable abort (CWE-617) instead of CWE-125 — either way the missing bound is confirmed.

Potential int64 overflow of cell_size * 4 and input_size + cell_size (lines 53, 58, 103, 109): the wrapped expressions are used consistently in checks and allocations, and no security-relevant consumer of a wrapped value is visible in the fragment; demoted with no CWE.

No claim is made that the peephole vectors are unsafe when use_peephole_ == false; the witness relies on use_peephole_ == true, which the fragment does not constrain.

verdict.summary: Nonce k is deterministically forced to 1 on the g_rng_function==NULL path (tmp[0]=1), so every signature in that configuration reuses the same k and an attacker observing two signatures can recover the ECDSA private key.

evidence.reason: k is an internal-helper input with only the range guard `0 < k < curve_n` (line 47) applied; that guard admits k=1. On the `!g_rng_function` branch (lines 65-66), tmp is set to the deterministic value {1,0,0,...} instead of a fresh random value, and lines 69-71 compute k' = 1*k = 1, k = 1/k' = 1, k = 1/k = 1. Every call of the shown function on this admitted path therefore uses the identical nonce k=1 in EccPoint_mult (line 55) and in the modular inversion chain (lines 69-71); the NULL state of g_rng_function is admitted by the branch itself and no statement in the fragment enforces nonce freshness. Every guard on the path (lines 8, 10, 16, 21, 27) admits the witness, and the size checks at lines 33/37 are not executed because line 31 requires axis_ != -1. Primary CWE-617.

Secondary confirmed finding: step==0 makes `from += step` a no-op, stalling the loop at lines 20-21 (CWE-835, non-termination).

For any step >= 2 there are loop-entry positions admitted by line 10 (`from < end`) with `end - from < step`, so `from` becomes > `end`. The guard at the sink only excludes `from == end`; for `from > end` the left operand `data != *from` forces the dereference. Witness: buffer B[0..4], from=B, end=B+5, step=2; third iteration enters with from=B+4 (line 10 admits), line 13 sets from=B+6, line 14 evaluates `B+6 == B+5` false then dereferences `*(B+6)`, 2 bytes past the last valid byte and 1 past `end`. The equality check executes at the sink on the same statement and cannot cover the overshoot; no other guard precedes line 14 on the path.

CWE-835 non-termination: with step==0 (admitted — line 1 gives `int` with no shown constraint), line 13 leaves `from` unchanged and line 14 establishes `*from == data` on the else path; line 20's condition `(from < end) && (*from == data)` is permanently true while line 21 (`from += step`) is a no-op, so the loop never advances and never exits. No guard in the fragment excludes step==0, making the stall reachable on an admitted input (unbounded hang).

assumptions: The buffer [from, end) is a valid object at entry with `end` as its exclusive boundary — this is the fragment's own visible read window and boundary.
`byte` is an 8-bit unsigned type (consistent with `data >= 0xc0` comparisons).
`int` is 32-bit for the line-8 `step * MAX_RUN_COUNT` overflow consideration.
Parameters from/end/step/file were instantiated inside their declared domains to construct witnesses.
limitations: Division by zero at line 29 (`(from - start) / step`) is not a confirmed finding: with step==0 the inner loop at line 20 never exits, so line 29 is unreachable on that input (sink cannot be reached while the divisor is zero).
Line 8 `int max_run = step * MAX_RUN_COUNT` can overflow for |step| > ~143165576; the wrap is UB and its downstream effect is covered by the non-termination finding, so it is not separately reported.
Negative `step` also moves `from` below the buffer start and produces OOB reads (same CWE-125 mechanism as the primary evidence); not given a separate evidence item.

Discarded `gp_fputc` return values (lines 16, 24, 25, 29, 31) mean output errors are silently ignored — a robustness/error-handling concern, not a security finding without a downstream security decision.

If an unshown caller always passed step == 1, lines 13-14 would be safe — but that invariant is not visible in the fragment and cannot be used to demote the finding; the absence of the constraint in the shown code is itself the defect.

verdict.summary: In pjmedia_rtcp_fb_parse_rpsi, the RTCP length field is compared raw (< 3, line 18) before ntohs; on little-endian hosts a wire length of 1 (bytes 0x00 0x01, stored 0x0100 = 256) passes, so rpsi_len = (1-2)*4 = -4 converts to an enormous pj_size_t (line 24). The subsequent length guard (line 25) becomes vacuous (rpsi_len+12 wraps to 8), and parsing dereferences offsets sizeof(fb_common) and +1 past the buffer (lines 29, 43) and returns an RPSI string with an attacker-influenced ~536 MB length from a tiny buffer (line 45): OOB read (CWE-125) enabled by signed-to-unsigned conversion (CWE-195).

evidence.reason: OOB read (CWE-125): length==sizeof(pjmedia_rtcp_fb_common) is admitted by line 12; wire RTCP length V=1 (bytes 0x00 0x01) passes the line-18 raw host-order comparison on LE (0x0100=256, not < 3); line 24 yields (1-2)*4 = -4 converted to pj_size_t 0xFFFFFFFC, making the line-25 guard 'length < rpsi_len+12' vacuous (wraps to 8); p is set to offset sizeof(*hdr) (line 28) and the dereference at line 29 reads one byte past the admitted minimal buffer.

OOB read (CWE-125), same root cause: with the wrapped rpsi_len, the line-25 check is vacuous and the line-37 bit-length guard (rpsi_len*8 = 0xFFFFFFE0, not < 16+padlen) passes; after line 29 advances p, this dereference reads offset sizeof(*hdr)+1 — two bytes past a buffer of length sizeof(pjmedia_rtcp_fb_common) (reached whenever the OOB padlen byte is < 32, line 31).

Unvalidated-size flow (CWE-125): rpsi_bit_len derives from the wrapped attacker size (line 44, % 4,294,967,2xx), so the length argument equals 536,870,906 for padlen=0 while p stands at offset sizeof(*hdr)+2 and the admitted buffer holds only length bytes; no shown statement bounds this length against the buffer (line 25's guard is defeated by the wrap), so the returned rpsi string advertises an attacker-influenced huge size consumed OOB downstream.

assumptions: sizeof(pjmedia_rtcp_fb_common) is the standard 12-byte RTCP FB header (4-byte RTCP common + two 32-bit SSRCs); the OOB conclusion uses length == that size, so it holds for any such size.
Little-endian host assumed for the concrete witness (raw hdr->rtcp_common.length = 0x0100 for wire bytes 0x00 0x01); big-endian hosts reject V=1 at line 18.
pj_size_t is 32-bit for the concrete magnitudes (0xFFFFFFFC, 536,870,906); on 64-bit builds the same wrap occurs with larger magnitudes.
rpsi_bit_len is an unsigned width type (pj_size_t-like) for the line-45 magnitude; if it were signed 32-bit the exact pj_strset length would differ but would still be unvalidated against the buffer.
limitations: The line-18 raw comparison is effective on big-endian targets; the finding is demonstrated for little-endian targets.
The rpsi_bit_len field type and the pj_strset parameter types are not declared in the fragment, so the exact downstream magnitude at line 45 is inferred from standard PJLIB types.
The values read OOB at lines 29/43 (padlen, pt) are not attacker-controlled when the buffer is minimal; the OOB read itself is the confirmed flaw regardless of the byte values.

pjsip debug-build assertion behavior of PJ_ASSERT_RETURN is build-configuration-dependent; the return semantics (used here) prevent a NULL deref and any abort claim is debug-only, so it is recorded as a robustness concern only.
Severity is judged on this fragment only (remote OOB read / oversized-length propagation); no full exploit chain or RCE is demonstrated here.

verdict.summary: The SELinux ptrace_traceme hook performs the standard PROCESS__PTRACE authorization check via avc_has_perm on the parent→current SID pair (lines 3-5) and returns the decision directly, so a denial propagates and no path bypasses the check. The fragment contains no memory, injection, crypto, file, loop, or status-handling operations; the only unconstrained input, the parent pointer, is passed to task_sid_obj whose body is not shown and which is not an index/size/length sink, so a NULL-dereference cannot be confirmed from this fragment.

assumptions: avc_has_perm (lines 3-5) returns a non-zero status on denial and the fragment's direct 'return avc_has_perm(...)' propagates that status to the caller, so a denied PTRACE request is rejected.
SECCLASS_PROCESS and PROCESS__PTRACE (line 5) are constants selecting the process class and ptrace permission; no alternative class/permission is used anywhere in the fragment.
limitations: Demoted NULL-dereference candidate: parent (line 1) is unconstrained in the fragment, but the dereference would occur inside task_sid_obj (line 4), whose body is not shown and which is not a standard or index/size/length-consuming helper, so the failure is not demonstrated by the shown code.
task_sid_obj(current) (line 4) relies on the kernel 'current' task being valid; that framework invariant is not visible inside the fragment and cannot be used to justify either safety or a finding.

The correctness of the SID pair (which label transitions are permitted) depends on SELinux policy and task-label state external to the fragment; a policy misconfiguration is not expressible as a code-level defect here.

No branch, loop, buffer, format string, or other sink exists in the fragment, so no other vulnerability class had an anchor; the not-vulnerable verdict rests on the visible authorization gate rather than on a fully enumerated policy bound.

verdict.summary: The argc/argv loop in crun_command_exec has an off-by-one bound: `for (i = 0; i < argc - first_arg; i++)` reads `argv[first_arg + i + 1]` and on the final admitted iteration (`i = argc - first_arg - 1`) reaches `argv[argc]`, the NULL terminator, which is passed to `xstrdup` and dereferenced (NULL deref, CWE-476, line 44) on every invocation without --process. Independently, the LISTEN_FDS environment value is parsed with strtoll and never validated (no non-negative or errno check), so a negative or huge value overflows `crun_context.preserve_fds += crun_context.listen_fds` (CWE-190, line 31), corrupting the fd-preservation boundary of the container exec.

evidence.reason: Loop bound at line 43 (`i < argc - first_arg`, admits i = 0..argc-first_arg-1) lets the last iteration compute index `first_arg + i + 1 = argc`; `argv[argc]` is the NULL terminator of the argc/argv contract, so xstrdup receives NULL at line 44 on every non---process path (line 17 admits argc-first_arg >= 1). strdup semantics dereference the argument, causing a NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476). Witness: argc=3, first_arg=1, argv={"crun","ctr","/bin/sh",NULL} -> guard line 43 admits i=1 -> xstrdup(argv[3]=NULL); no shown statement excludes this boundary, and the write at line 45 shows the extra duplicated element is spurious. Deterministic crash/DoS; off-by-one is the root cause.

LISTEN_FDS is an environment value (entry-point input) parsed at line 30 with strtoll and no constraint: no errno/ERANGE check, no non-negative check, no upper bound; the only guard, line 28, admits any non-NULL string. An admitted value such as "-1" (or any magnitude beyond the destination field width) flows into `crun_context.preserve_fds += crun_context.listen_fds` at line 31, underflowing/overflowing the signed fd-preservation count used to decide which descriptors survive the container exec (CWE-190). The residual range entering the arithmetic is the full strtoll domain because the fragment never narrows it; the downstream fd-close/preserve consumer is outside the fragment, so this finding is range-based and capped at confidence 0.55.

assumptions: argc/argv form the C main() pair, so argv[argc] is the NULL terminator element; the shown code itself indexes up to the argc boundary.
Line numbers are counted from the first line of the fragment (`crun_command_exec (struct crun_global_arguments ...)` = line 1).
exec_options.process is NULL to enter the argument-copying branch at line 36; line 17 then requires at least 2 remaining arguments.
xstrdup is a strdup-style helper (duplicates its argument, checking allocation); passing NULL is out of its string-typed contract.
limitations: CWE-190 confidence is capped at 0.55: the width of libcrun_context_t.preserve_fds/listen_fds and the downstream fd-close/preserve consumer are not visible in the fragment, so the corruption is demonstrated as a residual-range flow rather than an exact demonstrated overflow.
process->args_len = argc (line 41) overstates the copied length, but the array is zero-filled and sized argc+1 (line 42), so no write out-of-bounds is demonstrable from the fragment.

Whether a NULL-aware xstrdup would convert the line-44 defect into a mere truncated-argument-list logic issue cannot be verified from the fragment; the name-implied strdup semantics are used per the call-site confirmation standard.
make_oci_process_user and dup_array internals are not shown; no finding is asserted on them.
init_libcrun_context's use of argv[first_arg] (lines 19, 92) is protected by the line 17 count assertion and is not reported.

verdict.summary: selinux_ptrace_traceme dereferences the parent parameter via task_sid_subj(parent) on every path with no NULL check; NULL is a member of the parameter's unconstrained declared pointer domain, so a NULL parent causes a kernel NULL-pointer dereference at the ptrace hook.

evidence.reason: The parameter `parent` (line 1, declared `struct task_struct *`) has an unconstrained residual range that includes NULL because the fragment imposes no validation on it. It flows unchanged into `task_sid_subj(parent)` at line 4, which dereferences the task pointer to read the subject SID. There are no conditionals in the fragment, so every invocation reaches this dereference; a NULL value satisfied every (absent) guard and triggers a kernel NULL-pointer dereference. Primary mechanism: CWE-476 NULL pointer dereference.

assumptions: `task_sid_subj(parent)` consumes the task pointer to extract the task's subject SID, i.e., it dereferences its argument (name-implied semantics); the shown code supplies the unconstrained pointer.

`current` is treated as framework/OS-provided data; its dereference is not a candidate under the NULL-deref standard because it is neither a parameter, a container-extracted pointer, nor a call return.
The return value of `avc_has_perm` is propagated to the caller of `selinux_ptrace_traceme` (line 3), so no return-status handling flaw exists.
limitations: A NULL value for `parent` is not produced by any statement in the fragment; its arrival depends on callers outside the shown code, which caps confidence at 0.62 per the residual-range/brittle-boundary guidance.
Whether a NULL `parent` is attacker-reachable in the actual ptrace path cannot be determined from this fragment.

No integer, injection, crypto, file-handling, loop-termination, or buffer-capacity candidates exist in this fragment; the avc_has_perm check itself is an access-control decision with correctly ordered subject/object SIDs.

verdict.summary: The NE segment parser reads the untrusted NE-header field bin->ne_header->SegCount (line 7) and indexes bin->segment_entries[i] (line 12) with it, with no visible capacity or count bound on the array anywhere in the fragment — a missing-bound OOB read (CWE-125) over up to SegCount-1 entries. Independently, the guard at line 3 checks bin and bin->segment_entries but not bin->ne_header, so a NULL ne_header reaches the unconditional dereference bin->ne_header->SegCount at line 7 (CWE-476), crashing the parser on crafted input.

evidence.reason: CWE-125 OOB read: the loop bound bin->ne_header->SegCount (line 7) is a file-supplied value with full declared domain and is not constrained by the only guard on the path (line 3), which establishes only that bin and bin->segment_entries are non-NULL. The loop admits every i in [0, SegCount-1], and the sink at line 12 indexes bin->segment_entries at those values; the fragment contains no statement establishing the array's element count or capping SegCount against it, so for any SegCount exceeding the (unshown) allocation count the reads of se->length/minAllocSz/flags/offset at lines 13-19 operate on out-of-bounds memory. Missing bound on an input-derived index is the defect itself; no backing allocation needs to be exhibited.

CWE-476 NULL dereference: bin->ne_header is a pointer payload field of the parsed-file object whose residual range after the guard at line 3 still includes NULL, because line 3 tests only !bin and !bin->segment_entries and no statement in the fragment initializes or checks ne_header. The input state {bin non-NULL, segment_entries non-NULL, ne_header == NULL} passes every guard on the path (line 3 admits it; line 9 is unrelated) and the loop condition dereferences bin->ne_header at line 7 without any NULL check, crashing before the first iteration. The shown guard's own treatment of the sibling field segment_entries demonstrates this field class is caller-suppliable as NULL; the missing check on ne_header is the confirmed defect.

assumptions: bin and its members (ne_header, segment_entries, alignment) are populated by the NE loader from untrusted file data; the fragment itself provides no initializer or validator for ne_header or SegCount.
After line 3, bin->segment_entries is non-NULL but its element count is never established by any statement in the fragment.

SegCount and se->* fields are treated as file-derived integers of their NE-header types (small unsigned counts); the shown code performs no narrowing, so no integer-overflow claim is made for the 64-bit multiply at line 18.
limitations: The exact OOB magnitude for CWE-125 is a range claim: the concrete over-read size depends on the unshown allocation count of segment_entries; the finding rests on the missing visible capacity/bound per the unvalidated-size-flow standard.
Unchecked returns of r_list_newf (line 6) and r_str_newf (line 19) would only fault on non-attacker-scaled allocation failure; recorded as robustness concerns, not findings.
Internals of __translate_perms and downstream consumers of bs fields are outside the fragment and were not used for any verdict.

verdict.summary: handle_PORT discards the return value of sscanf (line 14); a PORT argument with fewer than six comma-separated integers leaves locals a–f (declared uninitialized at line 3) untouched, and the indeterminate values are read at line 15 (snprintf arguments) and line 25 (data_port = e*256 + f), flowing into inet_aton/ERR/DBG logging, ctrl->data_address, and ctrl->data_port (CWE-457).

evidence.snippet: snprintf(addr, sizeof(addr), "%d.%d.%d.%d", a, b, c, d);
evidence.reason: sscanf at line 14 writes only conversions that match and its return is discarded; a and-f are declared uninitialized at line 3, so an entry-point input such as "1,2,3" leaves d (and e,f) indeterminate. The snprintf at line 15 reads those indeterminate ints with no intervening check or initialization, so indeterminate stack bytes are formatted into addr and reach inet_aton (line 18), ERR/DBG logs (lines 19, 27), and strlcpy into ctrl->data_address (line 24). The inet_aton guard at line 18 runs after this read and cannot protect it. Primary mechanism: use of uninitialized variable (CWE-457).

Same root cause as the line-15 read: with an entry-point PORT argument like "1,2,3,4,5", only five conversions succeed at line 14 (f is never written), and since line 3 declares f uninitialized, line 25 reads indeterminate f and stores the result into ctrl->data_port on any path that passes the line-18 inet_aton guard (which validates only the IP string, never e/f or the conversion count). Primary mechanism: use of uninitialized variable feeding a security-relevant endpoint value (CWE-457).

assumptions: str is the caller-supplied argument of the FTP PORT command (entry-point input) whose content the fragment never constrains.
sscanf assigns only arguments whose conversions succeed; failed conversions leave the corresponding argument untouched (C semantics), and a–f are declared uninitialized at line 3.
snprintf (line 15) bounds addr by sizeof(addr) and strlcpy (line 24) bounds the copy by sizeof(ctrl->data_address), so addr and data_address cannot overflow in the shown code.
limitations: Port-component validation is absent (e,f admit the full int domain; e*256+f can overflow signed int or produce an out-of-range port), but ctrl->data_port's only shown consumers are the store at line 25 itself and the DBG %d read at line 27; the real consumer (e.g., a connect) is outside the fragment, so CWE-190 was not confirmed.
No NULL-check finding is reported for ctrl/str: no shown statement derives a possibly-NULL pointer in the fragment; treated as framework/robustness concern only.
The value of INET_ADDRSTRLEN is not quoted in the fragment, so the safety of the addr copy rests on the sizeof argument of snprintf, which is visible and sufficient.
Loop phase not applicable: the fragment contains no loops.

verdict.summary: call_qftf_func dereferences the list pointer returned by the user-configurable 'quickfixtextfunc' callback without a NULL check: at line 42 the callback's return payload is assigned to qftf_list, and line 43 unconditionally executes qftf_list->lv_refcount++. The only guard, line 40 (rettv.v_type == VAR_LIST), constrains the type tag but not vval.v_list, whose pointer domain includes NULL, so a callback returning a null list (v:_null_list) crashes Vim via NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476).

evidence.reason: The dereferenced pointer qftf_list is assigned at line 42 from rettv.vval.v_list, the return payload of the callback invoked at line 38 (cb is the user-configurable 'quickfixtextfunc' callback selected at lines 3 and 14-15). The only guard before the sink, line 40 (if (rettv.v_type == VAR_LIST)), admits every VAR_LIST typval regardless of vval.v_list, whose declared pointer domain includes NULL; the fragment places no constraint on it (no '!= NULL' check exists between line 42 and line 43, and line 37's NULL initialization is overwritten by line 42). A callback returning a null list therefore passes line 40 and is dereferenced at line 43, causing a NULL pointer dereference crash, primary CWE-476.

assumptions: A typval_T with v_type == VAR_LIST may carry a NULL vval.v_list; no statement in the fragment ties the type tag to a non-NULL pointer (line 40 constrains only the tag).

The callback invoked via call_callback at line 38 is user-configurable ('quickfixtextfunc' global at line 3 or per-list callback at lines 14-15), so its return value is entry-point-class user-config data.
Reference counting is balanced on the shown paths: list refcount incremented at line 43 before clear_tv at line 45; dict refcount incremented at line 33 before dict_unref at line 47.
limitations: qfl NULL-deref at lines 14 and 30 is demoted: the fragment neither derives NULL for the parameter nor shows any channel that nulls it; producing it would require an unshown caller.
Static 'recursive' flag (lines 5-9, 50) could remain TRUE if call_callback unwound via an exception/longjmp, but no such machinery is visible in the fragment, so it is unconfirmable.
start_idx/end_idx flow through the dict untransformed; the fragment contains no index/size sink consuming them.
No capacity/offset arithmetic exists in the fragment, so no OOB or integer-overflow candidate arises.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability is confirmable in the shown fragment. All error paths assign `status` (lines 16, 25, 31) before reaching `return status;` (line 57), so the return value is never uninitialized. The only free, `kfree(rsi_dev->tx_buffer)` (line 53), is reachable solely on the path where the NULL check at line 24 has passed, so no NULL or double free occurs. All allocations use compile-time sizes (lines 7, 23) and no attacker-derived value flows to any sink; the only format-style calls (lines 30, 49) use literal format strings. Demoted concerns (NULL for `adapter`/`pfunction` via unshown caller contract, and a single probe-time leak) are recorded in limitations.

assumptions: `kzalloc` at line 7 is NULL-checked at line 8; every statement at line 11 and later executes with `rsi_dev` non-NULL.
`kmalloc(2048, GFP_KERNEL)` at line 23 is NULL-checked at line 24; the free at line 53 is reached only via lines 29-33, after line 24 excluded NULL.

`status` is assigned on every path that reaches `fail_eps` (lines 16, 25, 31) before the corresponding goto (lines 17, 26, 32); the only other exit, line 9, returns a literal without reading `status`.

All buffer sizes and constants used as sizes/capacities are compile-time literals visible in the fragment (sizeof(*rsi_dev) at line 7, 2048 at line 23, 252 at lines 35-36, MAX_DEBUGFS_ENTRIES-1 at line 46).
limitations: `adapter` and `pfunction` are dereferenced (lines 11-21) with no NULL check, but no shown statement can produce NULL for them; their non-NULL status depends on an unshown caller/kernel probe contract, so the NULL-deref candidate is a robustness concern, not a confirmed finding.

`rsi_dev` is not freed on the `fail_eps` paths (lines 17, 26), a single probe-time leak; the fragment shows no attacker-controlled volume to compound the leak, so it is not a confirmed security finding.
`interface_to_usbdev(pfunction)`'s return value (line 12) is not validated, but it is only stored and never dereferenced within the fragment.

Whether `rsi_find_bulk_in_and_out_endpoints` (line 15) and `rsi_usb_init_rx` (line 29) themselves process attacker-controlled endpoint descriptor data is outside the fragment; the shown code checks both return values and routes failures to cleanup.

verdict.summary: string_scan_range has a confirmed heap out-of-bounds read: with an admitted range such as from=2,to=3, len=1 (lines 22-23), buf is calloc(1,1) (line 27), and the guard `needle < to - 4` at line 77 underflows (ut64) for to<4, so r_read_le32 at line 78 reads 4 bytes from a 1-byte buffer (3-byte over-read). Separately, the `needle -= 2` backward at line 188 can exactly undo all progress for a two-rune ASCII string followed by NUL when min>=3, making the outer loop at line 72 non-terminating (CWE-835).

evidence.reason: Heap over-read (CWE-125). from=2,to=3 is admitted by the only range guards: line 15 (from==to false), line 18 (from>to false), line 23 (len=(st64)(to-from)=1 passes `len<1||len>ST32_MAX`), and buf is calloc(1,1) at line 27 (capacity 1 byte). needle=2 enters the loop at line 72, and line 77's guard `needle < to - 4` evaluates 3-4 in ut64, wrapping to a huge value, so it admits needle=2; the sink at line 78 then reads 4 bytes (r_read_le32) from the 1-byte allocation, over-reading by 3 bytes. No statement in the fragment bounds to>=4.

Non-termination (CWE-835). With min=3 (admitted: line 28 rejects only min==0) and file bytes 0x61 0x62 0x00 at from (read at line 42), the inner loop at line 129 decodes two printable ASCII runes (runes=2) and breaks on NUL, leaving needle = str_start+2; the guard at line 186 admits this state (runes<min, runes>=2, ASCII, needle<to) and the backup at line 188 rewinds needle to str_start. The next outer-loop iteration at line 72 re-detects the identical ASCII state and rewinds again, so needle never advances and the loop runs forever for any to > str_start+2. No shown statement bounds needle before the decrement.

assumptions: from/to are entry-point range inputs; their only shown constraints are from<to (lines 15-21) and 1 <= (to-from) <= ST32_MAX (line 23), so to<4 with len<=3 is admitted.
min is admitted for any int != 0 (line 28), including min>=3 used by the CWE-835 witness.
r_read_le32 performs a standard 4-byte little-endian load at the given pointer.
R_STRING_SCAN_BUFFER_SIZE is not shown; all tmp[] writes are bounded by the shown sizeof(tmp)-relative guards (lines 129, 166, 184) and are not findings.
limitations: charset-path outlen narrowing (line 47: int outlen = len * 4; overflows for len >= 2^29 admitted by line 23) is environment-gated on RABIN2_CHARSET and its impact depends on r_charset_encode_str's handling of a negative capacity; not counted as confirmed.
bf is dereferenced at line 3 before r_return_val_if_fail(bf, -1) at line 10; a NULL bf requires internal-caller misuse and is treated as robustness, not an entry-point finding.
The return of r_buf_read_at (line 42) is ignored; a short read leaves zero-filled buf, a robustness concern only.
The escape-branch tmp writes (lines 166-171) are protected by the shown guard ((i+32) < sizeof(tmp) && r < 93) and are not findings.
Exact value of ST32_MAX is not visible in the fragment; it does not affect either demonstrated witness.

verdict.summary: The fragment is the patched form of Vim's get_visual_text() (CVE-2024-4786 class). The character-wise multibyte path computes *lenp from unconstrained visual columns (lines 20/25) and reads at *pp + *lenp - 1 in line 34, which is an OOB read when the selection starts with a multi-byte lead byte and extends to the end of the line (e.g., UTF-8 line "a<C3><A9>", cursor col 0, VIsual.col 2 gives *lenp 3 and an end pilot at the NUL). The visible guard at lines 36-39 re-anchors the length to the last byte of the start character when *pp is a lead byte with a non-NUL successor, forcing *pp + (*lenp - 1) inside the line for exactly that failing class; the remaining lead-byte-at-line-end layout is confined by *pp[1] != NUL so the line 34 read stays within the buffer. No other injection, memory, crypto, or control-flow sinks are present.

assumptions: ml_get_curline() and ml_get_pos() return valid, NUL-terminated line-buffer pointers for the current window line (standard Vim buffer contract the fragment relies on).

MB_BYTE2LEN()/*mb_ptr2len() implement Vim's multibyte encoding conventions, where a lead byte Leaf must be followed by the remaining bytes of the character on the line; lines 36-39 use exactly this to bound the length.
VIsual.col and curwin->w_cursor.col are colnr_T integers (stored into int *lenp at lines 20/25) and the fragment never bounds either against the line length.
limitations: Pre-fix OOB/wrong-length behavior of line 34 can be demonstrated with the multi-byte-line witness (cursor col 0, VIsual.col = 2, trailing 2-byte character), giving *lenp 3 and an end pilot on the NUL; that witness passes lines 9, 21, and 33 exactly and is then absorbed by lines 38-39, which are the protective statements that make the fragment not vulnerable.

No NULL check on the results of ml_get_pos()/ml_get_curline() exists in the fragment; treated as a robustness concern because those functions have no attacker-directed failure mode in the shown code and no security-relevant operation runs on a failure state.

Whether VIsual.col can be set to a column past the line's last character in real invocations is enforced outside the fragment; the verdict rests on the in-fragment guard, and confidence is therefore capped below the 0.75-0.9 band for a single fully decisive protective statement.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The memset at line 10 writes exactly the size requested at line 6 from the same constant (MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE) and is guarded by the line 7 NULL check; the skb_pull at line 14 is bounded to 1..63 bytes by the line 13 non-zero guard, excluding the 64-byte pull; and the line 15 error check fully isolates the failure path (free + return -EINVAL) from the success path (queue + return 0). Possible NULL dereference of the 'common' parameter and tailroom reduction affecting rsi_prepare_beacon are unconfirmed robustness concerns recorded in limitations.

assumptions: dev_alloc_skb(MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE) (line 6) provides at least MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE writable bytes after skb->data, and line 10 uses the identical constant, so the memset size equals the requested capacity.
