The only loop guard `bytes < size` (line 50) bounds reads against the attacker-derived `size`, not against any visible capacity of `directory_table` (no allocation/extent for the table appears in the fragment), so reads at offsets up to ~INT_MAX are admitted; CWE-125 missing bound. The write side of this same memcpy is bounded by guard 81 (admits dire->size in [0, SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN-1]) and the line 5 name capacity SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN+1, so the failure is the read, not the stack buffer.

Read sink: header copy at index `bytes` admitted by `while(bytes < size)` (50) with `size` derived from unvalidated `(*i)->data` (48); no visible capacity for `directory_table` bounds `bytes`, so on a crafted inode with a large `data` field the read executes at offsets far beyond the table allocation (CWE-125).

Read sink (swap branch): same unvalidated index `bytes`/`size` flow (lines 42, 47, 48, 50) feeding `directory_table + bytes` with no visible capacity bound on the table; large attacker-chosen `(*i)->data` admits reads past the allocation (CWE-125).

Read sink: entry-header copy indexed by `bytes`, executed for up to SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT iterations per outer pass (guard 64) even after `bytes` reaches `size` (no per-entry bound re-check inside lines 69-107), with `size`/`bytes` unconstrained by any visible `directory_table` capacity (lines 47-48, 50) -- CWE-125 missing bound on the read index.

Read sink (swap branch): same unvalidated `bytes`/`size` flow (lines 42, 47, 48, 50) into `directory_table + bytes`; no visible capacity for `directory_table` exists in the fragment, so the index domain up to ~INT_MAX is admitted and reads can pass the allocation end on a crafted image (CWE-125).

assumptions: Line 5-6 declares the only local buffer as `sizeof(squashfs_dir_entry_2) + SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1`, so the `dire->name` area has capacity `SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1`; this is what makes the line 81 guard sufficient for the write side.

Guards 64 and 81 bound per-header entry count and per-entry name length by the constants SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT / SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN; exact constant values are not shown and the analysis is expressed relative to them.
limitations: The classic dire->name stack write overflow is NOT present: guard 81-83 admits dire->size in [0, SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN-1] (excludes [SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN, 255]) and, with the line 5 capacity, the memcpy of size+1 bytes and the NUL at index size+1 stay in bounds; this is the named protective statement and it precedes the sink (81 before 86-88).

The OOB crossing point for `directory_table` cannot be named because the table's allocation size is not shown; the finding is therefore a residual-range/missing-bound claim, capped at confidence 0.55.
The inner loop (69-107) can continue reading after `bytes` has passed `size` (no per-entry `bytes < size` check); treated as the same missing-bound class, not a separate finding.
NULL dereference of `*i` from `read_inode` (17 into 25-32) has no NULL-producing path visible in the fragment (`EXIT_UNSQUASH` may abort internally) -- demoted.
`strcpy` destination `dir_ent.name` capacity at line 100 is not visible -- no verdict either way.

int overflow of `bytes`/`size` at the exact size == INT_MAX boundary depends on the unshown declared type of `(*i)->data`; a brittle boundary claim, not independently confirmed (no secondary CWE reported).
Potential log injection via `TRACE("%s", dire->name)` (89-91) is not confirmable: the argument is NUL-terminated at 88 and no log consumer semantics are shown.

verdict.summary: The loop at line 43 iterates one element too far ('i < argc - first_arg' instead of 'i < argc - first_arg - 1'), so the last iteration of line 44 reads argv[argc] — the NULL terminator slot per the fragment's own argc+1 model — and passes NULL to xstrdup, whose strdup semantics dereference it, crashing the process on every exec without --process. The correct bound would exclude the terminator slot.

evidence.reason: CWE-476: argv/argc/first_arg are entry-point inputs; line 43's guard admits i up to argc-first_arg-1, making the read index first_arg+i+1 = argc at the last iteration. The fragment models the vector as argc+1 slots with the NULL terminator at index argc (lines 42, 45), so the admitted value at that slot is NULL, and line 44 passes it to xstrdup (strdup semantics dereference a non-NULL string), yielding a NULL-pointer dereference on every exec path that reaches the else branch (process == NULL at line 34). No constraint or NULL check exists between line 43 and the sink; the correct loop bound is argc - first_arg - 1. Write index i stays within the line-42 capacity (argc+1), so the failure is the NULL dereference, not an OOB write.

assumptions: argv is modeled as having argc+1 slots with a NULL terminator at index argc, matching the C argv contract and the fragment's own convention at lines 42 (argc+1 allocation) and 45 (terminator write).
xstrdup is a strdup-family helper: its parameter is consumed as a non-NULL NUL-terminated string; passing NULL is out-of-domain and dereferenced.
Process==NULL (line 34) is the branch condition that makes the loop reachable; first_arg is the argp_parse output at line 16.
limitations: LISTEN_FDS (lines 28-31): strtoll can return out-of-range values and preserve_fds += listen_fds is unbounded, but the crun_context field types and downstream consumption of preserve_fds are not shown, so a narrowing/overflow or semantic impact cannot be confirmed; also no negativity check is shown.

process->args_len = argc (line 41) exceeds the number of elements actually initialized (argc - first_arg + 1), but no consumer of args_len is visible in the fragment, so no impact can be demonstrated.

If a caller passed a degraded argv array (fewer than argc+1 slots), the last read would be an OOB read; the caller's invocation is not shown, and under the standard contract the slot is the in-bounds NULL terminator, so the confirmed mechanism remains the NULL dereference.

All rsize arithmetic in the found block stays non-negative for every admitted match position. assumptions: r_size(ref) returns the byte length of a t_string operand, and op1->value.bytes / op->value.bytes point to data of that r_size length (string-ref contract implied by check_read_type(..., t_string) at L12-L13 and by the fragment deriving every bound from these r_size values).
Line numbering starts at the function signature search_impl(...) as line 1.

count wraps to UINT_MAX at the final evaluation of while (count--) (L31), but the loop exits at that point and the no-match path returns immediately (L33-L34); on the found path the goto (L28) precedes the decrement, so the wrapped value is never consumed.

With a backward search and an empty pattern, the early goto found (L20-L21) runs before the backward pointer adjustment (L22-L23), so the empty match is reported at the start of the string rather than the end; all produced substring ranges remain within [base, base+L), so this is a semantics quirk with no security impact.

The overall operand-stack result layout (whether make_true(op) at L49 targets the intended top-of-stack slot) cannot be confirmed from the fragment alone because the bodies of the push/make_true macros are not shown; this is a functional-correctness concern, not a demonstrated security vulnerability.
No injection, crypto, file, auth, or resource-exhaustion sinks exist in the fragment, so no other vulnerability class is applicable.

verdict.summary: The unsigned index parameter `u` reaches the array-subscript sinks `fm->hdf[u]` (line 6) and `fm->hd[u]` (lines 10 and 13) with no upper-bound check anywhere in the fragment. The only guard, `if (u < HTTP_HDR_FIRST) return (0);` (line 8), bounds only from below (and executes after the line-6 access), leaving the full upper tail of `u`'s declared domain admitted. For any finite capacity of the `hdf`/`hd` arrays, an admitted value `u` at or beyond that capacity causes an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). Confidence is capped because the array capacity itself is not visible in the fragment, making the witness a residual-range claim rather than an exact demonstrated excess.

evidence.reason: Primary sink: array subscript `fm->hdf[u]` reads element `u` with no preceding guard. `u` is an internal-helper parameter of type `unsigned` whose residual range at this point is the full declared domain [0, UINT_MAX]; the only bound check in the fragment (line 8, `u < HTTP_HDR_FIRST`) executes after this access and, being a lower bound, cannot keep `u` below the (unshown) element count of `hdf`. For any finite capacity L of `hdf`, u = L is in the admitted set and reads one element past the array, so the missing upper-bound validation is the confirmed CWE-125 out-of-bounds-read mechanism; the exact excess cannot be quantified because the capacity is not declared in the shown code.

Array subscript `fm->hd[u]` feeds `strchr` with `u` in residual range [HTTP_HDR_FIRST, UINT_MAX]. Guard line 8 admits every `u >= HTTP_HDR_FIRST` and provides no upper bound, so for any finite capacity L of `hd`, the admitted value u = L (with L >= HTTP_HDR_FIRST) reads element L, one past the array, before the scan; this is the same missing-bound CWE-125 out-of-bounds read as the primary sink, on the `hd[]` array.

Second `hd[u]` subscript on the same path: `u` remains in residual range [HTTP_HDR_FIRST, UINT_MAX] on the continuing path (line 8 passed, line 11 passed with `e != NULL`), with no upper-bound check between the parameter and this sink. The admitted value u = L (any finite capacity L of `hd`, L >= HTTP_HDR_FIRST) indexes element L out of bounds, a CWE-125 read passing the address of an out-of-range `http_hdr` object into `http_hdr_flags`.

assumptions: `HTTP_HDR_FIRST` is a named constant used as a lower bound; its numeric value is not shown and is irrelevant to the upper-bound finding.
`fm->hdf` and `fm->hd` are C arrays whose element counts are fixed by the (unshown) `struct http` definition; the fragment never derives or validates any capacity for them.
`http_hdr_flags()` is treated by its name-implied semantics as a lookup that parses the header name region ending at `e` and may return NULL; its internals are not shown.
limitations: The OOB witness is a residual-range claim (u at or beyond the unshown array capacity), not an exact demonstrated excess, because no array capacity is visible in the fragment; this is what caps confidence at 0.55.

A NULL-deref of `fm` was considered: `fm->hdf[u]` and `fm->hd[u]` dereference the pointer parameter unconditionally, but no shown path produces NULL for `fm`, so this is recorded as a robustness concern, not a confirmed finding.
NUL-termination of `fm->hd[u].b` (required for a well-defined `strchr`) is not derivable from the fragment and was not treated as a finding.
The guards at lines 11 (`e == NULL`) and 14 (`f != NULL && (f->flag & how)`) correctly protect their respective dereferences and do not involve `u`; they are not vulnerabilities.
No attacker origin for the caller of `http_isfiltered` is visible; per the analysis rules this does not demote the parameter-derived unvalidated-index finding.

verdict.summary: Preallocating the stack-map elements computes the allocation size as a 32-bit product, elem_size * smap->map.max_entries (line 6), which wraps for large map-config values; bpf_map_area_alloc then receives a truncated, too-small byte count while pcpu_freelist_populate (lines 15-16) subsequently writes max_entries elements of elem_size bytes into that undersized region, producing a kernel heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) rooted in the integer overflow (CWE-190), with no size bound or capacity check visible in the fragment.

evidence.reason: The storage region sized at line 6 is (elem_size * max_entries) mod 2^32 in u32 arithmetic, but this call hands the callee slot size elem_size and count max_entries, whose required span elem_size * max_entries can be >= 2^32 (e.g. elem_size = 2^16 via value_size, max_entries = 2^16 + 1 wraps the line-6 size to 2^16 while the populate writes span ~2^32 + 2^16 bytes). The last written offset (max_entries-1)*elem_size exceeds the line-6 capacity, and the only prior guard (line 8) admits every non-NULL pointer without bounding size — heap OOB write, CWE-787, fed by the CWE-190 overflow at line 6.

value_size and max_entries are u32 map-config fields with unconstrained residual ranges [0, 2^32-1] (no check in the fragment); elem_size is also u32 (line 3). The product elem_size * max_entries wraps modulo 2^32, so the byte count consumed by bpf_map_area_alloc is the truncated value instead of the required elem_size * max_entries, while the consumer at lines 15-16 assumes the full unwrapped product — the corrupted allocation size is the root-cause CWE-190 that enables the CWE-787 overflow.

assumptions: smap->map.value_size and smap->map.max_entries are u32 map-config fields populated from BPF_MAP_CREATE attributes with no validation visible in this fragment.
bpf_map_area_alloc honors the passed byte count; allocation of the wrapped (too-small) size is possible for overflowing inputs.
pcpu_freelist_populate writes freelist links spanning max_entries elements of elem_size bytes each inside the region given to it.
No upper bound on max_entries or value_size exists anywhere in the fragment (lines 3, 6, 15-16).
limitations: Line 20 references 'smp', which is not declared in this fragment (the parameter is 'smap'); the shown error-label path cannot compile — a code defect, but not evaluated as a runtime vulnerability.

The numeric value of sizeof(struct stack_map_bucket) is not shown, so the witness is a residual-range claim (elem_size >= 2^16 reachable via value_size) rather than an exact constant-only witness; confidence is capped accordingly.

Overflow requires elem_size * max_entries >= 2^32; if the wrapped size is 0 and kmalloc returns NULL, the line-8 guard returns -ENOMEM, but small-positive wrapped sizes (e.g. 2^16) still expose the OOB path when the allocation succeeds.
Successful allocation of the wrapped size is an environment assumption; the size mismatch itself is confirmed by the shown u32 arithmetic.
max_entries == 0 or non-wrapping products do not overflow and are not implicated.

Line 74's NULL check is on the else-branch of line 60, executes after line 33, and cannot protect this sink.

The allocation at line 26 is then skb->len-2 = 1 byte (visible capacity), and memcpy at lines 31-32 copies transaction->aid_len = 0xFF = 255 bytes into it (excess 254 bytes, heap overflow, CWE-787) while reading indices 2..256 of the 3-byte skb (OOB read past skb->len, CWE-125). Same admitted short-frame path (skb->len <= 6, data[0]==AID_TAG, aid_len = data[1] in 0..255): index aid_len+2 is at least 2 and up to 257 while skb->len-1 <= 5, so this read is out of bounds for every aid_len >= skb->len-1 (CWE-125). The condition itself sits after the overflowing memcpy at lines 31-32 and only gates the later return, not the copy.
On the same path, skb->data[aid_len + 3] reads an index up to 258 against an skb of length at most 6, an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) whose value then feeds the params memcpy at lines 40-41.

The memcpy source skb->data + aid_len + 4 with length params_len (0..255) reads indices from aid_len+4 to aid_len+4+params_len-1; for any admitted short frame (skb->len <= 6, aid_len up to 255) this is far beyond skb->len, a confirmed OOB read (CWE-125) on the same taint flow.

assumptions: skb is the HCI event payload delivered to the event callback, classified entry-point input: the fragment imposes no minimum skb->len and no cap on skb->data[1] before use.
skb->len is unsigned, so skb->len - 2 at line 26 wraps for skb->len < 2.

NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH is taken as 5 (threshold 7) per the ETSI table quoted at lines 15-21 ('AID 81 5 to 16'). The witness only needs skb->len < NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH + 2 and skb->data[0] == NFC_EVT_TRANSACTION_AID_TAG; the numeric tag value is irrelevant because data[0] is attacker-chosen and equal to the constant.

The witness skb->len=3, data[0]=AID_TAG, data[1]=0xFF is non-degenerate (non-empty frame with tag present) and every magnitude traces to a shown statement (guard admission at lines 22-23, allocation skb->len - 2 at line 26, u8 byte at line 30).
limitations: hdev/ndev NULL dereference at line 5: no NULL producer exists on any shown path; the framework precondition is not visible, so this is treated as robustness, not a finding.
skb leak on early returns (lines 24, 28, 37, 47) and the default branch: per-event leak of one skb, DoS-only and volume-dependent, not asserted as a CWE.
The guard's own OOB read skb->data[0] at line 23 for skb->len == 0 is subsumed by the same missing-length-validation family and is not needed for the primary verdict.

The second memcpy's write side (into the flexible params area) is not asserted independently because the struct layout of nfc_evt_transaction is not visible; the primary write overflow is fully provable from the visible allocation skb->len - 2 alone.

The low-level fixes that would neutralize these findings (changing && to ||, or bounding aid_len against the allocation) are absent from the shown code; none of the shown statements provides the protective bound.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds heap read in squashfs_opendir: the cursor 'bytes' and the region bound 'size' are derived exclusively from unvalidated filesystem metadata ((*i)->start, (*i)->offset, (*i)->data, directory-table contents) and are never checked against any capacity of directory_table. The loop guard `bytes < size` is self-referential, and the reads at directory_table + bytes (lines 51, 65, 75-76) execute with no bound tying them to the actual allocation, allowing a crafted image to drive reads past the end of the directory table.

evidence.reason: bytes (long long) is built at lines 41-48 from unconstrained entry-point metadata (sBlk.s.directory_table_start, (*i)->start, lookup_entry result which only excludes -1, (*i)->offset) and is used here as an offset into directory_table. The only guard on the path, line 50 `while(bytes < size)`, compares bytes against size which is derived at line 49 from the same attacker-controlled metadata ((*i)->data) and is never validated against any visible capacity of directory_table. No shown statement bounds bytes relative to the allocation; the header read can therefore occur past the end of the buffer (missing-bound/unvalidated-size flow, OOB read, CWE-125).

Same taint as the header read: bytes has been advanced by sizeof(dirh) at line 56 (and by sizeof(*dire)/dire->size+1 at lines 67/102 on later iterations) without any re-check against size or against any capacity of directory_table; the entry read at directory_table + bytes can run beyond both the attacker-claimed region (bytes >= size) and the actual allocation. The guards at lines 59 and 70 bound dir_count and name length only and do not constrain bytes. OOB heap read, CWE-125.

The memcpy source directory_table + bytes uses the same unvalidated attacker-derived offset; the destination dire->name is provably in-bounds only because guard 70 (line 70, `dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN`) admits dire->size < SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN, capping dire->size+1 at SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN within the NAME_LEN+1 name area of the buffer declared at line 5. The source side, however, has no bound tying bytes to directory_table's allocation, so the copy reads out of bounds on a crafted image (OOB read, CWE-125).

assumptions: Buffer capacity at line 5 is sizeof(struct squashfs_dir_entry) + SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1; with guard 70 admitting dire->size < SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN, the memcpy (<= NAME_LEN bytes) and NUL write at dire->name[dire->size+1] (index <= NAME_LEN) stay inside that buffer.
Guard 59 bounds the per-header entry count to dir_count <= SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT (constant value not shown in the fragment).

dir->dirs is regrown by realloc at lines 88-95 so that dirs[dir->dir_count] at lines 96-100 is within the freshly enlarged capacity unless dir->dir_count approaches INT_MAX (a magnitude not derivable from shown bounds).
limitations: NULL dereference of *i at lines 25-30/32/41/48-49 depends on read_inode returning NULL, whose failure semantics are not shown; not confirmed.
strcpy into dir->dirs[dir->dir_count].name at line 96: destination field capacity (struct dir_ent.name) is not visible, so an overflow can be neither confirmed nor excluded.

Sign of dire->size is not derivable from the fragment (struct squashfs_dir_entry not shown); a negative size would pass guard 70 and could turn dire->size+1 into a huge size_t, but this is unconfirmable.

Integer narrowing at line 49 (size = (*i)->data + bytes - 3 into int) can truncate, but the truncated value is always smaller than the true value above 2^31, so it only shortens the loop; it has no independent security consequence beyond the reported missing-bound read.
realloc size arithmetic at lines 89-90 could overflow int only with ~2^31 entries, requiring a directory region whose magnitude cannot be derived from the shown code; not confirmed.

TRACE lines 54-55 print long long bytes with %d (format/type mismatch, log-only UB); TRACE at line 85 prints attacker-influenced dire->name but log injection depends on check_name admitting control characters, whose body is not shown.

No value of SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT, SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN, DIR_ENT_SIZE, or any capacity of directory_table is visible; the OOB-read finding is therefore a missing-bound (residual-range) finding rather than one with an exact numeric witness, which is reflected in the confidence.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in tipc_crypto_key_rcv: skey->keylen is read as a u32 from attacker-controlled TIPC message data (line 24) with no bound, then used as the memcpy length at lines 26-27, writing up to 2^32-1 bytes into skey->key, whose capacity inside the kmalloc(size) buffer (line 17, size is a u16 <= 65535) is at most size - 20 bytes. The only size sanity check (line 30) executes after the copy, so it cannot prevent the overflow.

evidence.reason: CWE-787 heap OOB write: skey->keylen (u32, full residual range [0, 2^32-1] after the load at line 24 from msg data; no shown constraint before this copy) is the memcpy length. The destination skey->key is the flexible member inside the kmalloc(size) object allocated at line 17, where size is u16 (line 6, [0,65535]); the flexible array starts at offset 4 + TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME, so capacity is size - (4 + TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME) <= 65535 - 4. Any admitted message with keylen > size - 20 (e.g., size=64, keylen=256, passing the line 10 fresh-key guard) overflows the heap object. The sanity check at line 30 (size != tipc_aead_key_size(skey)) executes after this sink in path order and only kfrees the already-corrupted buffer, so it provides no protection.

assumptions: struct tipc_aead_key layout implied by the accesses: u32 keylen at offset 0, char alg_name[TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME], and a flexible char key[] member starting at offset sizeof(__be32) + TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME = 4 + TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME.
tipc_aead_key_size(skey) = sizeof(*skey) + skey->keylen = (4 + TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME) + keylen, as implied by its use at line 30.
The message payload pointer data (line 7) is considered to have the header-announced length size (line 6).
The overflow conclusion is independent of the numeric value of the unshown macro TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME: key[] capacity is at most size - 4 <= 65531, far below the u32 keylen maximum.
limitations: Read-side OOB read of the message payload (line 24 reads 4 bytes at offset TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME; lines 26-27 read keylen bytes past the announced size) is the twin of the confirmed write overflow and is not reported as a separate CWE.
Unaligned dereference at line 24 (*((__be32 *)(data + TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME))) is an architecture-dependent robustness/UB concern, not the confirmed security mechanism.
tx from line 3 is dereferenced at line 46 with no NULL check in the shown code, but no NULL-producing statement or attacker-directed failure is shown, so it is noted only here.
The guard at line 18 (kmalloc failure) is correctly handled and not a finding.

verdict.summary: A crafted squashfs image controls the directory-entry size field loaded at L77-78. The only guard, L82-85, rejects only sizes >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN and admits negative values; e.g., size 0xFFFE (-2) passes the guard and makes the memcpy length at L88 (dire->size + 1 == -1) convert to SIZE_MAX as size_t, overflowing the stack buffer declared at L5-6 (CWE-121 stack buffer overflow; CWE-195 signed-to-unsigned length conversion).

evidence.reason: Sink: memcpy writes dire->size + 1 bytes into dire->name, which lies inside the local stack array declared at L5-6 (capacity sizeof(squashfs_dir_entry_3) + SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1). dire->size is loaded from attacker-controlled image bytes at L77-78 (or L73-75) and the only constraint on it, the guard at L82 (dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN), admits every value below SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN, including negatives (e.g., -2). For such a value the length dire->size + 1 is negative (-1) and is converted to SIZE_MAX in memcpy's size_t parameter (CWE-195), producing a write of ~2^64 bytes into the L5-6 stack buffer (CWE-121) plus an equally large read from directory_table + bytes. The guard executes before the sink (L82-85 then L87-88) but its admitted set contains the failing witness, so it does not protect the operation; no lower-bound check on dire->size exists anywhere in the fragment.

assumptions: SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN, SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT, and DIR_ENT_SIZE are positive constants defined outside the fragment; only the comparisons using them are visible.
directory_table, directory_table_hash, sBlk.s.directory_table_start, and swap are provided by the image-loading layer, and directory_table contains attacker-controlled on-disk bytes.
The stack buffer capacity visible for the memcpy write side is the declaration at L5-6.
limitations: The declared type of the dir-entry size field is not visible in the fragment; the primary finding (and the dir_count loop candidate) rely on the standard signed 16-bit interpretation of the on-disk field. If the fields are unsigned, the negative-value witnesses are unconstructible and the L82/L65 upper-bound guards would be sufficient.

dir_count wrap candidate: dirh.count = 0xFFFFFFFE makes dir_count = -1 at L59, which passes L65 and makes while(dir_count--) at L70 non-terminating with unbounded reads and realloc growth (CWE-835/CWE-400). Not independently evidenced due to the same unshown field type.

OOB read from directory_table (CWE-125 missing bound): bytes (L42, L48) and size (L49) are derived from unconstrained image fields with no visible capacity for directory_table; a range-level candidate only.
strcpy at L101 into dir->dirs[dir->dir_count].name has an unshown destination capacity; source length is bounded by the NUL placement at L89, so an overflow is not confirmable.
read_inode's return is dereferenced without a NULL check (L25-29, L32); no NULL producer is shown, so this is a robustness concern.

The guard at L44 only discards the -1 sentinel of lookup_entry; residual negative values and unbounded positive values are not validated against the extent of directory_table (missing bound, as above).

verdict.summary: issuerAndThisUpdateCheck performs an out-of-bounds heap read when parsing the GSER issuer/thisUpdate value: if the thisUpdate value region contains no closing quote (or the issuer value region is empty), the scan exits by exhaustion and lines 113-114 advance x.bv_val one byte past the end of in->bv_val while underflowing x.bv_len; the space-eating loop at line 123 then dereferences x.bv_val[0] out of bounds. A deterministic 51-byte witness '{issuer rdnSequence:"",thisUpdate "XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX}' passes every guard (lines 18/20/34/41/51/57/82/90/99/111) and reads in->bv_val[51], 1 byte past the 51-byte buffer. An additional variant with an empty issuer value reads past the buffer at line 65.

evidence.reason: in is entry-point input whose residual range after the shown guards includes any length>=38 brace-delimited string; the witness '{issuer rdnSequence:"",thisUpdate "XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX}' (51 bytes) passes lines 18, 20, 34, 41, 51, 57, 82, 90, 99, and 111 (tu->bv_len==15, not <15). Because the thisUpdate value contains no closing quote, the scan at lines 106-110 exits by exhaustion with tu->bv_len == x.bv_len == 15, so line 113 advances x.bv_val to in->bv_val+51 (one past the 51-byte buffer whose last byte is accessed at line 20) and line 114 makes x.bv_len -1/wrapped. Line 123 then evaluates x.bv_val[0] == in->bv_val[51] before the && x.bv_len operand, dereferencing 1 byte past the buffer: confirmed CWE-125 OOB read.

With the empty-issuer witness '{issuer' + 20 spaces + 'rdnSequence:"}' (41 bytes, capacity indices 0..40 evidenced by line 20), guards at lines 18/20/41/51/57 all admit the input; lines 58-59 decrement x.bv_len from 0 so the bound wraps to a huge value, re-entering the scan at line 64; line 65 then reads is->bv_val[1] == in->bv_val[41], 1 byte past the buffer (deterministic). Further reads continue while the scan fails to find a quote byte. Confirmed CWE-125 OOB read.

assumptions: in->bv_len is the capacity of in->bv_val (indices 0..in->bv_len-1); the fragment's own access to in->bv_val[in->bv_len-1] at line 20 evidences this bound.

The primary line-123 OOB read does not depend on ber_len_t being unsigned: line 113 already advances x.bv_val one past the buffer, and the loop condition dereferences x.bv_val[0] before testing x.bv_len, which is nonzero in either signedness.
limitations: NULL dereference of parameters in/is/tu (lines 18/20, 61-62, 103-104): dereferenced with no NULL check, but no shown path produces NULL for them, so demoted per the NULL-cannot-be-produced exclusion.

Unchecked slap_sl_malloc result at line 148 (used at lines 153/155) and the discarded ber_dupbv_x result at line 142: depend on allocation failure, which is only attacker-directed if the input length exhausts memory; demoted as environment-failure robustness.
The line-65 issuer variant requires x.bv_len to wrap (unsigned ber_len_t) for loop re-entry; the primary line-123 witness has no such dependency.
The unquote loop at lines 147-156 is verified in-bounds for writes; it can read the in-bounds byte after the closing quote and copy it into the output (logic oddity, not memory-unsafe).

The read-before-length-check ordering in the space-eating loops (lines 29/46/95/123) is not an OOB by itself: with x.bv_len==0 and no prior underflow, x.bv_val points at the in-bounds '}' by the invariant x.bv_val + x.bv_len == in->bv_val + in->bv_len - 1.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The case-fold expansion loop is fully guarded: invalid code points are rejected (lines 24-27), the combinatorial expansion is capped by the alt_num threshold break (lines 55-56), the empty-string case is excluded (line 15), and every length/count that reaches a consuming sink (onig_node_str_cat line 51, expand_case_fold_string_alt line 66) is bounded by the visible items array capacity (line 8) and by the validated code-point range [p, end). All allocation and list-add results are NULL/status checked before use; no OOB, integer overflow, NULL-deref (beyond generic internal-helper parameter domain), non-termination, or error-handling flaw is demonstrable from the shown statements.

assumptions: ONIGENC_GET_CASE_FOLD_CODES_BY_STR writes at most ONIGENC_GET_CASE_FOLD_CODES_MAX_NUM entries into the 'items' array declared at line 8, bounding the returned count n used at lines 55, 66.

enclen(reg->enc, p) returns the byte length in [1, end - p] of the code point at p, whose completeness inside [p, end) is established by the successful decode in the ONIGENC_GET_CASE_FOLD_CODES_BY_STR call at lines 22-23; this keeps p + len within [start, end].
Internal-helper parameters node and reg are non-NULL at the call sites by the regex-compiler contract; the fragment itself contains no NULL check for them.
limitations: C1 demoted: an out-of-bounds read at line 51 would require enclen to return a length exceeding end - p, which contradicts the decode performed at lines 22-23; no witness passes every shown guard, and no visible capacity violation is constructible.

C2 demoted: expand_case_fold_string_alt(n, items, ...) at line 66 is safe because the visible declaration at line 8 bounds n by the items array capacity; the call is in-domain for the whole admitted set.
C3 demoted: alt_num *= (n + 1) at line 55 cannot overflow int because the line-56 break fires after at most 4 multiplications (factors >= 2), well below INT_MAX.
C4 demoted: infinite loop would require len == 0 at line 93, which no shown statement can produce on an input admitted by line 15 and validated at lines 22-23.

C5 demoted: unconditional dereference of node/reg (lines 9, 11, 22, 29, 124) with no NULL check is a generic internal-helper parameter concern; the fragment shows no producer of NULL, so it is recorded here rather than as the verdict.

Robustness-only: if onig_node_list_add/onig_node_new_str/expand_case_fold_make_rem_string fail, the fragment frees the affected nodes and returns ONIGERR_MEMORY (lines 128-133); allocation failure is not attacker-directed and every failure path is handled, so no error-handling finding is issued.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The input-derived length len = strlen(uri) is bounded before every consumption: len > INT_MAX - EXPAND_SPARE guards the len + EXPAND_SPARE allocation arithmetic (lines 71-73, 98-100), the #if UINT_MAX >= SIZE_MAX guards bound the size_t product (78-82, 105-109), the realloc gate at line 69 keeps capacity >= len, and the allocated capacity len + EXPAND_SPARE exceeds the memcpy length len (line 120) and the store index len - 1 (line 122). Namespace-array reads at lines 39 and 43 are short-circuited by len > xmlLen / len > xmlnsLen so indices stay within the 37- and 30-element arrays. The fragment is the fixed counterpart; residual NULL/NUL-termination concerns are caller-contract robustness only.

assumptions: uri and prefix->name are NUL-terminated XML_Char strings supplied by the caller; the sentinel loop at line 38 relies on uri's terminating NUL.
EXPAND_SPARE is a positive compile-time constant, and INT_MAX, SIZE_MAX, UINT_MAX are standard macros.
In the free-list branch, b->uriAlloc is the intact capacity of a previously allocated b->uri, so len <= b->uriAlloc (line 69) implies sufficient capacity.
xmlNamespace has 37 elements (xmlLen = 36, line 8); xmlnsNamespace has 30 elements (xmlnsLen = 29, lines 12-13).
limitations: NULL-dereference of uri (lines 23, 127), parser->m_dtd (line 127), and bindingsPtr (lines 131-132) without shown NULL checks is a caller-contract robustness concern; no shown statement can produce NULL.
An over-read of uri in the line-38 sentinel loop would require a caller-supplied non-NUL-terminated buffer, which the fragment never derives; treated as a C-string contract concern, not a finding.
A uri length at or beyond INT_MAX is not demonstrable from the fragment and is in any case rejected by the len > INT_MAX - EXPAND_SPARE guards (lines 71, 98) before use.
The fragment contains no injection (format/command/SQL/log/header/URL), weak-crypto, temp-file, or authorization sinks.

The shown overflow guards on both allocation paths indicate the fragment is the patched/fixed counterpart of the Expat addBinding integer-overflow issue; no protective statement is missing from the shown code.

verdict.summary: The per-record length guard at line 53 rejects requests whose trailing data is smaller than the record about to be swapped. Because xkbSelectEventsReq is 16 bytes (four-byte header plus the six CARD16 selector fields referenced at lines 5-12), every reachable dataLeft value is congruent to 0 mod 4 (line 23 and line 67), so the size-1 path's guard/consumption mismatch (guard admits dataLeft == 2, consumption is 4 at lines 63-67) can never wrap the unsigned counter and no out-of-bounds access exists. Not vulnerable.

assumptions: xkbSelectEventsReq is 16 bytes: the standard 4-byte request header (swaps(&stuff->length), line 5) plus the six CARD16 fields deviceSpec, affectWhich, clear, selectAll, affectMap, map referenced at lines 7-12; therefore SIZEOF(xkbSelectEventsReq) is congruent to 0 (mod 4).

client->req_len is the received request length in 4-byte words and equals the delivered request buffer size; REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE (line 6) enforces the fixed-header minimum, so dataLeft at line 23 is >= 0 and congruent to 0 (mod 4).
swaps()/swapl() are the standard in-place byte-swap macros (read-modify-write through the given pointer) and return no status.
limitations: Demoted candidate: on the size-1 path (lines 44-47, 63-67) guard line 53 admits dataLeft == 2 while 4 bytes are consumed, which would wrap unsigned dataLeft to 0xFFFFFFFE and enable an out-of-bounds swap if dataLeft == 2 were reachable; it is not, because line 23 and all decrements at line 67 keep dataLeft congruent to 0 (mod 4). A request layout with SIZEOF congruent to 2 (mod 4) (e.g., 14 bytes with only five selector fields) would change this verdict, but that contradicts the six CARD16 fields visible in the shown code.

The final leftover check `if (dataLeft > 2)` (line 69) is not the protective statement; leftover values are also congruent to 0 (mod 4), so excess data always trips it, but no partial-record read occurs before it.
Internals of REQUEST/REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE/swaps, SIZEOF(xkbSelectEventsReq), XkbMapNotify, and the Xkb event-class constants are not shown; standard X11 semantics are assumed.

verdict.summary: No confirmable vulnerability in the fragment. The only caller-memory write (*handle at line 13) is protected by the NULL guard if(handle) at line 12, which excludes NULL from the dereference path; the array access at line 9 is bounded by the strict loop condition i < MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS (line 7), allowing i at most MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS-1; MemorySet at line 15 uses the compile-time constant sizeof(OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES); and the loop provably terminates on every input. The fragment contains no entry-point input reaching any security-relevant sink.

assumptions: MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS is a positive compile-time constant, so the loop over i in [0, MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS-1] terminates.
i is declared UINT32 (line 5), and the store at line 13 assigns a UINT32 result to the TPMI_DH_OBJECT target without a visible narrowing cast.
Line 12 (if(handle)) restricts every execution of *handle at line 13 to non-NULL handle values; NULL is the only value in the parameter's declared domain that would fault the write.
limitations: The element count of the global array s_objects is not declared in the fragment, so the in-bounds reading of line 9 relies on the unshown pairing of MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS with the array size; correspondingly, no OOB claim could be confirmed against a visible capacity.

The values of MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS, TRANSIENT_FIRST, and CLEAR are unshown; a UINT32 wrap in i + TRANSIENT_FIRST (line 13) cannot be demonstrated, and the validity range of the produced handle (e.g., TRANSIENT_FIRST..TRANSIENT_LAST) is outside the fragment.
Caller behavior is unshown: whether callers pass NULL for handle, dereference the NULL return at line 19, or validate the written handle value is out of scope for this fragment.
Concurrency or TOCTOU on the occupied flag across contexts is not analyzable from the single-threaded control flow shown here.
The discarded return of MemorySet (line 15) is not treated as an error-status flaw because its arguments are constants, not attacker-derived data.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The early guard at line 12 (attempt cancellable cancelled OR task completed/cancelled) with the early return at lines 13-17 is the protective statement: every path that reaches the later data->task uses (line 38, g_task_get_cancellable at line 98) or data uses (lines 45-112) requires the enclosing task to be still live (neither completed nor cancelled), so no use-after-free witness survives. Remaining candidates (unchecked user_data/attempt/data NULL deref at lines 5-6, potential double-unref of attempt if it is a member of connection_attempts, NULL protocol in g_set_error at line 107) depend on unshown contracts or membership and are recorded in limitations.

assumptions: Line 12: `if (g_cancellable_is_cancelled (attempt->cancellable) || task_completed_or_cancelled (data->task))` — per its name and usage, task_completed_or_cancelled reports that the enclosing task has already completed or been cancelled; the early return at lines 13-17 keeps all continuation paths in the admitted set {attempt not cancelled, task not completed, task not cancelled}.

Line 48: `for (l = data->connection_attempts; l; l = g_slist_next (l))` — iteration terminates on the GSList NULL sentinel with g_slist_next as the only progress step; the fragment performs no index or capacity arithmetic.

Whether the current `attempt` is also a member of `data->connection_attempts` is not visible in the fragment, which is why the unref at line 56 cannot be proven to be a double-unref with the loop unref at line 52.
limitations: NULL dereference of user_data/attempt/data (lines 5-6): the pointers are unchecked, but no shown statement derives NULL for them and they are the initiating async API's registered callback payload; a NULL here is a robustness/callback-contract concern, not demonstrated by the fragment's own logic. No CWE assigned.
Potential double-unref of `attempt` (loop line 52 plus line 56) cannot be confirmed because membership of `attempt` in `data->connection_attempts` is not shown.
`g_set_error` at lines 107-109 passes `protocol` as %s with no shown NULL constraint or downstream log/command/query consumer; no injection mechanism is confirmable within the fragment.

The exact internal semantics of task_completed_or_cancelled are not shown; the verdict relies on its name and the guard's usage, which is why confidence is capped at the 0.75-0.9 not-vulnerable band (0.82).

verdict.summary: OP_JMPUW in mrb_vm_exec derives the jump target at line 302 from the bytecode operand and uses it at line 322 as `pc = irep->iseq + a` with no check that `a < irep->ilen` on the main execution path. The only `ilen` bound is an assertion in the CHECKPOINT_RESTORE branch (line 308), which is not executed on the normal path; the catch-handler guard at line 314 is skipped when `catch_handler_find` returns NULL and compares against a handler range rather than `ilen`. A crafted bytecode program can therefore make `a` exceed `irep->ilen` (or wrap negative) and drive an out-of-bounds read of the instruction stream (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: Bytecode-derived value `a` (Phase 1 taint; computed at line 302 as `(uint32_t)((pc - irep->iseq) + (int16_t)a)`, residual range including all values >= `irep->ilen` and values wrapped near 2^32 by the uint32 cast) is consumed here as an index into the `irep->iseq` buffer whose capacity `irep->ilen` is visible only in the line-308 assertion. That assertion executes only in the CHECKPOINT_RESTORE branch, not on the CHECKPOINT_MAIN path, and is compiled out in release builds; the only other guard (line 314, inside `if (ch)`) is skipped when `catch_handler_find` returns NULL (line 312 handles NULL) and bounds against ch->begin/end rather than ilen. A witness with `ilen=100`, operand 32767, and no ENSURE handler yields `a=32867` at the sink, forming an out-of-bounds pointer whose next opcode fetch reads past the buffer: CWE-125 out-of-bounds read.

assumptions: Bytecode executed by mrb_vm_exec is treated as entry-point input because no shown statement constrains or validates `irep`/`proc` fields.
The visible capacity of `irep->iseq` is `irep->ilen` (line 308); `ch == NULL` is an explicitly handled outcome of `catch_handler_find` (line 311-312).
The `(int16_t)a` cast at line 302 fixes the operand's effective offset domain to [-32768, 32767] per the shown code.
limitations: Other opcodes (OP_MOVE line 48, OP_GETUPVAR lines 249-256, OP_SETUPVAR lines 265-268, OP_JMP line 276) exhibit the same missing bytecode-operand validation; they are not reported as separate findings and would all be neutralized by a bytecode validator or by trusting only compiler-generated code.
If untrusted bytecode execution is outside the threat model, the finding is not exploitable; severity and confidence are calibrated for the entry-point interpretation used here.
OP_ENTER argument-unpacking paths were examined but no independently demonstrable overflow was confirmed from the fragment alone.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. Every attacker-controlled value reaching a security-relevant consumption point is constrained by a visible protective statement: netlink length validation before tcmsg reads (L31-34 then L36), the TCA_KIND length guard before the name[IFNAMSIZ] buffer is used (L65-69, L6), the chain_index upper-bound check before tcf_chain_get (L92-97), the protocol/kind presence checks on the creation path (L123), and IS_ERR/NULL checks before every block/chain/tp/q dereference. err is assigned on all error and success paths, and the EAGAIN replay loop re-derives state with balanced locking.

assumptions: IFNAMSIZ=16 for the name[] declaration at L6 (kernel uapi constant referenced by the declaration).
nlmsg_parse_deprecated(n, sizeof(*t), ...) at L31 validates that the payload holds at least sizeof(struct tcmsg) and enforces attribute bounds via rtm_tca_policy before t = nlmsg_data(n) at L36.
nlattr array entries tca[] are NULL when an attribute is absent, which the presence tests at L65, L91, L123, L158 rely on.
tcf_proto_check_kind(tca[TCA_KIND], name) at L65 both caps the copied kind string into name and reports overlong kinds via its nonzero return, which the calling code treats as 'name too long' (L66).
tcf_chain_get and tcf_chain_tp_find report failure via NULL/IS_ERR, as the checks at L98, L107 use.
TC_ACT_EXT_VAL_MASK bounds chain_index; its exact value is not defined in the fragment, but the guard at L92-96 exists and runs before the only consumer at L97.
limitations: The internal contract of tcf_block_release(q, block, ...) at L210 is not shown; on the __tcf_block_find error path (L85-88) an ERR_PTR reaches it. The fragment's own dereference of block (L89) is properly IS_ERR-guarded, so this is an unconfirmable callee-semantics concern, not a finding.
Whether __tcf_block_find can return a NULL (non-ERR) block on some input is not visible; the fragment checks only IS_ERR at L85. Any NULL deref claim would need callee behavior not shown.

Whether tcf_proto_check_kind is fully length-safe internally is not shown; the visible caller-side guard (L65-69) rejects a nonzero return and is treated as an overlong-name error, and no shorter-string input can overflow name[IFNAMSIZ].
Replay spin (L215-219) would require chain->flushing (L116-118) to persist indefinitely; this is a transient concurrency condition, not an attacker-settable input in the shown code.
No memory, injection, crypto, file, or authz sink inside the fragment consumes an unconstrained input-derived index, size, string, path, or status.

verdict.summary: The most dangerous operation — consuming rex.line/rex.input after getvvcol(), which the fragment itself documents as able to flush rex.line (line 69) — is protected: lines 70-71 re-fetch the line via reg_getline(rex.lnum) and re-derive rex.input = rex.line + col before the sink win_linetabsize(wp, rex.line, col) at line 73, so the flushed pointer never reaches the sink. Remaining concerns (unvalidated pointer-difference col, unchecked reg_getline NULL, MAXCOL wrap at line 55, end==0 underflow at line 74) lack witnesses expressible in the shown code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: rex.line and rex.input initially point into the same line of the buffer; the re-fetch at lines 70-71 restores them consistently with the same col before line 73 consumes them.
reg_getline(rex.lnum) returns the live line for the match line; line 48 constrains the match line to the visual range and the engine produced the match on it.
limitations: col = (colnr_T)(rex.input - rex.line) at line 51 is unconstrained and flows into rex.line + col (line 71) and win_linetabsize(..., col) (line 73), but a witness (rex.input before the line start or beyond its end, or a line-length beyond colnr_T's range) is not produced by any shown statement and the line capacity is not visible, so this remains a missing-bound range claim capped below reportable confidence (CWE-125).

The return of reg_getline (line 70) is not NULL-checked before rex.line + col (line 71) and win_linetabsize (line 73); no shown path produces NULL and the failure is not attacker-directed, so it is treated as robustness, not a NULL-dereference finding.

bot.col + (*p_sel != 'e') at line 55 can wrap if bot.col == MAXCOL in characterwise mode; the fragment names MAXCOL as an admitted field value only in the Ctrl_V branch (line 66) and no shown statement produces bot.col == MAXCOL in 'v' mode; impact would be a wrong-reject of a match, not a memory-safety error.

end - (*p_sel == 'e') at line 74 can underflow when end == 0 and *p_sel == 'e'; getvvcol's output of end == 0 is not established by a shown statement and the effect is a wrong-accept within lines already bounded by line 48, with no security-relevant consumer confirmed in the fragment.
The function contains no loops, so loop-termination analysis is not applicable.

verdict.summary: In the Ctrl_V branch, the byte-length argument to win_linetabsize is derived from the unconstrained pointer difference rex.input - rex.line without any visible bound or capacity check, so an admitted value of that difference exceeding the line's allocation causes an out-of-bounds read of the line buffer (CWE-125). The guard at line 69 executes only after the call and checks the result, not the length argument.

evidence.reason: The length argument (colnr_T)(rex.input - rex.line) is the narrowed ptrdiff of two pointers (rex.input, rex.line) that no shown statement constrains or bounds (Phase 1 item 8); over that residual domain the length admits values larger than the line object's capacity, which is not declared anywhere in the fragment, so the missing bound is itself the finding (unvalidated-size flow). The sink consumes the value as a byte length over rex.line inside win_linetabsize; guards on the path (lines 14, 48, 58, 60-67) constrain only buffer identity, lnum, mode, and start/end, and the only pointer-derived check (line 69) executes after the call, too late to prevent the out-of-bounds read. Primary mechanism: out-of-bounds read via unvalidated size (CWE-125).

assumptions: colnr_T is Vim's 32-bit signed integer column type and win_linetabsize's third parameter is a byte length that the function reads as line[0..len); the type width and callee semantics are not declared in the fragment but are required to interpret line 68 as a length-consuming read sink.
MAXCOL equals the maximum colnr_T value (Vim's INT_MAX) for the demoted overflow candidate at line 55.
limitations: The OOB witness is a range claim, not a single demonstrated value: the fragment shows no allocation/capacity for rex.line and no guarantee that rex.input stays within it; if the regex engine elsewhere guarantees rex.input inside the line, no over-read occurs, but such an invariant is not visible in the fragment and cannot be used either way.

bot.col + (*p_sel != 'e') at line 55 can wrap when bot.col == MAXCOL (CWE-190/CWE-682); demoted because the corrupted comparison only rejects otherwise-valid visual-area matches and has no security-relevant consumer.

end - (*p_sel == 'e') at line 69 evaluates to -1 when end == 0 and the selection is exclusive, making cols > -1 always true and rejecting column-0 block selections; logic flaw with no security impact.
NULL dereference of p_sel/curbuf would require unshown environment invariants to fail and is not attacker-directed; robustness concern only.
No loops, injection sinks, crypto, or file/access-control operations exist in the fragment; no other candidates were identified.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled squashfs image fields drive directory-table read offsets (lines 41-52, via bytes/size from (*i)->data, (*i)->offset and lookup_entry) with no visible bound to the table's storage, causing out-of-bounds reads (CWE-125); additionally, the attacker-derived filename is copied at line 90 into struct dir_ent.name, whose capacity is not visible, an unvalidated-size write (CWE-787, lower confidence). The local stack buffer (lines 5-6, 76-78) is protected by the line 71 sizing guard and is not a finding.

evidence.reason: bytes (line 42) originates from image-controlled state (directory_table_hash, start at line 41) plus (*i)->offset (line 48); size = (*i)->data + bytes - 3 (line 49). The only guards before the read are line 44 (-1 check) and line 51 (bytes < size), neither of which ties bytes/size to any capacity of directory_table declared in the fragment. For (*i)->data in [4, 2^32-1] (admitted by the line 32 == 3 check), the loop reads at offsets up to size-1 (≈ data + bytes0 - 4): an input-derived index with no visible target bound, i.e., the missing-bound OOB read, CWE-125.

Same input-derived bytes (lines 41-49) is used as the table offset; guards 44 and 51 admit every bytes < size with attacker-set size and nothing bounds bytes against directory_table's storage. The entry-size guard at line 71 executes after this read, so it cannot protect it. Missing-bound OOB read, CWE-125, on the same unvalidated-size flow.

The destination (stack buffer, lines 5-6) is protected by the line 71 guard admitting dire->size <= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN-1 and the +SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN+1 tail capacity. The source read directory_table + bytes remains governed only by the attacker-set bytes/size (lines 41-49, 51) with no visible directory_table capacity, so the source access is a missing-bound OOB read, CWE-125.

dire->name length is fixed by line 78 to dire->size + 1 <= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN (admitted by guard line 71), and dire->name bytes are image-controlled with no sanitization. The destination field .name of struct dir_ent has no visible capacity in the fragment; the only sizing statement (realloc at lines 83-84) sizes whole struct dir_ent elements. An input-derived string of up to SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN bytes plus NUL is written with no visible destination bound: unvalidated-size OOB write, CWE-787 (missing-capacity flow).

assumptions: SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN, SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT and DIR_ENT_SIZE are compile-time constants; only their symbolic use is visible, and the local-buffer bound proof relies only on offsetof(name) <= sizeof(struct squashfs_dir_entry), which holds because name is a member of that struct.

directory_table, directory_table_hash and sBlk are globals populated from the squashfs image; no capacity for directory_table is declared in the fragment, which is the premise of the missing-bound finding.
sizeof(dirh) and sizeof(*dire) are positive, so bytes strictly increases and the outer loop terminates (CWE-835 not applicable).
limitations: The local stack buffer writes (lines 76-78) are NOT vulnerable: line 5 capacity (+ SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1) plus line 71 guard (rejects size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN) bound the write to within the buffer for every admitted size.
NULL dereference of *i after read_inode (line 17) is demoted: the fragment shows no path on which read_inode produces NULL.

Integer overflow of dir_count / realloc size is demoted: per-entry bytes advance (>= 11) bounds total entries to about data/11, below INT_MAX for a 32-bit data field; the field's width is not shown, so the overflow is not demonstrated.

TRACE("%s", dire->name) (lines 79-80) can emit image-supplied newlines into the log (log-injection class), but TRACE is a debug macro and the log backend is not shown; kept as a low-severity limitation rather than a confirmed CWE.
The CWE-787 secondary finding is capped at low confidence because the destination .name capacity is not visible in the fragment; the confirmed mechanism is the missing bound itself.

verdict.summary: NULL pointer dereference in the gzip-header EXTRA handler of inflate(): line 144 dereferences state->head (state->head->extra_len) before the NULL checks at lines 145-147 execute. A gzip stream with the FEXTRA flag (FLG=0x04) and a non-zero XLEN crashes inflate() when the application has not supplied a header buffer (state->head == Z_NULL), enabling denial of service on decompression of attacker-controlled input.

evidence.reason: CWE-476 NULL pointer dereference. state->head is a pointer field of the inflate_state struct obtained at line 28; no shown statement initializes it to non-NULL or constrains it, and the fragment itself treats Z_NULL as an anticipated value (null tests at lines 52, 98, 107, 116, 129, 135, 169, 180, 191, 202, 216). Line 144 dereferences state->head unconditionally whenever the attacker-controlled FEXTRA flag (line 126, state->flags & 0x0400) and a non-zero XLEN (line 128, state->length) yield copy >= 1 (lines 141-143); the NULL checks at lines 145-147 execute only after the dereference and cannot protect it. Witness: gzip header 1f 8b 08 04 00000000 00 00 0100 00 with state->head == Z_NULL and wrap bit 2 set — guards at 43, 88, 93, 126, 143 all admit (CM=8, FLG=0x04 with reserved bits clear, XLEN=1, copy=1), and line 144 loads through a NULL state->head, crashing the process.

assumptions: GUNZIP is defined so the gzip header case group (lines 42-223) is active; it is the zlib default build configuration.

NEEDBITS/PULLBYTE/INITBITS/DROPBITS/BITS/LOAD/RESTORE are standard zlib macros not shown in the fragment; their name-implied semantics (bit accumulation into hold; goto inf_leave on input exhaustion) are used.
state->wrap bit 2 must be set by the application (gzip decoding) to reach the gzip header path per line 43.
state->head is Z_NULL by default when the application does not call inflateGetHeader; the fragment provides no initialization or invariant establishing non-NULL.
limitations: state->lens[] writes at lines 334/338/362/397 cannot exceed index 315 from the visible guards (ncode <= 19 via line 332; nlen <= 286 and ndist <= 30 via line 321; have + copy <= nlen + ndist via line 391); the exact declared lens[] capacity is not shown, but no out-of-domain index is derivable, so no OOB finding is confirmed.

The MATCH window copy at lines 571-576 relies on wnext/wsize/whave invariants maintained by updatewindow() (not shown) and is defended by the sane check at line 552; a window out-of-bounds cannot be confirmed from the fragment.

The zmemcpy at lines 148-150 is fully bounded when state->head is non-NULL (line 147 requires len < extra_max; length is capped at extra_max - len; len and copy are each <= 65535 from the 16-bit XLEN at lines 128/130, so len + copy <= ~131070 and the unsigned comparison at line 149 cannot wrap).
NAME/COMMENT writes at lines 172/194 are guarded by state->length < name_max/comm_max; whether a caller can configure those limits larger than the supplied buffers is outside the fragment.
1U << len at line 77 is safe because line 72 rejects len > 15, capping the shift at 1U << 15.

No error/status-handling flaw is confirmed: inflate_table returns (lines 342/417/426) are checked at 344/419/428 and updatewindow at 660; NEEDBITS input exhaustion routes through inf_leave by implied macro semantics.
The switch default at lines 646-647 returns Z_STREAM_ERROR only for an illegal state->mode value, which is not directly attacker-controlled in the fragment.
zlib's documented behavior requires the caller to pre-size gzip header buffers via inflateGetHeader; caller-capacity mismatches are outside this fragment.

verdict.summary: NULL pointer dereference: constant-pool lookups keyed by attacker-controlled inner_name_idx/inner_class_info_idx can return NULL; the guard branches only print (lines 44-46, 50-52) and execution continues, passing NULL as the object argument to r_bin_java_get_item_name_from_bin_cp_list at lines 47 and 53, which dereferences it to read the item name.

evidence.reason: obj is the unchecked lookup result from line 43, keyed by icattr->inner_name_idx (attacker-controlled USHORT from buffer, line 35, residual range 0..65535 with no constant-pool validation). The guard at lines 44-46 admits obj == NULL but only calls eprintf and falls through, so NULL reaches the call at line 47 and is passed to r_bin_java_get_item_name_from_bin_cp_list, whose name-implied semantics dereference the object to fetch its name: NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476). No shown statement excludes NULL between the guard and the sink; witness: inner_name_idx not present in the CP list.

Reached when the line-47 lookup yields NULL (line 48) and the fallback lookup at line 49, keyed by attacker-controlled icattr->inner_class_info_idx (line 31, residual 0..65535), also returns NULL: the guard at lines 50-52 admits obj == NULL but only prints, and line 53 unconditionally passes NULL to r_bin_java_get_item_name_from_bin_cp_list, dereferencing it to read the name: NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476), distinct sink from line 47.

assumptions: buffer has size sz (the buffer/size pairing used consistently by the guards at lines 9 and 23 and by the reads at lines 18, 31, 33, 35, 37).
R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT(buffer, offset) reads exactly 2 bytes starting at buffer+offset.
R_BIN_JAVA_GLOBAL_BIN is a valid global CP-list handle for the lookup helpers.
r_bin_java_get_item_name_from_bin_cp_list dereferences its object argument to read the item name (name-implied callee semantics; callee body not shown).
limitations: IFDBG log sink (line 62) writes attacker-controlled name content with %s (possible log/content injection), but is debug-gated and demoted.
NULL returns from r_list_newf (line 20)/R_NEW0 (line 27) would make r_list_append (line 63) crash on a single allocation failure; not attacker-scaled, so robustness only.
attr->size = offset (line 65) under-reports consumed bytes after an early break (lines 25/58); no security-relevant consumer is shown in the fragment.

Overflow of buf_offset + offset + 8 (lines 9, 23) would require buf_offset near UINT64_MAX; not derivable from the fragment (no OOB read on buffer is otherwise demonstrable because the guards enforce offset + 8 <= sz before each guarded read).
Resource exhaustion via number_of_classes up to 65535 is bounded by the shown buffer-size guard and loop bound; not reported as a distinct finding.

verdict.summary: Stack buffer overflow in spell_suggest(): the second vim_strncpy (lines 135-137) writes into wcopy[MAXWLEN+2] (declared at line 5) at offset stp->st_wordlen with length sug.su_badlen - stp->st_orglen. None of the fields from spell_find_suggest() are bounded anywhere in the fragment, and the only guard (line 134, su_badlen > st_orglen) fixes only the sign of the length, not the total span. A witness such as st_wordlen = MAXWLEN, st_orglen = 0, su_badlen = 2 passes every guard and writes the terminating NUL one byte past the buffer (index MAXWLEN+2 vs last valid MAXWLEN+1), a confirmed 1-byte stack out-of-bounds write.

evidence.reason: Sink writes into wcopy whose capacity is MAXWLEN+2 (declared at line 5, valid indices 0..MAXWLEN+1). The destination offset stp->st_wordlen and length sug.su_badlen - stp->st_orglen come from the spell_find_suggest() output (lines 88-89) with no bounding statement between the call and this sink; their residual ranges are the full int domains. The guard at line 134 (sug.su_badlen > stp->st_orglen) admits only positive lengths but imposes no cap on st_wordlen or on st_wordlen + (su_badlen - st_orglen). Witness (all magnitudes derived from the visible constant MAXWLEN): st_wordlen = MAXWLEN, st_orglen = 0, su_badlen = 2 passes line 134 (2 > 0), and vim_strncpy writes its terminating NUL at wcopy[MAXWLEN+2], one byte past the last valid index MAXWLEN+1 - a confirmed CWE-787 stack out-of-bounds write.

assumptions: MAXWLEN is a compile-time positive constant visible at line 5 where the only capacity for wcopy is declared (wcopy[MAXWLEN + 2]).
vim_strncpy copies at most n bytes and then writes a terminating NUL, needing n+1 destination bytes (name-implied strncpy-family semantics).
sug.su_ga.ga_len counts the elements stored in sug.su_ga, and SUG(sug.su_ga, i) (line 129) yields the i-th suggest_T element, so stp->st_wordlen/st_orglen/... are struct fields read from that array.
limitations: Candidate 2 (heap write mismatch at lines 215-221): alloc(STRLEN(line) - stp->st_orglen + stp->st_wordlen + 1) can wrap in size_t when st_orglen > STRLEN(line) (no shown bound); on 64-bit targets the wrapped size stays enormous so alloc fails and the p != NULL guard at line 216 prevents writes, and the STRCPY/STRCAT overflow case requires an arbitrary line length/offset not derivable from any shown statement - range claim only, not reported as evidence.

The visual-selection badlen computation (lines 40-45) casts colnr_T columns to int and may truncate very large columns; it feeds spell_find_suggest whose internal use is not shown, so it is not independently confirmable here.

%.*s precision arguments derived from sug.su_badlen / stp->st_orglen (lines 111-112, 151-152, 202-204) are precision-bounded reads that stop at the NUL inside the copied line buffer; no overrun is demonstrated.

No use-after-free or missing-status-handling flaw was confirmed inside the fragment: vim_strsave is NULL-checked (79-80), alloc at line 216 is NULL-checked, u_save_cursor() is compared to OK (190), and prompt_for_number's result is range-guarded (190).
sug.su_badptr is assumed by the engine to point into the copied line; the primary finding does not depend on that, and no separate OOB-read finding was confirmed from it.

verdict.summary: r_bin_java_inner_classes_attr_new dereferences a CP-list lookup result that its own guards admit can be NULL: lines 40-42 and 46-48 only log when obj is NULL, then lines 43 and 49 pass that possibly-NULL obj to r_bin_java_get_item_name_from_bin_cp_list, whose name-implied semantics read fields of obj (CWE-476, NULL dereference on malformed class input). Independently, the first attribute read at line 14 consumes 2 bytes at offset 6 with no check against sz; the only size guard (line 19, `offset + 8 > sz`) executes inside the loop after that read, so an input with sz < 8 reads past the buffer end (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: obj is the return of r_bin_java_get_item_from_bin_cp_list (line 39), whose residual range includes NULL: the fragment's own branch at lines 40-42 (`if (obj == NULL) eprintf(...)`) admits NULL but neither returns nor skips the use. The value (possibly NULL, from an attacker-chosen ushort inner_name_idx against the parsed constant pool) is passed to a name getter that must dereference the object to produce its name (name-implied callee semantics), making line 43 an unchecked dereference of an admitted NULL lookup result: CWE-476.

Second instance of the same defect: obj is the return of the lookup at line 45; when the lookup fails, the branch at lines 46-48 admits NULL but only calls eprintf, and the NULL value still flows into r_bin_java_get_item_name_from_bin_cp_list at line 49, which reads the object's fields (name-implied semantics). The downstream NULL checks at lines 44/50 execute only after these dereferencing calls, so they cannot protect this sink: CWE-476.

R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT reads 2 bytes at buffer[offset..offset+1] with offset == 6 (line 8 `offset += 6;` from the ut64 initialized at line 6). sz is an unconstrained entry-point input (ut64, full domain [0, 2^64-1]); no statement before line 14 bounds it. The fragment's own capacity contract for buffer is sz, evidenced by the guard at line 19 (`if (offset + 8 > sz) break;`), but that guard executes after line 14, inside the loop that starts at line 17, so it cannot protect this read. Witness: sz = 6 with a 6-byte buffer (attr non-NULL per the guard at line 9) reaches line 14, which reads indices 6 and 7, both past the buffer end; with sz = 7, index 7 is out of bounds. The missing bound is the 2-byte over-read: CWE-125.

assumptions: R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT reads 2 big-endian bytes at buffer[offset] and buffer[offset+1] (standard radare2 macro semantics).
sz is the byte capacity of buffer, exactly as the fragment itself uses it in the guard at line 19 (`if (offset + 8 > sz)`), which admits loop reads only when offset+8 <= sz.

r_bin_java_get_item_name_from_bin_cp_list consumes its obj argument (must read object fields to produce the name), so a NULL argument is out of its required domain (name-implied callee semantics; callee body not shown).

The most protective reading of r_bin_java_default_attr_new is that it needs the 6-byte header (returns non-NULL for sz >= 6); even under that strongest reading, sz in {6,7} still reaches line 14 with an out-of-bounds read.
limitations: The NULL-dereference verdict depends on name-implied callee behavior; if r_bin_java_get_item_name_from_bin_cp_list internally NULL-checks its argument, that specific crash is neutralized — but no shown statement excludes NULL from lines 43/49.

Path at lines 51-53 (`icattr->name = r_str_dup (NULL, "NULL"); ... free (icattr); break;`) leaks flags_str (line 35) and the duplicated name because the entry is freed without being appended; each call loses at most 65535 small allocations, so it is a bounded leak, not a confirmed security finding.
The return of r_list_newf (line 16) is not NULL-checked before r_list_append (line 59), but the failure is an allocation failure not scaled by attacker input, so it is a robustness concern.
IFDBG eprintf at line 58 logs attacker-influenced name bytes (potential log injection) but is compile-time debug-only, so it was not promoted to a finding.

curpos = buf_offset + offset (line 18) could wrap in ut64 for pathological buf_offset, but the result is only stored into icattr->file_offset metadata with no security-relevant consumer, so it is not a finding.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown fragment. The allocation size `size = bytes_per_line * hh` (line 92) is validated by the exact-division overflow check `size / bytes_per_line != hh` (line 93), which admits only the exact non-wrapped product and rejects every wrapped outcome before `g_malloc(size)` (line 95). The `%s` writes into `name_and_type[MAX_SIZE]` (lines 33/62/64/66/68/70) are bounded by `fgets(line, MAX_SIZE, ...)` (line 30) plus the length guard `strlen(line) == MAX_SIZE-1` (line 31), which leaves admitted tokens of at most `MAX_SIZE-2` characters, i.e. at most `MAX_SIZE-1` bytes written into a `MAX_SIZE`-byte buffer (line 11). The two-byte pixel loop (lines 101-107) is only entered when `version10p == 1`; for that branch the padding logic (lines 86-91) forces an even `bytes_per_line`, hence an even `size`, so the loop performs at most `size/2` iterations and writes at most `2 * (size/2) = size` bytes into the `size`-byte allocation; the one-byte loop (lines 112-115) writes exactly `size` bytes. All candidate memory-safety and logic findings fail the reachability or taint tests.

assumptions: `MAX_SIZE` is the declared capacity of both `line` (line 9) and `name_and_type` (line 11); `fgets(line, MAX_SIZE, fstream)` therefore stores at most `MAX_SIZE-1` characters plus a terminating NUL.
`guint` is treated as an unsigned 32-bit integer of the same width as `int`, so after the `value <= 0` guards (lines 41-42, 46-47) `ww` and `hh` hold values in [1, INT_MAX].

Standard two's-complement wrap-around is assumed so that the division at line 93 is able to detect a wrapped product from line 92; every wrapped outcome returns before any downstream use, so no corrupted value reaches a sink.
The fragment's `g_malloc` is GLib's allocation routine; its OOM behavior is not shown in the fragment, so nothing about a NULL return or abort is relied on for any verdict.
limitations: Demoted — odd-size one-byte heap overwrite in the version10p loop: the only odd values of `size` occur on the `version10p == 0` path (e.g., `ww=1`, `hh=3` gives `bytes_per_line=1`, `size=3`), but that path executes the one-byte loop (lines 112-115) which writes exactly `size` bytes. The two-byte loop (lines 101-107) requires `version10p == 1`; for that branch `bytes_per_line = (ww+7)/8 + padding` is always even (padding=1 when `ww%16` is in 1..8 gives an odd `(ww+7)/8` plus 1; padding=0 when `ww%16` is 0 or 9..15 gives an even `(ww+7)/8`), so `size` is always even and total writes are exactly `2*(size/2) = size`.

Demoted — `%s` token overflow into `name_and_type`: admitted lines satisfy `strlen(line) <= MAX_SIZE-2` (line 31 rejects `== MAX_SIZE-1`, and `fgets` caps at `MAX_SIZE-1`), so any token is at most `MAX_SIZE-2` characters and `sscanf` writes at most `MAX_SIZE-1` bytes into the `MAX_SIZE` array (line 11); no excess.

Robustness only — `g_malloc(size)` (line 95) is unchecked and `size` (bounded to `<= INT_MAX` by lines 92-94) is attacker-scalable, so a very large declared bitmap could exhaust memory or trip GLib's OOM abort; the failure behavior of `g_malloc` is not visible in the fragment, so no CWE is assigned.
Hotspot values (lines 50-58) are not range-checked, but `hx`/`hy` only flow out through output parameters (lines 127-130) and no security-relevant sink consumes them inside the fragment.

The multiplication at line 92 is formally signed-overflow UB before line 93's check, but the check is the visible protective statement, and all wrapped outcomes return; no wrapped value is consumed by a security-relevant operation.

verdict.summary: Guest-controlled RTAS args.nargs (read from guest memory at line 16) is used with no bounds check as an array index at line 28: args.rets = &args.args[be32_to_cpu(args.nargs)]. verdict.summary: The gzip FEXTRA length is read from the stream into state->head->extra_len (line 130, range [0,65535]) and copied into the caller-provided extra buffer without any bound against state->head->extra_max. When extra_len exceeds extra_max (e.g., 300 vs 2, with chunked input per line 157), len = extra_len - state->length (line 146) exceeds extra_max, and the length expression at lines 148-149 computes extra_max - len as an unsigned underflow (~4294967294), so the zmemcpy at line 147 writes ~4 GiB from attacker bytes to extra + len, which is already past the buffer: a confirmed heap out-of-bounds write (CVE-2022-37434 class).
