verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability: the u64 arithmetic (line 4 cast and u64 declaration at line 3) keeps elem_size exact, the line-7 product is computed in u64 and cannot 32-bit-truncate, the allocate/freelist-init returns are fully checked (lines 9-10, 13-14), and the populate footprint (lines 16-17) equals the allocation size (line 7). The only potential excess is a u64 wrap of elem_size * max_entries, which requires sizeof(struct stack_map_bucket) >= 3; that magnitude is not derivable from the fragment, so no witness can be confirmed.

assumptions: smap->map.value_size and smap->map.max_entries are treated as u32 (full domains [0, 2^32-1]); their declarations are not visible in the fragment, and the explicit (u64) cast at line 4 is consistent with a <=32-bit type.
sizeof(struct stack_map_bucket) is a positive constant C >= 1; its value is not visible in the fragment, so no magnitude larger than 1 is assumed for it.

bpf_map_area_alloc / pcpu_freelist_init / pcpu_freelist_populate bodies are not shown; their semantics are taken from their names and standard kernel usage (allocation with a size argument; populate writing 'elements' nodes at stride 'size').
smap->map.numa_node is used only as a NUMA hint and has no security-relevant consumer.
limitations: Integer-overflow candidate demoted with no CWE: u64 wrap of 'elem_size * smap->map.max_entries' (line 7) occurs only when sizeof(struct stack_map_bucket) >= 3, a magnitude not established by any shown statement; with C <= 2 the maximum admitted in-domain product fits u64, and the pcpu_freelist_populate span (lines 16-17) then equals the allocation size; the OOB consequence additionally depends on bpf_map_area_alloc succeeding on the wrapped size.
NULL-dereference of smap demoted as a robustness concern: the fragment shows no statement that can produce a NULL smap, so the NULL cannot be produced on any shown path.
A possible u64-to-u32 narrowing of elem_size at the pcpu_freelist_populate call (line 16) cannot be confirmed because the callee's parameter types are not shown.
The fragment imposes no in-fragment validation on value_size/max_entries; caller-side map-create checks (not shown) cannot be used to justify either a safe or unsafe verdict.
No other vulnerability classes apply: the fragment contains no string/format/exec/SQL/XPath/log/crypto/file or path sinks.

verdict.summary: The fragment is the patched counterpart of the tc_new_tfilter concurrent-flush race: the create path is gated by the explicit statement 'if (chain->flushing) { err = -EAGAIN; goto errout_locked; }' (lines 119-122), which executes while chain->filter_chain_lock is still held (acquired line 107, released line 142) and therefore before the dangerous tcf_proto_create(name, protocol, prio, chain, rtnl_held, extack) call (lines 143-144); the EAGAIN value is drained by the replay loop (lines 218-225) only after cleanup, so no create or tp use can run against a flushing chain. All other input-derived cardinalities are constrained before use: chain_index is bounded by TC_ACT_EXT_VAL_MASK (lines 94-99) before tcf_chain_get (line 100), the classifier kind is length-checked to IFNAMSIZ (lines 65-69) before name is consumed, and missing kind/protocol and missing NLM_F_CREATE are rejected before creation (lines 126-136). No confirmed vulnerability.

assumptions: tca is declared with TCA_MAX + 1 slots (line 5) and nlmsg_parse_deprecated caps the maximum attribute type at TCA_MAX (line 31), so all later tca[TCA_CHAIN]/tca[TCA_KIND] indices are in-array.
t = nlmsg_data(n) (line 36) is reached only after nlmsg_parse_deprecated returns >= 0 (lines 33-34), placing the tcmsg body inside the validated message.

chain->filter_chain_lock is held from line 107 through the tp == NULL branch (unlock at line 142), so the flushing check at line 119 and the create at line 143 are ordered under the same lock that a concurrent flush uses to set chain->flushing.
TC_H_MIN/TC_H_MAJ (lines 37-38) extract 16-bit fields from the u32 tcm_info, so protocol and prio cannot widen or narrow in the shown code.
limitations: Demoted: char name[IFNAMSIZ] (line 6) has no visible initializer and its only writer is the not-shown tcf_proto_check_kind() out-parameter (line 65); whether it writes name when tca[TCA_KIND] == NULL is not derivable from the fragment, so the potential uninitialized read in tcf_proto_is_unlocked(name) (line 77) cannot be confirmed and gets no CWE.

Demoted: the attribute-length/type invariants for tca[TCA_CHAIN] (and other attrs) fed to nla_get_u32 (line 94) live in the not-shown rtm_tca_policy (line 32); under the fragment-only rule neither a safety bound nor a confirmed OOB is derivable.

Demoted: refcount/list semantics of tcf_chain_tp_find, tcf_proto_create, tcf_chain_tp_insert_unique, tcf_chain_tp_delete_empty, tcf_proto_put (lines 108, 143, 151, 205, 209) and the classifier ops->get/change argument handling (lines 167, 192) are callee-internal and not shown; no confirmed finding is derivable from the fragment.

Demoted: the replay loop (lines 218-225) repeats while err == -EAGAIN, which depends on the transient kernel-internal flushing state; no attacker-controlled progress variable is stalled by the shown code, so non-termination is not confirmed.

verdict.summary: The fragment is the patched tipc_crypto_key_rcv: the keylen read at line 16 is protected by the minimum-size guard at line 11, and both memcpy sinks (lines 41-43) are exact-fit for the entire admitted set because line 19 enforces size == keylen + sizeof(struct tipc_aead_key) and line 20 caps keylen at TIPC_AEAD_KEY_SIZE_MAX. No witness passes every guard and fails a sink; no vulnerability is confirmed in the shown code.

assumptions: data (line 7) references a packet data region of size bytes: the comment at line 10 and the min-size guard at line 11 rely on size as the data-region length, and the source of the line 43 memcpy ends exactly at offset size.
struct tipc_aead_key is laid out as alg_name[TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME], a 4-byte keylen field, and a trailing flexible key[] array, as implied by the fragment's own offsets at lines 16 and 42.
skey->key is a flexible array member, so its offset equals sizeof(struct tipc_aead_key) and its capacity equals size - sizeof(struct tipc_aead_key), which the line 19 equality makes exactly keylen.
TIPC_AEAD_KEYLEN_MIN is non-negative, so the line 11 floor implies size >= sizeof(struct tipc_aead_key) >= TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME + 4, covering the line 16 keylen read.
msg_data_sz returns a u16 value, so size has the full declared domain 0..65535 as its starting residual range.
limitations: The bodies of msg_data_sz / msg_key_gen / msg_data are not shown; if a malformed message could make msg_data_sz report a value larger than the actual packet data length, the fragment's bounds would not help, but that requires a caller/framing invariant (skb-length validation) outside the fragment and is not confirmable here.

The numeric values of TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME, TIPC_AEAD_KEYLEN_MIN, and TIPC_AEAD_KEY_SIZE_MAX are not shown; the exact-fit reasoning depends only on keylen being capped and on the exact equality, not on their specific values.
tx->wq is dereferenced at line 56 without a NULL check on tipc_net(rx->net)->crypto_tx (line 3); no attacker-directed NULL producer is visible, so this is treated as a robustness concern.

skey->keylen stores the host-order keylen into the __be32 member at line 40 and is read back raw as the line 43 memcpy length; the value is identical (<= TIPC_AEAD_KEY_SIZE_MAX) so no in-fragment effect, and downstream byte-order handling is outside the fragment.
An unchecked-environment-failure NULL (e.g., kmalloc failing at line 33) is handled at line 34 and does not reach a security-relevant operation.

verdict.summary: Not vulnerable. The Opt_name path bounds param->size to [1, MAX_CGROUP_ROOT_NAMELEN - 1] via the guards at lines 65 and 67 before the validation loop at line 70 consumes it as its iteration bound; the loop uses strict inequality (max index param->size - 1, well within the value's own size), so no input-derived value reaches a read, store, or log sink with an unconstrained residual range. Demoted concerns (OOB read dependent on an unshown buffer invariant, log injection via param->key, functional always-reject of names) are recorded in limitations.

assumptions: MAX_CGROUP_ROOT_NAMELEN is a positive compile-time constant; the guard at line 67 defines the admitted set param->size <= MAX_CGROUP_ROOT_NAMELEN - 1 on the Opt_name path.
for_each_subsys(ss, i) yields only in-range subsystem indices (macro contract, not visible in fragment), so (1 << i) at line 25 and the strcmp at line 20 use kernel-bounded i.
fs_parse (line 8) returns one of the Opt_* constants for opt >= 0, all of which are handled by the switch at line 33; no unmatched positive value is security-relevant.
limitations: The in-bounds property of the reads param->string[i] (lines 70-71) relies on the fs_parameter contract that param->string points to a buffer of at least param->size bytes; that contract is not visible in the fragment, so an OOB-read claim cannot be anchored to a shown statement (it would require an unshown buffer smaller than param->size).

Under the convention where param->size includes the terminating NUL, the whitelist loop reads the NUL at index param->size - 1 and rejects every name (line 76) - a functional regression for named v1 mounts, not a security finding (the failure only affects the caller's own mount attempt).

param->key is unconstrained and is passed as a %s argument to invalfc at lines 23-24 and 28; a key containing CR/LF would be written verbatim to the kernel log (CWE-117 candidate), but no sanitization or consumer is shown and this is judged an environment-dependent concern, not the fragment's demonstrated defect.
ctx->release_agent (line 57) and fc->source (line 15) are stored without a visible length/content cap; any downstream copy occurs outside the fragment, so no sink can be confirmed here.
cgroup_fc2context(fc) at line 3 is dereferenced without a NULL check; fc is a framework-provided context and the failure is not attacker-directed, so this is a robustness concern only.

verdict.summary: On builds with uECC_VLI_NATIVE_LITTLE_ENDIAN, uECC_sign_with_k passes its bcopy() arguments in reverse order (bcopy is src-first). Line 52 writes BITS_TO_BYTES(curve->num_n_bits) bytes of the blinding value from tmp into the caller's const private_key buffer, destroying the secret key, and tmp is never loaded with d so the signature math at line 59 uses the wrong value. Line 68 then copies from signature+num_bytes into s instead of storing s into the output, so the s component is never written. The function returns 1 at line 72 with a corrupted key and an invalid signature.

evidence.reason: bcopy(src, dst, n) copies from the first argument to the second, so this unconditional write deposits BITS_TO_BYTES(curve->num_n_bits) bytes of tmp (blinding value {1,0,...} from lines 35-36 or RNG output from line 37) into the private_key buffer declared const at line 1. private_key is an internal-helper pointer with no NULL, capacity, or writability check anywhere before this sink; the parallel branch at line 54 ('/* tmp = d */') shows the intended direction is private_key -> tmp. The write corrupts the caller's secret key in-domain for size but out-of-domain as a destination (CWE-787), and because tmp is never loaded with d, line 59 computes s with the wrong value and line 72 still returns 1 with an invalid signature.

Same argument-order inversion: bcopy(src, dst, n) copies curve->num_bytes bytes from signature+num_bytes into local s, so the s component of the signature buffer (which on this path holds the y-coordinate bytes left by EccPoint_mult through the p alias at lines 12/27) is never overwritten with the computed s. The emitted signature is therefore [r || garbage], yet the function returns 1 at line 72. Same root cause (CWE-787-family wrong-destination write) as the line 52 sink.

assumptions: Standard libc semantics for bcopy: void bcopy(const void *src, void *dst, size_t n), where the first argument is the source (POSIX/BSD).
The branch guarded by #if uECC_VLI_NATIVE_LITTLE_ENDIAN (lines 11-15, 51-55, 67-71) is compiled into the analyzed build; it is part of the shown code.
BITS_TO_BYTES(curve->num_n_bits) is the length used for both the private-key transfer (lines 52/54) and is a per-curve constant.
limitations: The capacities of the private_key and signature caller buffers are not visible in the fragment, so no specific byte excess over a buffer capacity is claimed for the line 52 or line 68 writes; the confirmed defects are the wrong-direction copies into out-of-domain destinations and the resulting invalid signature reported as success.
s[num_n_words - 1] (line 57) would underflow only for a degenerate curve with num_n_bits == 0, which no shown statement derives; rejected under the degenerate-input rule (no CWE).
The discarded return of uECC_vli_modInv (line 44) is an error-handling concern, but no shown statement can produce a non-invertible k' (tmp is 1 or n-bounded), so CWE-754 is unconfirmed.
hash_size passed to bits2int (line 61) is unchecked, but the callee's clamp/read semantics and the message_hash capacity are not shown, so the OOB-read claim is unconfirmable.

EccPoint_mult via the p alias (lines 12/27) and uECC_vli_set(s, p, num_words) (line 58) cannot be proven out-of-bounds because UECC_MAX_WORDS and the curve field relationships are not visible in the fragment.
The nativeToBytes writes at lines 48/70 rely on a caller-provided signature capacity (2*num_bytes) that is not shown, so no OOB claim is made for them.

verdict.summary: The fragment is the patched form of sys_setrlimit: the guard at L17-18 (resource == RLIMIT_NOFILE && rlim_max > NR_OPEN -> -EPERM) bounds every stored RLIMIT_NOFILE value before the write at L25, and the cur <= max check at L11-12 bounds rlim_cur as well; the resource bound at L7-8 protects the rlim array index at L13. No confirmed vulnerability.

assumptions: current->signal->rlim is an array whose element count is RLIM_NLIMITS, the same named constant used by the guard at L7, so resource in [0, RLIM_NLIMITS-1] indexes it in-bounds at L13.
rlim_cur/rlim_max (rlim_t) are unsigned, so the comparisons at L11, L17, and L41 are unsigned with no negative values.
RLIM_INFINITY equals the maximal unsigned long value, so the equality check at L37 excludes exactly one value.
limitations: Demoted overflow concern: secs_to_cputime(rlim_cur) at L54 can wrap for rlim_cur greater than about 1.84e10 seconds, admitted via the it_prof_secs == 0 branch at L41, but the wrapped cputime is consumed only as a per-process CPU timer expiry at L57, never as an allocation size, index, length, capacity, or security-gating value; no CWE-190 finding.
Demoted status-handling wart: silent success (return 0) when the RLIMIT_CPU update is not applied, acknowledged in the comment at L31-36; no security-relevant operation runs on that failure state.
The fragment contains no loop constructs, so loop-termination analysis is empty.
copy_from_user faults, capability denials, and the LSM hook return are all correctly converted to error returns; no residual error-handling flaw found.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the shown fragment. The name path is protected by visible guards that execute before any use: L63 rejects size 0 and L65 rejects sizes above MAX_CGROUP_ROOT_NAMELEN - 1 before the validation loop (L68) and the store (L79), and L68-74 whitelists the name characters. Every other dangerous-looking operation cannot be demonstrated within the shown code: the `1 << i` mask write at L23 depends on the unshown `for_each_subsys` bound and the unshown width of `ctx->subsys_mask`; `isalnum(c)` on a possibly-negative char depends on unshown `char` signedness and libc behavior; `strcmp`/`invalfc` on `param->key` depends on unshown framework NUL-termination; and the `release_agent`/`source` string stores have no size/length consumer in the fragment. No attacker value can be shown to reach any failing sink.

assumptions: The shown name path enforces, before any use, 1 <= param->size <= MAX_CGROUP_ROOT_NAMELEN - 1 via the checks at L63 (`if (!param->size)`) and L65 (`if (param->size > MAX_CGROUP_ROOT_NAMELEN - 1)`); both checks precede the loop at L68 and the store at L79.

`ctx->name`, `ctx->release_agent`, and `fc->source` are only assigned pointers in the fragment (L13, L55, L79); the fragment contains no copy, length computation, or dereference of these stored strings.

String values reach their use sites by the shown path only after a valid store from `param->string`; framework guarantees about NUL-termination or lifetime of `param->string`/`param->key` are not visible and are not used to justify any positive or negative verdict.
limitations: The mask write `ctx->subsys_mask |= (1 << i);` (L23) is unconfirmable: the iteration range of `for_each_subsys(ss, i)` (L17) and the declared type/width of `ctx->subsys_mask` are not present in the fragment, so neither a concrete out-of-domain `i` nor a truncation can be demonstrated.

The name-length guard at L65 caps the admitted range to [1, MAX_CGROUP_ROOT_NAMELEN - 1], but the numeric value of MAX_CGROUP_ROOT_NAMELEN and the downstream consumer of `ctx->name` (where an oversized name could overflow) are outside the fragment; for every structurally admitted size the check rejects nonconforming values, but no admitted value can be shown to fail a visible sink.

`char c = param->string[i];` at L69 followed by `isalnum(c)` at L70 is undefined for negative `c` only if `char` is signed, which is implementation-defined and not shown; the precise libc behavior and exploitability are not established by the fragment, so this is recorded as a robustness concern rather than a confirmed OOB.

`strcmp(param->key, ...)` (L10, L18) and `invalfc(..., param->key)` (L21, L26) rely on framework-provided NUL-terminated keys; the fragment shows no statement that could produce an unterminated `param->key`, and kernel log output is not treated as a security boundary.

A NULL `param->string` combined with `param->size > 0` is not produced by any statement in the fragment and conflicts with the framework string-value contract; the witness is invalid as a degenerate input.

`release_agent` and `source` are stored without a visible length bound, but the fragment contains no operation that consumes their size or contents, so no sink and no failure can be anchored in the shown code.

verdict.summary: The EVT_TRANSACTION handler trusts skb->len and packet bytes without sufficient bounds checks: the short-packet guard at lines 22-24 uses &&, so a packet with skb->data[0] == NFC_EVT_TRANSACTION_AID_TAG and skb->len < 7 passes; skb->len - 2 then sizes a heap allocation that cannot hold struct nfc_evt_transaction (1 byte for skb->len=3), and memcpy at lines 36-37 writes transaction->aid past that allocation (CWE-787), with additional OOB reads of skb->data at lines 40 and 44. An NFC-proximity attacker can corrupt kernel heap memory.

evidence.reason: Heap OOB write: with the admitted input skb->len=3, data[0]=0x81, data[1]=1, the guard at line 22 (skb->len < NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH + 2 && skb->data[0] != NFC_EVT_TRANSACTION_AID_TAG) is false and passes; line 26 allocates skb->len - 2 = 1 byte; line 33 admits aid_len=1; this memcpy then writes 1 byte into transaction->aid, which lies after the u8 aid_len member and therefore beyond the 1-byte allocation. Primary CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write via an input-derived size/offset).

OOB read of skb->data: for admitted input skb->len=3, data[0]=0x81, data[1]=1, guard A at line 22 passes, aid_len=1 passes line 33, and index aid_len+2 = 3 exceeds the valid range 0..2 of the 3-byte skb. There is no skb->len >= aid_len + 3 check on this path; line 40 is a confirmed CWE-125 read from the same missing-length-validation defect.

OOB read of skb->data: for admitted input skb->len=4, data[0]=0x81, data[1]=1, data[3]=0x82, guard A at line 22 passes, aid_len=1 passes line 33, line 40 reads the in-bounds tag at index 3, and line 44 reads index aid_len+3 = 4, which equals skb->len and is therefore outside the packet buffer. No shown length check guards this index; same missing-bounds defect as the primary finding.

assumptions: NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH is 5 as stated in the specification comment (ETSI 102 622), making the line 22 bound NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH + 2 = 7; the witnesses use skb->len = 3 and 4, which are below it.

struct nfc_evt_transaction contains at least the u8 aid_len field and the aid array sized via sizeof(transaction->aid), so a 1-byte allocation cannot contain the struct head; member order is assumed to be aid_len followed by aid as the code's field usage implies.
devm_kzalloc(dev, 1, GFP_KERNEL) succeeds on the normal path so that the overflow witness executes (an allocation failure would return -ENOMEM at line 27, but that failure is not attacker-directed).
limitations: NULL-dereference of skb or hdev is not reported: no shown statement produces NULL for these framework callback parameters, so per the 'NULL cannot be produced on any shown path' limitation this is robustness hardening, not a demonstrated finding.

skb->len = 0 reads skb->data[0] at line 23 and skb->len = 1/2 makes skb->len - 2 underflow or causes devm_kzalloc(0) to return a non-NULL zero-size pointer; these are additional robustness/DoS concerns of the same guard flaw rather than independently confirmed memory-corruption witnesses.

The params_len check at line 47 uses (skb->len - 2) - sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction); for small skb->len the unsigned arithmetic underflows, so the cap is ineffective; it also executes after the line 36-37 write, so it cannot protect the primary overflow.
memcpy at lines 50-51 (params) requires assuming the value of the already OOB byte read at line 40, so its reachability is not independently demonstrated and it is left out of evidence.
Return-status handling of nfc_se_connectivity/nfc_se_transaction is not analyzed beyond storing r, because the callee bodies are not shown.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read of idxt.offsets: curr_number is an internal-helper parameter with no constraint in the shown code, yet it is used immediately in the subscripts idxt.offsets[curr_number + 1] and idxt.offsets[curr_number] at line 7 (and as the position at line 8), with no visible capacity or bound for the offsets array. The entry_number guard at line 10 executes after the reads and constrains only entry_number, so it cannot protect them; the missing bound on curr_number is the defect (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: curr_number (size_t, residual range [0, SIZE_MAX]) is unconstrained by any statement in the fragment and reaches the array-subscript sink idxt.offsets[curr_number + 1] before any guard: the only potentially related check, `if (entry_number >= indx->total_entries_count)` at line 10, executes after this read and constrains only entry_number = curr_number + entry_offset, not the subscript. No capacity or element count for idxt.offsets is declared or derived in the shown code, so the fragment consumes an input-derived index with no visible bound (missing-bound / unvalidated-size flow); any curr_number with curr_number + 1 >= element_count(idxt.offsets) reads one element past the array -> out-of-bounds read (CWE-125, primary). The same tainted index reaches the mobi_buffer_setpos argument on line 8.

assumptions: char text[INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX + 1] (line 26) is a fixed-size stack buffer whose capacity constant is symbolic; its numeric value is not shown.

uint32_t tagvalues[INDX_TAGVALUES_MAX] (line 112) is guarded by the identical constant in both consuming loop conditions (lines 115 and 124), so its writes are in-bounds for any value of the constant.

ptagx is allocated with tagx->tags_count elements (line 56) and the first tag loop (lines 64-100) writes it at most once per iteration, so ptagx_count <= tags_count; the second loop (line 108) indexes tags (allocated with tag_count at line 101) with i < ptagx_count.
The malloc at line 37 allocates label_length + 1 bytes, exactly matching the strncpy length argument at line 42.
Guard at line 10 bounds entry_number to [0, indx->total_entries_count), but the capacity of indx->entries is not shown and was not inferred from the guard bound.
limitations: NULL-dereference candidates: tagx, ordt, and buf are pointer parameters dereferenced without NULL checks (ordt->ordt2 at line 28, tagx->control_byte_count at line 46, buf->maxlen at line 15). They match the letter of the NULL-deref rule but are demoted as robustness concerns (crash-only impact) and are not the primary mechanism.

Label/text overflow (lines 26-42): label_length is re-derived from mobi_getstring_ordt/mobi_indx_get_label returns with no visible comparison to INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX, so a write past text or an over-read by strncpy is possible only if label_length exceeds INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX; the constant's value and the callees' write semantics are not shown, so the excess cannot be demonstrated by visible arithmetic.

control_bytes[0] read (line 70) and control_bytes++ (line 66): buf->offset is captured at line 45 without a visible check against buf->maxlen, and the allocation size of buf->data and mobi_buffer_seek's clamping semantics are not shown, so an out-of-allocation read cannot be proven.

Asymmetric error handling: on the ordt2 path (lines 28-29) buf->error is not checked after mobi_getstring_ordt, unlike the else path (lines 31-35); the failure behavior depends on unshown callee reads and was not confirmed as a security-relevant state.

Unsigned underflow of entry_length (line 7 when offsets[curr_number + 1] < offsets[curr_number]) and possible size_t wrap of buf->offset + entry_length (lines 16, 20): a wrapped value only shrinks the stored window (line 20) or is rejected by the line-16 guard, so no memory overrun is demonstrable; treated as logic/robustness only.

Malloc-size overflow at lines 56/101 would require tagx->tags_count > SIZE_MAX/sizeof(MOBIPtagx), a magnitude not shown and not constrained; the loop structure keeps all subsequent writes within tags_count elements.

Non-termination of the loop at line 124 depends on mobi_buffer_get_varlen advancing len when the buffer window is exhausted, which is callee behavior not shown; write counts there are capped by INDX_TAGVALUES_MAX.
OOB write to indx->entries[entry_number] (lines 37, 42, 47-48, 101, 131, 141-143) is guarded by line 10 but the array capacity is not shown; no confirmed exceedance of a visible capacity.

verdict.summary: In VREPLACE mode, line 196 `new_line[curwin->w_cursor.col] = NUL;` indexes the heap copy made by `vim_strsave(ml_get_curline())` at line 191 (capacity STRLEN+1 bytes) with the unclamped editor column `curwin->w_cursor.col`. The fragment stores that unconstrained post-change cursor column at lines 133-136 and never compares or clamps it to the new line's length before line 196, so a cursor column beyond the line end performs a 1-byte heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The minimal local fix is to clamp `curwin->w_cursor.col` to `STRLEN(new_line)` immediately before line 196.

evidence.reason: The array index is `curwin->w_cursor.col`, a colnr_T value whose residual range the shown code never constrains: on the VREPLACE paths it is set from the post-change cursor column (lines 81/84), stored back unclamped at lines 133-136, and then used at line 196 with no length comparison or clamp anywhere between. The target `new_line` is allocated at line 191 by `vim_strsave(ml_get_curline())`, giving a heap capacity of exactly STRLEN(new_line)+1 bytes. The only guards on the path (lines 187 and 192) check allocation NULLs, not the index, so their admitted sets do not exclude out-of-range values. Any admitted editor state where the post-change cursor column exceeds STRLEN(new_line) writes one byte past the heap buffer; primary CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write), confirmed as an unvalidated-index flow with a non-empty residual-range intersection.

assumptions: `vim_strsave()` allocates exactly strlen+1 bytes and returns NULL on failure (NULL is checked at lines 187-188 and 192-193).
`ml_get_curline()` returns the NUL-terminated current text line, so `new_line`'s capacity is STRLEN(new_line)+1 bytes (line 191).
`alloc(i+1)` at line 114 returns an i+1-byte buffer or NULL (checked at line 115).
`vim_strsave`, `alloc`, `ins_str`, `vim_free` are the Vim utilities implied by their names and by the NULL handling in the fragment; their internals are outside the fragment.
limitations: The concrete excess (`curwin->w_cursor.col - STRLEN(new_line)`) is not derivable solely from values shown in the fragment; confirmation rests on the residual range of `curwin->w_cursor.col` (full colnr_T domain, unconstrained by the shown code), so this is a range-based finding rather than an exact simulated witness — confidence capped at 0.6.

Demoted: a potential OOB read via `mb_ptr2len(ptr + new_cursor_col)` (line 99) on the first iteration (`new_cursor_col == -1`, line 93) is excluded by the guard `new_cursor_col >= 0` at line 98, which routes that iteration to `++new_cursor_col` (line 101).
Demoted: reads of `ptr[new_cursor_col]` (line 102) are bounded because the NUL-termination break at lines 102-103 fires as soon as the index reaches STRLEN.

Demoted: `ptr[i] = NUL` / `ptr[i] = ' '` (lines 118/120) are in-bounds because `i = (int)curwin->w_virtcol - vcol` (line 113) is non-negative: the loop (line 95) only enters its last iteration with vcol <= virtcol, and `vcol = last_vcol` (line 106) restores that pre-increment value.
Demoted: NULL dereference of `orig_line`, `new_line`, and `ptr` is guarded at lines 187-188, 192-193, and 115.
`amount` is forwarded unvalidated to `set_indent(amount, ...)` (line 55); since `set_indent`'s body is not shown, any allocation/resource impact there is unconfirmed.
Column arithmetic (lines 81, 113, 117) could overflow `int` only at magnitudes near 2^31, which the fragment does not demonstrate.

verdict.summary: NULL-pointer dereference (CWE-476): internal parameters `prefix` (deref at line 33, also lines 30/122-129/134), `uri` (`*uri` at line 30), and `bindingsPtr` (`*bindingsPtr` at lines 130-131) are dereferenced with no NULL check, and NULL lies in each parameter's unconstrained declared domain; no shown statement excludes it, so a NULL value crashes the parser. The integer-overflow guards at lines 69-71/97-99 (admitting only len <= INT_MAX - EXPAND_SPARE) and 77-81/104-108, plus the capacity guard at line 67, fully protect the len-derived allocations and the memcpy at line 119, so the historical overflow class is not a finding here.

evidence.reason: `prefix` is an internal-helper parameter whose full declared domain (including NULL) is left unconstrained by every shown statement; on the path with witness `prefix = NULL, uri = "u"`, line 30 short-circuits (`*uri == '\0'` false), then line 33 evaluates `prefix->name`, dereferencing a NULL `prefix` before the field-level guard `prefix->name &&` can do anything (the guard itself faults on a NULL pointer). No `prefix == NULL` check exists between entry and this dereference. Primary mechanism: NULL dereference (CWE-476), crashing the parser (DoS).

`uri` is dereferenced at line 30, the first executable statement on every call path, with no NULL check anywhere in the fragment; witness `uri = NULL` reaches `*uri` unconstrained (full declared domain retained, no constraining statement shown) and faults. Primary mechanism: NULL dereference (CWE-476).

`bindingsPtr` is dereferenced at lines 130-131 on every successful path (e.g. prefix="p", uri="u" passes misses at lines 56-61), with no NULL check shown; witness `bindingsPtr = NULL` faults at `*bindingsPtr`. Its full declared domain includes NULL because no shown statement constrains it. Primary mechanism: NULL dereference (CWE-476).

assumptions: `uri` is a NUL-terminated string; the loop at line 45 terminates on the NUL at `uri[len]`, bounding reads of `uri` itself.

`EXPAND_SPARE` is a non-negative compile-time constant (value not shown), so `len + EXPAND_SPARE >= len` makes the memcpy at line 119 fit the allocation at lines 83-84/110-111; the guards at 69-71/97-99 admit only `len <= INT_MAX - EXPAND_SPARE`, so `len + EXPAND_SPARE` cannot overflow int.
`b->uriAlloc` reflects the actual allocation of `b->uri`; the shown code maintains it with `b->uriAlloc = len + EXPAND_SPARE` (lines 88, 116).
`xmlNamespace` has 37 elements (36 chars + NUL) so `xmlLen = 36`; `xmlnsNamespace` has 30 elements (29 chars + NUL) so `xmlnsLen = 29`.
limitations: The historical integer-overflow/allocation-size class is neutralized here: guards 69-71/97-99 admit only `len <= INT_MAX - EXPAND_SPARE` and guards 77-81/104-108 bound the size_t product on the relevant platforms, so no admitted `len` overflows `len + EXPAND_SPARE`, and the allocation capacity exceeds `len`; the memcpy (119) and `b->uri[len-1]` (121) are in-bounds.

Overflow of `int len` inside the loop at line 45 would require a URI longer than INT_MAX characters; no concrete witness of that magnitude can be derived from the shown statements (a range claim only), so it is recorded here, not as a confirmed finding.
`EXPAND_SPARE`'s definition is outside the fragment; the memcpy-in-bounds conclusion assumes it is non-negative.
`parser` is a framework handle whose non-NULL-ness is not established by shown statements; a NULL `parser` is an unconfirmable environment concern, not a finding.
The return value of `parser->m_startNamespaceDeclHandler` (lines 134-135) is discarded; a failing handler would be unreported, an error-handling robustness concern, not a confirmed security flaw.
The short-circuits at lines 46 and 50 (`len > xmlLen` / `len > xmlnsLen`) prevent any out-of-bounds read of the static namespace arrays; no finding there.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The fragment is the guarded version of Vim's command-line editor: recursion is capped by the visible depth check (lines 72-77, with ++depth at 40 and --depth at 1008), and every indexed access to ccline.cmdbuff is in-bounds over the shown invariants — the K_RIGHT guard (line 547) excludes cmdpos >= cmdlen before any advance, the K_LEFT guards (lines 569, 579) exclude cmdpos == 0 and index -1, and Ctrl_U's cmdlen -= j (lines 489-490) cannot underflow because every shown mutator keeps 0 <= cmdpos <= cmdlen (lines 698, 707). All input-driven index/length flows into the shown buffer are provably in-domain; the only remaining concerns depend on unshown callee bodies and are recorded in limitations.

assumptions: ccline.cmdbuff is NUL-terminated at index ccline.cmdlen; this is a stated invariant the shown code re-establishes at line 495 ('Truncate at the end, required for multi-byte chars.') and at line 879.

The invariant 0 <= ccline.cmdpos <= ccline.cmdlen is maintained by every shown mutator: ccline.cmdpos = 0 (line 698), ccline.cmdpos = ccline.cmdlen (line 707), K_RIGHT guarded by line 547 before each increment, K_LEFT guarded by line 569 before each decrement.
The recursion counter depth changes only via ++depth (line 40) and --depth (line 1008), so the check at line 72 (depth == 50) caps recursion at exactly 50 levels.
mb_ptr2len and mb_head_off obey standard bounded multibyte semantics (never read past the NUL, never subtract past the character head).
limitations: Callee bodies are not shown for put_on_cmdline (lines 873, 880, 885), cmdline_paste (616, 619, 625), bracketed_paste (835), cmdline_insert_reg (528), cmdline_erase_chars (462), nextwild/ExpandOne, do_cmdkey_command (236), and cmdline_left_right_mouse (641); if any of them violated the 0 <= cmdpos <= cmdlen / NUL-termination invariants, the Ctrl_U path (ccline.cmdlen -= j at 490; ccline.cmdbuff[ccline.cmdlen] = NUL at 495) could underflow or write out of bounds — demoted because no shown statement can derive cmdpos > cmdlen.
IObuff's capacity is not declared in the fragment; IObuff[j] = NUL at line 879 assumes mb_char2bytes returns at most the buffer size minus one (standard Vim contract, not visible here).
vim_strsave return at line 961 is stored without a NULL check; a failure would be an unattacker-directed OOM, so it is a robustness concern, not a finding.
Unsupported-environment livelocks (e.g., safe_vgetc() delivering only K_IGNORE/K_NOP forever at lines 226-230) are input-supply conditions, not defects of the shown logic.

getcmdline_int can recurse through autocommands triggered at lines 153, 912, and 983; the recursion hazard is capped by the depth check at lines 72-77, which is the protective statement for that class.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in TCP octet-count framing: the store at line 42 writes an attacker-chosen digit at pMsg[iMsg] without the iMsg < iMaxLine bound that every other writer in the fragment enforces. iMsg can already equal iMaxLine on entry (stuffing-delimiter path at lines 90-96 keeps the stale iMsg, and the counting path clamps to iMaxLine at line 115), and repeated octet-count digit episodes push the index beyond iMaxLine without any reset, so a remote sender can corrupt the message buffer past any capacity consistent with the fragment's own iMaxLine bound.

evidence.reason: CWE-787 OOB write: c is the entry-point TCP byte admitted by isdigit at line 32 ('0'..'9'), and the index pThis->iMsg has fragment-derived residual [0, iMaxLine] that reaches exactly iMaxLine (write at iMaxLine-1 admitted by the line 102 guard, delimiter path at lines 90-96 leaves iMaxLine untouched; counting path at line 119 with clamp at line 115) and then grows without bound: line 42 executes for every digit with no iMsg < iMaxLine check (contrast line 102-103 and the clamp at line 113-115), up to 10 digits per episode (line 33 admits iOctetsRemain <= 200000000; the 10th digit trips lines 39-40 but line 42 still writes), and the stale iMsg is retained through eAtStrtFram at lines 96/126 with no reset (reset exists only at line 64), so repeated LF+digit cycles write at iMaxLine+10..iMaxLine+19 and beyond. The fragment shows no allocation for pMsg; the visible bound it enforces for every other message write is iMaxLine, which this sink provably exceeds — the missing bound is the defect.

assumptions: iMaxLine is the fragment's de facto message-buffer write cap: enforced at lines 102-103 (iMsg < iMaxLine) and 113-115 (octatesToCopy = iMaxLine - iMsg).
int is at least 32-bit, so iOctetsRemain*10 + (c-'0') at line 34 cannot wrap on the admitted set (max 2,000,000,009 < INT_MAX).
bSuppOctetFram must be true for the octet-counting path, which is the framing feature this code implements.
limitations: Demoted: char c = **buff at line 10 with buffLen == 0 or buff == NULL is an OOB read/NULL deref whose degenerate precondition is not derived by any shown statement and depends on an unshown caller contract.

Demoted: line 121 *buff += (octatesToCopy + octatesToDiscard - 1) would move the pointer backward if the sum were 0, but reachable entries to the counting branch have iOctetsRemain >= 1 and buffLen >= 1 (buffLen == 0 is not derived in the fragment).

Demoted: after the emergency flush, lines 81 and 94 can both submit the same full buffer before iMsg is reset — duplicate-submission logic with no independent memory or injection mechanism in the fragment.
Demoted: no format-string issue; every LogError/DBGPRINTF argument list matches its format, and the %.*s precision at line 80 is bounded by min(i,32) with i <= buffLen.

verdict.summary: The timeseries branch dereferences the boost::optional<BucketUnpacker> parameter with *bucketUnpacker (lines 121 and 133) after only checking that the namespace is a timeseries buckets collection (line 84); no statement engages or validates the optional, so a disengaged optional is in the parameter's residual domain and the dereference triggers a boost assertion/undefined behavior (server abort / DoS).

evidence.reason: bucketUnpacker (declared line 5 as boost::optional<BucketUnpacker>, an internal-helper parameter with no shown constraint) is dereferenced unconditionally. The only guard on the path is line 84 (expCtx->ns.isTimeseriesBucketsCollection()), which constrains only the namespace and has no relation to optional engagement; no has_value()/is_initialized() check appears anywhere in lines 1-161. Residual range therefore includes the disengaged (boost::none) state. Dereferencing a disengaged optional is a precondition violation: boost::optional::operator* asserts (abort) or reads uninitialized storage (UB) — a NULL/absent-value dereference (CWE-476) reachable on the admitted path (timeseries ns, disengaged optional, sampleSize/numRecords such that the line 28 early-return is not taken, e.g. sampleSize=0, numRecords=0).

Second independent dereference of the same unvalidated optional in the timeseries branch: no statement between line 5 and line 133 checks bucketUnpacker's engagement, so the disengaged state admitted by the line 84 guard reaches this second sink and again produces the CWE-476 failure (boost assertion abort or uninitialized-storage access) for the same residual-range reason as the line 121 sink.

assumptions: boost::optional<BucketUnpacker>::operator* has standard semantics: dereferencing a disengaged optional fires a BOOST_ASSERT (abort in normal builds) or is undefined behavior.
gTimeseriesBucketMaxCount is a scalar numeric server parameter; the fragment only uses it inside double arithmetic (lines 28, 114, 127).
Line numbers are taken from the fragment as presented.
limitations: Division-by-zero / NaN ratio (lines 113-115): with numRecords==0 and sampleSize==0, the line 28 guard (sampleSize > kCoefficient * numRecords * gTimeseriesBucketMaxCount) admits the path because 0 > 0.0 is false, and sampleSize / (0.01 * 0 * maxCount) = 0.0/0.0 = NaN is passed to TrialStage as minAdvancedToWorkRatio (lines 135-140). The failure mode inside TrialStage is not shown, so the downstream security impact (plan-choice logic) cannot be confirmed; recorded without a CWE.

The non-timeseries/sharded ratio at line 62 is protected: line 14 executes before it on every reaching path and admits only numRecords > 100 (denominator numRecords*0.05 > 5.0) with sampleSize <= numRecords*0.05 on the same guard, so no division failure or overflow occurs there.

css->getCollectionDescription(opCtx) (line 54) and css->getOwnershipFilter(...) (lines 66-67) dereference CollectionShardingState::get(...) without a null check; a null return would require a framework contract violation not shown and not attacker-directed, so it is not treated as a confirmed finding.

invariant(opCtx->lockState()->isCollectionLockedForMode(coll->ns(), MODE_IS)) (line 10) aborts only on caller contract violation (double-locking / unlocked caller), which is not attacker-controlled per the shown code.

The fragment contains no loops, no buffer/array/copy operations, no injection sinks (format strings, shell, SQL, HTML, logs, URLs), and no crypto/file operations, so no other vulnerability classes are present.
The rsRandCursor null check (lines 35-37) and execStatus isOK() check (lines 152-154) are correctly handled; execStatus.getValue() at line 159 is only reached after the isOK() guard.

A caller-side invariant that bucketUnpacker is always engaged on the timeseries path is not visible in this fragment and, per analysis scope, cannot be used to downgrade the finding; it is noted only as an unconfirmed practical mitigant.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The exact-length guard `if (ticklen + 6 != n)` (line 27) executes before every sink and confines `ticklen` to [0, 65535] with `ticklen == n - 6`, so the `OPENSSL_malloc` size (line 36), `memcpy` length (line 41), and `EVP_Digest` length (line 44) all equal the remaining message bytes and the allocation size; integer overflow is impossible for a 16-bit `ticklen`, and the malloc result is checked before dereference.

assumptions: ss l_get_message (lines 8-11) returns the full received message length `n` and leaves `s->init_msg` pointing at `n` received bytes; this is the libssl message API contract and the capacity the fragment relies on.
n2s (line 25) reads two big-endian bytes, giving `ticklen` a residual range of [0, 65535].
limitations: The protective statement is line 27: its admitted set is {(n, ticklen) : n >= 6, 0 <= ticklen <= 65535, ticklen == n - 6}; all other pairs are rejected before the sinks at lines 36, 41, and 44 (guard line 27 precedes sinks in path order).

The admitted degenerate case `ticklen == 0` / `n == 6` depends on implementation-defined `malloc(0)` behavior, but a NULL result is handled at lines 37-40 without dereference, so it is only a robustness concern.
The body of `ssl_get_message` is not shown; any violation of its length contract would not be demonstrable from the fragment itself.
The unused variable `d` (lines 6 and 23) is a code-quality issue, not a security defect.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in qtm_decompress: on the window-wrap match path (match_offset > window_posn), the decompressor copies match_length bytes to &window[window_posn] with no clamp against qtm->window_size. The only visible clamp (lines 112-113) lives in the mutually exclusive else branch, and the guard at line 98 bounds only the source offset j, not the dest copy extent, so a decoded match length exceeding the remaining window space writes past the window (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: match_length (derived at line 80 from decoded sym/extra with no visible cap) is copied unclamped starting at &window[window_posn] (line 92) on the wrap path admitted by lines 95-98 (j = match_offset - window_posn <= qtm->window_size). The clamp at lines 112-113 is in the exclusive else branch (line 110) and never executes here, so the last dest index window_posn + match_length - 1 exceeds the window capacity qtm->window_size when match_length >= window_size - window_posn + 1, producing a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

assumptions: window capacity is qtm->window_size bytes; the fragment itself treats it as the window bound at lines 98, 112, and 135.
out_bytes is non-negative after the line 12 check (residual range [0, OFF_MAX]).
QTM_FRAME_SIZE is a positive frame constant (referenced at lines 47, 123, 124).
qtm->window_posn and qtm->frame_start are arbitrary in-range values loaded at lines 30-31; P = window_posn with 1 <= P <= W-1 is within the residual range.
limitations: The overflow witness is a residual-range construction: exact magnitudes (qtm->window_size, qtm->position_base/extra_bits/length_base/length_extra entries) are not literal constants in the fragment, so confidence is capped at 0.64; an unshown invariant such as a decoder that caps match_length would dissolve the finding, but no such invariant appears in the shown code.

sym decoded by QTM_GET_SYMBOL is used unchanged as an index into qtm->extra_bits/position_base/length_base/length_extra (lines 65, 66, 72, 73, 79, 80, 83, 84) with no visible array bound; demoted to a range concern (possible OOB table read) because the table capacities are not shown.

The assignment at line 46 narrows an off_t expression into unsigned int frame_end; modulo truncation can only shrink the loop bound, and no security-relevant consumption of the truncated value was derivable.
The literal-write path at line 59 could also exceed the window if frame_end exceeds window_size, but frame/window layout invariants are not shown; the wrap-branch finding stands independently.
The (int) casts of qtm->window_size at lines 98 and 112 assume window_size <= INT_MAX; a larger window_size value is not shown and would alter comparison behavior.

Match decoding macros (QTM_GET_SYMBOL, QTM_READ_BITS) are not shown, so their bounds are not assumed; the absence of any visible constraint on the derived lengths is the basis of the missing-bound finding.

verdict.summary: In the 'code not in table' branch (lines 40-45), code_out is assigned ctx->previous_code with no bound check, and the chain-walk loop (lines 72-74) uses code_out as a table index. ctx->previous_code is a context input with a full uint32_t residual range — no shown statement constrains it (the only assignment, line 67, executes after the use) — so values at or above the table capacity (2^LZW_CODE_MAX per the guard at line 32) reach table + code_out and cause an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: ctx->previous_code (uint32_t; never initialized or bounded by any shown statement — the context write at line 67 executes only after this use) flows to code_out at line 43, then into the table index at lines 73-74. Guards at lines 28 and 32 constrain only code_new, not previous_code. Witness (range claim): current_entry = 10, clear_code = 256, eoi_code = 257, code_new = 10 — admitted by line 28 (10 > 10 false), line 32 (10 >= 4096 false), line 36 (10 < 10 false) so the else branch is taken — previous_code = 100000; line 72 (100000 > 256) is true, so line 73 forms table + 100000 and line 74 reads out of bounds for the 2^LZW_CODE_MAX-entry table implied by the guard at line 32. Primary mechanism: out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

assumptions: LZW_CODE_MAX is a positive compile-time constant used at lines 32, 48, 58, and 61; 1 << LZW_CODE_MAX is the dictionary capacity implied by the shown guard (valid indices 0..(1<<LZW_CODE_MAX)-1).

ctx is an internal-helper/context parameter; its numeric fields (current_entry, clear_code, eoi_code, previous_code, previous_code_first) enter with their full declared domains because no shown statement constrains their initial values.
limitations: The checks at lines 28 and 32 fully bound code_new-indexed table reads (lines 39 and 66) to [0, (1<<LZW_CODE_MAX)-1]; those accesses are properly guarded and are not findings.
The dictionary-add write at table[current_entry] (line 49) is guarded by line 48 (current_entry < (1 << LZW_CODE_MAX)) and is in bounds.
Stack writes (*stack_pos++ at lines 42, 74, 77) have no declared stack_base capacity in the fragment, so a stack overflow could not be confirmed.

Chain non-termination (CWE-835) would depend on table contents populated outside the fragment; for entries written by the shown code the previous_entry chain strictly decreases, and the demonstrated failure is the initial OOB read, not non-termination.
The OOB-magnitude witness (previous_code = 100000) is a range claim over the full uint32_t domain rather than a value derived from a shown constant; confidence is capped accordingly.
If an unseen caller initializes previous_code to a bounded value on every entry, exploitability would change, but no such constraint is present in the fragment.

verdict.summary: The entry-point buffer 'buf' is consumed as a NUL-terminated C string by strcmp (lines 5, 12), by the handler lookup at line 22, and by the '%s' conversion at line 25, while the length parameter 'len' (line 1) is never used to bound the reads or establish termination. A non-NUL-terminated 'buf' therefore causes an out-of-bounds read of at least one byte (unbounded if no NUL follows); at line 25 the over-read bytes are also written back to the socket, enabling memory disclosure.

evidence.reason: CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. 'buf' is the line-1 entry-point parameter (declared length 'unsigned int len', never referenced anywhere in lines 2-33). The only guard on this path, the 'buf == NULL' short-circuit in this same line, admits every non-NULL byte sequence and neither requires nor enforces a NUL terminator within the 'len'-bounded region. With len=4 (member of the unconstrained unsigned int domain) and buf pointing to an exactly 4-byte object holding "help" with no NUL, strcmp here reads buf[4] - one byte past the declared region, unbounded further if no NUL appears.

CWE-125 out-of-bounds read, same mechanism and taint source as the line-5 sink. The path is reached only with buf != NULL (lines 5-10 early-return on NULL), and the guard admits every non-NULL buffer with unconstrained contents. With len=4 and buf = "list" in an exactly 4-byte object with no NUL, strcmp reads buf[4] past the declared region; without a NUL anywhere the read is unbounded.

CWE-125 call-site sink: qh_find_handler receives buf as its handler-name string argument (name-implied string comparison), with buf still in the residual range of non-NUL-terminated byte sequences; no bound derived from 'len' (line 1) is applied before this call, so the internal comparison can read past the end of the len-byte region. This is the missing-bound flow at the call site.

evidence.snippet: nsock_printf_nul(sd, "No handler named '%s' is registered\n", buf);
evidence.reason: CWE-125 out-of-bounds read with disclosure: reached when qh_find_handler returns NULL (line 23, guard satisfied by the witness, e.g., non-terminated "help" + trailing bytes never matching a registered name). The '%s' conversion scans buf to a NUL; with the residual range of buf (no NUL-termination guarantee, no sanitization or termination statement in the fragment, 'len' at line 1 unused) the read runs past the end of the len-byte region and the bytes are written to the connected socket, exposing adjacent memory to the attacker.

assumptions: Line 1's 'unsigned int len' is the byte length of the buffer pointed to by 'buf' - the only visible bound on buf in the fragment, and it is never referenced in the body.
strcmp and printf-family '%s' conversions consume their char* arguments until a NUL byte is found.
The 'qhandlers' list (line 14) is program-registered and NULL-sentinel-terminated; its elements are not derived from attacker input in the shown code.
limitations: The exact number of bytes read past the region cannot be quantified beyond '>= 1' because the backing allocation beyond 'len' is not shown; the finding rests on the missing-bound standard (the declared length 'len' is visible and is never used to bound the reads).
Raw-echo/response-injection via CR/LF in buf at line 25 is a shown write sink, but no downstream consumer with a broken trust boundary is visible in the fragment, so no CWE is assigned.
Line 29 has the same unbounded '%s' read, but reaching it requires 'qh->handler(...) > 200' at line 27, a value from unshown handler code, so a reachable witness cannot be constructed.

Return values of nsock_printf/nsock_printf_nul (lines 6/8, 15, 18, 25, 29) are discarded; a write failure is followed only by 'return 0' or loop continuation, with no security-relevant operation relying on the failed state.
NULL dereference of buf is excluded by line 5's short-circuit 'buf == NULL' check on every subsequent path.
qh->name / qh->description (line 15) come from program-registered handler data; description is NULL-guarded by the ternary, and a NULL name is not producible from the shown code.
The lines 14-16 loop terminates on the qhandlers NULL sentinel; its bounds are framework-controlled, not attacker-derived.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The lookup result qh is NULL-checked at line 23 before the indirect call at line 27, list entries are dereferenced only under the qh != NULL loop condition at line 14, and buf is consumed solely as a %s argument to constant-format nsock_printf_nul calls (lines 25, 29), so no injection, memory-safety, or NULL-deref finding is demonstrable from the shown code.

assumptions: buf is a NUL-terminated C string: the fragment's own use of *buf and strcmp (lines 5, 10, 12) requires this before any sink; no statement in the fragment produces a non-NUL-terminated buf.
qhandlers is a non-cyclic, NULL-terminated global list; no shown statement can create a cycle.
The handler field of registered query_handler entries is a valid non-NULL function pointer; no shown statement can set it to NULL.
limitations: A non-NUL-terminated buf would cause OOB reads inside strcmp/nsock_printf, but no shown producer or invariant can yield that state; it is a caller-side assumption only, so it is demoted with no CWE.

qh->handler(sd, "help", 4) (line 27) dispatches to an attacker-chosen registered handler with constant arguments; no in-fragment failure or security impact is demonstrated for any registered callee, so it is not a finding.
A cyclic qhandlers list could make the line 14 loop non-terminating (CWE-835), but no shown statement can produce such a list.
Discarded nsock_printf* return values (lines 6, 15, 18, 25, 29) are an error-handling robustness concern only; no security-relevant operation runs on the failure state.
The unused len parameter and constant 4 in the handler call are consistent with NUL-terminated strings; no length sink consumes them.
The > 200 threshold (line 27) has no security-relevant consumer of its admitted/excluded boundary, so it is not a confirmed CWE-697.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The only input-derived hazard is len reaching 0 when the first fgets chunk begins with a NUL byte (L37-L40), which would otherwise make buf[len-1] index one byte before the heap allocation. In this fragment that path is fully excluded: L61 'if (len >= 1 && buf[len - 1] == '\n')' excludes len == 0; the CTRL-Z disjunction at L45-L47 short-circuits before buf[len-1] for len <= 0; and L58's 'ga.ga_maxlen - ga.ga_len == 1' cannot hold for len == 0 because the loop-top ga_grow(&ga, 120) (L19-L20) guarantees ga.ga_maxlen - ga.ga_len >= 120. For len >= 1 every index (len-2, len-1, c) is within [0, maxlen-1], the buflines index at L26 is bounded by L24, and the NUL store at L31 is bounded by ga_grow(&ga,1) at L28. This is the fixed form of the function.

assumptions: ga_init2(&ga, 1, 250) (L13) establishes the garray_T contract: ga_len = 0, ga_maxlen = 0, ga_data = NULL, so iteration 1 starts from ga.ga_len = 0.

ga_grow(&ga, 120) (L20) plus the comment at L19 ('make room to read at least 120 (more) characters') guarantee ga.ga_maxlen - ga.ga_len >= 120 at every loop-top entry; ga_grow(&ga, 1) (L28) guarantees at least one free slot before the NUL store at L31.
fgets (L37) writes at most size-1 data bytes plus a NUL (standard contract), bounding each read chunk by ga.ga_maxlen - ga.ga_len - 1.
Entries of sp->buflines are NUL-terminated byte strings (Vim buffer-line invariant, producer outside the fragment), so ga_concat at L26 is length-bounded by the entry content.
sp->buf_lnum is a non-negative counter (no shown statement can make it negative; L27 only increments it).
limitations: If L61 lacked the 'len >= 1' conjunct (the historical vulnerable counterpart), a sourced file whose first fgets chunk begins with a NUL byte would set len = 0 at L40 and reach buf[len-1] = buf[-1] — a deterministic one-byte heap under-read before ga.ga_data (CWE-125). In this fragment that value is excluded at every use site (L45 short-circuit, L58 unsatisfiable equality, L61 guard), so it is not a finding here.

A NULL sp (dereferenced at L16), a NULL buflines entry, or a non-NUL-terminated buflines entry (ga_concat at L26) would crash; their presence depends on caller/data invariants not shown, so they are unconfirmed robustness concerns.

fgets returning NULL on a mid-line I/O error (L38-39) is treated as EOF and the partial line is returned for execution (L112); the triggering failure is not attacker-directed and no security-relevant operation runs on the failure state, so this is only an error-handling robustness note.
A negative initial sp->buf_lnum from the caller would bypass the L24 bound and under-read at L26; no shown derivation exists, unconfirmable.

The (int)STRLEN cast at L40 and the size argument ga.ga_maxlen - ga.ga_len at L37 cannot wrap or go negative within the shown admitted range (len <= ga_maxlen-1 <= INT_MAX-1, ga_maxlen >= ga_len+120).

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. On the path admitted by the SCM_UNBNDP(mode) guard at line 12 (guard precedes and does not constrain mask), the witness mask=0o2000 yields mode 0777 ^ 0o2000 = 0o2777, i.e. the directory is created setgid although the intended umask application gives 0o777. This is incorrect permission assignment to a critical resource (primary CWE-732); the wrong bitwise operator is the root cause, and no protective statement (no ~mask, no mask&0o777, no range check) exists between line 14 and the sink.

assumptions: mode_t is an unsigned integer type whose declared domain includes special permission bits such as 0o2000.

limitations: The real-world trigger requires an OS that retains umask bits outside 0777; on Linux, which masks umask to 0777, 0777 ^ mask equals 0777 & ~mask, but that invariant is outside the fragment and can only limit confidence, not neutralize the finding.

Cross-call integrity of w_tagstackidx under external mutation (autocommands/tagfunc) is not shown; no witness for an out-of-range index is derivable from the fragment alone.

verdict.summary: The internal-helper parameter *count (unsigned int, no constraint anywhere in the fragment) flows into t_malloc((*count + auth_count) * sizeof(*tab)) at line 15, memset(tab, 0, *count * sizeof(*tab)) at line 16, and tab += *count at line 17. The 32-bit addition overflows for *count > UINT_MAX - auth_count (e.g., *count = UINT_MAX, admitted by the declared type with no guard), so the allocation is wrapped to (auth_count-1) elements while memset writes UINT_MAX * sizeof(*tab) bytes (~68.7 GB), and tab advances far past the allocation before the tab[0..33] writes. Confirmed heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) with unsigned integer overflow as the root cause (CWE-190).

evidence.reason: Sink: with *count = UINT_MAX (residual range [0, UINT_MAX], no guard constrains it at lines 1-18), the multiplication promotes to size_t giving 4,294,967,295 * sizeof(*tab) bytes (~68.7 GB) written to a region that line 15 wrapped to (auth_count-1) * sizeof(*tab) bytes because *count + auth_count overflows in unsigned int. The write exceeds the allocation by UINT_MAX * sizeof(*tab) - (auth_count-1) * sizeof(*tab) bytes: confirmed heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), overflow root cause CWE-190.

Sink: the allocation element count is *count + auth_count computed in unsigned int, which wraps mod 2^32 for any *count in (UINT_MAX - auth_count, UINT_MAX] (e.g., UINT_MAX), so t_malloc receives (auth_count-1) * sizeof(*tab) bytes while the consumer at line 16 writes *count * sizeof(*tab) bytes and line 17 advances tab by *count elements. Unvalidated input-derived size flow (CWE-190) whose corrupted value is consumed as an allocation size and then by the overflow write at line 16.

Sink: tab is advanced by the unvalidated *count (UINT_MAX on the witness path), placing the pointer ~68.7 GB past the wrapped allocation from line 15; the subsequent unconditional tab[0]..tab[33] writes at lines 23-107 and the memcpy at lines 20-21 all operate out of bounds (CWE-787), with the same CWE-190 wrap as root cause.

assumptions: N_ELEMENTS(auth_request_var_expand_static_tab) >= 1 (C guarantees a non-empty array), which is sufficient for the *count = UINT_MAX wrap witness; the fragment's own writes tab[0]..tab[33] imply auth_count >= 34.
C usual arithmetic conversions: *count + auth_count is 32-bit unsigned addition; *count * sizeof(*tab) is computed in size_t after promotion.
sizeof(*tab) is a positive nonzero size, so the wrapped allocation is smaller than the memset byte count.
limitations: The exact value of auth_count is not visible in the fragment (N_ELEMENTS of an unshown array), so the precise wrap boundary (UINT_MAX - auth_count + 1) is a range claim; *count = UINT_MAX itself is definitely in the admitted set for any auth_count >= 1.

auth_request->user and other auth_request struct fields are consumed without NULL checks, but the dereferences occur in unshown callees (escape_func/strchr) and the pointer is a plain struct field with no shown NULL producer or lookup extraction, so no confirmed CWE-476.
t_malloc failure was not treated as a finding: it is an environment/allocation failure not attacker-directed in the fragment.

Whether production callers pass large *count values is not shown and was not used to demote the finding: as an internal-helper parameter, the full declared unsigned int domain is the residual range absent a shown constraint.
The individual writes tab[0..33] were not separately verified against auth_count as a capacity because the static table declaration is not in the fragment.

evidence.reason: Sink is the integer division 2147483647/desttypesize. desttypesize is a uint32 parameter (line 2) whose declared domain includes 0 and which the fragment never constrains (line 19 `(void) desttypesize;` is a no-op; the guard at line 14 excludes only target_count64==0 or typesize==0; the guard at line 26 only bounds target_count64*typesize). Primary CWE-369: divide by zero caused by a missing desttypesize==0 validation.

assumptions: uint32 desttypesize has declared domain [0, 2^32-1], including 0, per its declaration at line 2.
uint64 tdir_count/target_count64/maxcount are 64-bit unsigned; int typesize is 32-bit; TIFFDataWidth returns 1 for scalar byte types and 0 for unknown types (line 9, early return at line 14).
tmsize_t is wide enough to represent datasize (≤ 2^31-1) so the casts at lines 33, 47, 65 do not narrow.

Inline memcpy branches (lines 40, 58) read at most 4/8 bytes from the tdir_offset union, matching its shown width; no OOB finding.

Real-world exploitability depends on a caller passing desttypesize==0; no caller is shown in the fragment, and per the analysis rules the unconstrained parameter domain itself is the demonstrated defect (internal-helper parameter).

verdict.summary: krb5_sname_to_principal (lines 30-32) may fail, leaving princ NULL per its line-6 initialization; the failure status is silently overwritten at line 34 with no intervening check, and the possibly-NULL princip is passed to krb5_kt_get_entry (lines 34-38), which dereferences it - a NULL-pointer dereference / discarded-error flaw (CWE-476). The only later status checks (lines 39/42) execute after the sink and test only krb5_kt_get_entry's own return.

evidence.snippet:
krb5rc = krb5_kt_get_entry(krb5context, krb5keytab, 
                                princ,
                                0 /* IGNORE_VNO */,
                                0 /* IGNORE_ENCTYPE */,
                                &entry);
evidence.reason: The princ argument (line 35) is delivered to a keytab lookup that consumes a valid krb5_principal. princ's residual range is {NULL, valid}: line 6 initializes it to NULL, lines 30-32 are its only producer, and the producer's return value stored into krb5rc at line 30 is overwritten at line 34 with no test between lines 30 and 34, so a failed krb5_sname_to_principal leaves princ NULL and the sink is reached unguarded. The guards at lines 19/25 execute before line 30 and test krb5rc from krb5_kt_resolve/krb5_kt_default, not from krb5_sname_to_principal; the guards at lines 39/42 execute after the sink at line 35 and test only krb5_kt_get_entry's own result. Passing NULL to krb5_kt_get_entry is out of the argument domain and is dereferenced inside the lookup: CWE-476 NULL-pointer dereference via an unchecked error condition from a library call in the shown chain.

assumptions: princ is initialized to NULL at line 6, so a failed krb5_sname_to_principal leaves princ with the fragment-visible value NULL.
krb5_kt_get_entry's principal parameter requires a non-NULL krb5_principal (name-implied domain of a keytab entry lookup).
krb5keytab is valid after the line-19/line-25 guards (kb5_kt_resolve/krb5_kt_default failures exit before line 30).
limitations: kssl_ctx itself is dereferenced at line 15 with no NULL check, but no NULL producer exists on any shown path and the caller's contract is outside the fragment; treated as a robustness concern, not a confirmed finding.

KRB5_KT_NOTFOUND is mapped to rc=1 (lines 39-41), the same success value as a found entry (line 46); the semantics of the return to a caller are not shown, so the security impact of this logic quirk is unconfirmable and no CWE is attached.

If krb5_kt_get_entry tolerates a NULL principal and returns an error, lines 39/42 would catch it and the function would fail closed; the confirmed harm therefore depends on the name-implied dereference semantics, which caps confidence at 0.62.

The triggering condition is a range (any non-zero return of krb5_sname_to_principal, e.g., allocation or principal-construction failure), not a single fixed value derived in the fragment; there is no shown input value that deterministically forces the failure, so the witness is a range claim rather than an exact demonstrated value.

verdict.summary: The function dereferences the unchecked KSSL_CTX* parameter at `if (kssl_ctx->keytab_file)` (line 15) with no NULL test anywhere before it, so a NULL kssl_ctx reaches an unconditional dereference (CWE-476, crash/DoS); it also mishandles the krb5_kt_get_entry failure status KRB5_KT_NOTFOUND by setting rc=1 (line 43), reporting the keytab as available although the host key is absent (CWE-754).

evidence.reason: kssl_ctx is a KSSL_CTX* parameter whose full declared domain (including NULL) is never constrained by any statement in the fragment; the only earlier guard, `if ((krb5rc = krb5_init_context(&krb5context)))` (line 10), does not involve kssl_ctx and can pass with kssl_ctx==NULL, so execution reaches this first unconditional dereference (also repeated at line 17 and line 31) and dereferences NULL — confirmed NULL-pointer dereference, CWE-476.

The status returned by krb5_kt_get_entry (line 37), specifically KRB5_KT_NOTFOUND, is admitted by the equality test at line 42 after the keytab and principal were successfully set up (lines 19-20 and 34-35 not taken); this assignment converts that failure status into the same success value as the found case at line 49, and line 55 returns it, so the function reports the keytab as available while the service host key is missing — error/status-handling flaw, CWE-754.

assumptions: kssl_ctx is a KSSL_CTX* function parameter; a pointer type's declared domain includes NULL, and no fragment statement constrains it.
