evidence.reason: Undersized allocation: the size argument derives from file-controlled ldblk (line 202). For admitted SizeX=0x40000001, ldblk=(ssize_t)(4*0x40000001 mod 2^32)=4, so only 32 bytes are allocated for a scanline that the sink at line 314 treats as 0x100000004 bytes wide (columns=SizeX at line 236, depth=32 at line 201). No check in the shown code caps SizeX or ldblk; the comment's 'check phase' corresponds to no visible statement (line 243 checks only for zero). assumptions: 64-bit platform: size_t/ssize_t are 64-bit, unsigned int is 32-bit, and (ssize_t) sign-extends an unsigned int result whose high bit is set.

ImportQuantumPixels reads columns x channels x depth/8 bytes from the supplied source buffer for the imported region (standard import semantics, consistent with the per-scanline usage in lines 295-320).

limitations: Negative ldblk (SizeX >= 2^31 for miINT32) casts to a huge size_t at line 270, so AcquireQuantumMemory returns NULL and the code takes the clean ThrowReaderException at lines 271-272; that path is not memory-unsafe and is therefore demoted.
Resource-limit failure of SetImageExtent (line 265-267) would exit before the sink, but no resource limit is visible in the fragment, so it cannot be used to make the dangerous operation safe.
image->colors = one << image->depth (line 242) with depth=64 is an undefined shift of a 64-bit size_t; no security-relevant in-fragment consumer of the resulting value is shown, so it is demoted.

Frames==0 (line 133) makes --Frames (line 417) become UINT_MAX and loop via NEXT_FRAME; each pass still consumes file bytes and terminates via EOF-derived SizeX==0 at line 243, so non-termination is not confirmed; noted as a potential resource concern only.

The 4-byte ReadBlob into size_t size (lines 167, 178) can leave a partially/incorrectly filled value, but size is not used after line 178, so no security-relevant consumer exists; demoted.

verdict.summary: Not vulnerable. Every dangerous teardown operation is protected by an in-fragment statement: the NULL guard `if (!sp) return;` (lines 9-10) executes before the first `sp->` dereference (line 16) and excludes NULL from all later uses; `del_timer_sync(&sp->tx_t)` / `del_timer_sync(&sp->resync_t)` (lines 25-26) precede `kfree(sp->rbuff)`/`kfree(sp->xbuff)` (lines 31-32), so no timer callback can touch the freed buffers; `netif_stop_queue` (line 23), `unregister_netdev` (line 28) precede `free_netdev` (line 34) in the standard order; and the `refcount_dec_and_test`/`wait_for_completion` branch (lines 16-17) waits only when other users remain, which is the correct completion direction. No NULL, UAF, double-free, ordering, or status-handling defect is confirmable from the shown statements.

assumptions: Line 9 `if (!sp)` with return at line 10 executes before the first `sp->` dereference (line 16) on the only continuation path, so `sp` is non-NULL at every use (lines 16-17, 23, 25-26, 28, 31-32, 34).

`del_timer_sync(&sp->tx_t)` (line 25) and `del_timer_sync(&sp->resync_t)` (line 26) execute before `kfree(sp->rbuff)` and `kfree(sp->xbuff)` (lines 31-32) on the single continuation path, so no timer callback can run against the freed buffers.

The branch at line 16 waits only when `refcount_dec_and_test` returns false (other users remain) and proceeds when it returns true (this closure held the last reference), which is the correct direction for the `sp->dead` completion protocol.

No validation of len exists between line 76 and this write. Mechanism: out-of-bounds write/unsafe index following the CWE-681 truncation.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The inner scan is protected by the bound check `while (*s != NUL && c == mb_ptr2char(s))` (line 22): `mb_ptr2char(s)` is evaluated only while `*s != NUL`, and the only pointer advance `s += clen` (line 25) executes only after that guard admits a non-terminator position, so `s` cannot be advanced from or to a position at/past the NUL by the shown arithmetic, and both loops terminate (each iteration advances at least clen>=1 bytes). The run-shortening path `p = s - 1` (line 35) is reached only when `s > p`, and the outer `++p` then lands at most on the terminator. Remaining concerns (truncated/invalid trailing multibyte decode behavior, unchecked `gap`, `same_len` overflow on >2^31-byte runs) depend on unshown callee semantics or caller contracts and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: `str` is treated as a non-NULL, NUL-terminated C string after the `if (str == NULL)` guard at line 10; the fragment's own guards at lines 16 and 22 (`*p != NUL`, `*s != NUL`) operate inside that model and anchor all reads to the terminator position.

`clen = s - p` (line 21) is the byte length of the character decoded by `mb_cptr2char_adv` at line 20, and by standard multibyte-decode semantics a non-NUL character consumes at least one byte, so `clen >= 1` and every inner-loop advance is strictly positive.
For well-formed multibyte input, equal characters have equal byte length, so `s += clen` (line 25) keeps `s` aligned to character boundaries within the admitted set of line 22.
limitations: Truncated/invalid trailing multibyte sequences (e.g., a lead byte immediately before the NUL) could be decoded by the `mb_cptr2char_adv`/`mb_ptr2char` callees with a byte length extending past the terminator; the fragment shows no such derive, and the overrun would depend on callee-internal decode-length behavior not visible in the shown code, so it is demoted (no CWE).

`gap` (garray_T*) is dereferenced via `ga_concat`/`ga_concat_esc` without a NULL check, but NULL has no producer on any shown path (caller contract), so this is a robustness note, not a confirmed CWE-476.
`same_len` (int) could overflow only for a run exceeding INT_MAX bytes; the wrapped value would merely disable shortening and reaches no memory sink, so CWE-190 is not confirmed.

When a multibyte character is appended via the else branch, the `++p` at line 16 re-processes its continuation bytes one at a time, causing doubled escaping (a display bug); all accesses remain within [str, NUL), so it is non-security.

`NUMBUFLEN` is not defined in the fragment; line 32 uses a literal "%d" format with a fixed destination, and the buffer is NUL-terminated per standard snprintf semantics, so no overflow or injection is confirmable.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read of the global board table card[]: nr is admitted to [0, EM28XX_MAXBOARDS-1] only by the slot-bitmap guard at line 17 (`if (nr >= EM28XX_MAXBOARDS)`) and is then used to subscript card[] with no visible capacity for that table; the guard at line 159 (`(unsigned int)card[nr] < em28xx_bcount`) compares the element value instead of the index and reads card[nr] as its own operand on the same line, so it cannot protect the read. Any nr >= card[]'s entry count passes every shown guard and triggers the read at lines 159-160 (range claim; exact excess depends on the unshown table size). Independently, USB descriptor strings udev->manufacturer/udev->product (lines 93-94) are NULL-checked but never sanitized before being printed as %s by dev_info (lines 91-99), enabling log injection with embedded newlines.

Confirmed primary mechanism: OOB read via unvalidated index into a table with no visible bound (CWE-125).
evidence.reason: nr reaches this read with residual range [0, EM28XX_MAXBOARDS-1] (produced at line 16 by find_first_zero_bit over the EM28XX_MAXBOARDS-bit slot bitmap; guard line 17 admits exactly that set). card[] has no capacity declared in the fragment, and the line compares the element value to em28xx_bcount rather than the index to the table size, so the guard cannot restrict the index; the read executes for the whole admitted set, giving an out-of-bounds read whenever card[] has fewer than EM28XX_MAXBOARDS entries (CWE-125). The excess (nr - card_size state, up to EM28XX_MAXBOARDS-1) is not computable from the fragment, so this is a range claim; the protective reading (as if the author intended `nr < em28xx_bcount`) still leaves the read unguarded because the shown expression evaluates card[nr] first.

verdict.summary: DL_Dxf::handleLWPolylineData writes out of bounds on the heap: when group code 42 arrives while vertexIndex is -1 (set at line 17 and unchanged because the increment at line 26 requires groupCode==10), the branch guard `vertexIndex<maxVertices` at line 33 admits -1 and line 34 writes `vertices[4*(-1)+3]` = `vertices[-1]`, 8 bytes before the line-9 allocation (CWE-787). Additionally, `4*maxVertices` at line 9 overflows 32-bit signed int for any admitted maxVertices >= 2^29 (guard at line 5 only excludes <=0), corrupting the new[] size and the fill-loop indices at lines 11-14 (CWE-190).

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787). groupValue/groupCode are entry-point file inputs; the fragment sets vertexIndex=-1 at line 17 and increments it only for groupCode==10 (lines 25-26). For the order groupCode==90 (maxVertices=1 admitted by the >0 guard at line 5) followed by groupCode==42 with no vertex code in between, vertexIndex remains -1, and the only guard on this path, `vertexIndex<maxVertices` at line 33, admits -1 (-1 < 1). The sink index is 4*(-1)+3 = -1, which is before the 4-double allocation created at line 9 (capacity 4*maxVertices). Unlike the sibling branch at line 30, this branch has no `vertexIndex>=0` check, so the admitted value -1 is written at vertices[-1].

Integer overflow in an allocation size (CWE-190, secondary). maxVertices receives toInt(groupValue) at line 4 and the only constraint is `maxVertices>0` at line 5, leaving residual range [1, INT_MAX]. With 32-bit signed int arithmetic (loop counter declared `int i` at line 10), any admitted maxVertices >= 2^29 makes 4*maxVertices exceed INT_MAX and wrap, so the size consumed by new[] here is corrupted (huge size_t after sign conversion -> allocation failure/terminate, or a wrapped-small/zero allocation). The same wrap corrupts the fill-loop indices i*4..i*4+3 at lines 11-14, which then write past the (possibly zero-sized) allocation, combining with the primary CWE-787 write.

assumptions: maxVertices, vertexIndex, and vertices are member state that persists across invocations of this handler; groupCode and groupValue are per-entity DXF inputs supplied on each call (entry-point class).

maxVertices and vertexIndex behave as signed int per the shown usage: `if (maxVertices>0)` (line 5), `vertexIndex=-1` (line 17), `vertexIndex<maxVertices-1` (line 25), and the loop counter `int i` (line 10); toInt returns a signed int and toReal returns double.
Capacity of the buffer written at line 34 is the line-9 allocation: 4*maxVertices doubles, index domain [0, 4*maxVertices-1].
limitations: The DXF parser call-site that sequences group codes is outside the fragment; however, the 90-then-42 sequence is derived entirely from shown state transitions (line 17 sets -1; line 26 requires groupCode==10 to advance), so no external invariant is needed for the primary witness.
The integer-overflow finding assumes 32-bit signed int arithmetic for `4*maxVertices`; the member type is not literally declared in the fragment, which caps that finding's confidence at 0.6.
An uncaught std::bad_alloc from the wrapped size at line 9 is a denial-of-service outcome; the primary demonstrated corruption remains the line-34 negative-index heap write.
Leak of a previous vertices buffer when a subsequent groupCode==90 carries maxVertices<=0 (lines 5-16) is a single-shot robustness issue, not a security finding.
The write at line 31 is fully guarded by `vertexIndex>=0 && vertexIndex<maxVertices` at line 30 (max index 4*maxVertices-2) and is not a finding.

(line 41) and repeatX = x1-x0 (lines 78, 100-101) is unbounded: x0,y0,x1,y1 are entry-point ints with no shown constraint, and guard line 115 admits products >4 (witness bbox=(0,0,.5,.5), x0=1e9, x1=x0+3, y1=2 gives repeatX*repeatY=6>4, surface 2x2, matc[4]=5e8). The line 85-90 halving loop would not terminate for infinite kx, but infinite kx is blocked on practical paths by the line 81 surface cap or the line 35-40 isfinite check; treated as robustness only.

verdict.summary: In snd_pcm_oss_sync, the OSS period buffer is written by snd_pcm_format_set_silence with a sample count and buffer offset derived from runtime->oss.buffer_used/period_ptr/period_bytes that are never validated against each other or against the buffer capacity. evidence.reason: size = (8*(period_bytes - buffer_used)+7)/width (line 30) is derived from the unconstrained size_t fields runtime->oss.period_bytes and runtime->oss.buffer_used, guarded only by 'buffer_used > 0' (line 26). That guard sets no upper bound and never establishes buffer_used <= period_bytes, and no capacity of runtime->oss.buffer is visible. A witness buffer_used = period_bytes+1 passes the guard, makes (period_bytes - buffer_used) wrap to SIZE_MAX, and yields a huge size that snd_pcm_format_set_silence uses to write at buffer+buffer_used — an out-of-bounds write. This is the missing-bound (unvalidated-size flow) finding; primary mechanism CWE-787.

size = runtime->oss.period_bytes - runtime->oss.period_ptr (line 41) is unvalidated; guard 'period_ptr > 0' (line 37) sets only a lower bound and never establishes period_ptr <= period_bytes, and the buffer capacity is not visible. A witness period_ptr = period_bytes+1 passes the guard, underflows the subtraction to SIZE_MAX, and snd_pcm_format_set_silence is called with size*8/width (huge) writing at runtime->oss.buffer — an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787, missing bound).

assumptions: runtime->oss.buffer_used, runtime->oss.period_ptr, and runtime->oss.period_bytes are unsigned (size_t per kernel convention), so the subtractions at lines 30 and 41 can underflow; their exact types are not declared in the fragment.

verdict.summary: Unvalidated in-ICB file length `iinfo->i_lenAlloc` flows into PDE-buffer fprintf; only the nonzero check at line 9 is shown. For `iinfo->i_lenAlloc > PAGE_SIZE` (e.g., 4097 with 4 KiB pages), line 33 executes `memset(kaddr + iinfo->i_lenAlloc, 0x00, PAGE_SIZE - iinfo->i_lenAlloc)`: the length wraps to ~2^64-1 (CWE-190) and the destination starts past the end of the PAGE_SIZE page, while line 35-36 `memcpy(kaddr, ..., iinfo->i_lenAlloc)` copies more than PAGE_SIZE bytes into the page (CWE-787 OOB write). No upper-bound/capacity check protects these sinks; a crafted UDF image can corrupt kernel memory during ICB expansion.

evidence.reason: Sink line: memset destination offset = `iinfo->i_lenAlloc` (entry-point on-disk metadata; only shown constraint is the line 9 nonzero check, residual range `[1, field_max]`) and length = `PAGE_SIZE - ioffset` The page at `kaddr` has visible capacity `PAGE_SIZE` (the operand at line 34). For any admitted `iinfo->i_lenAlloc = PAGE_SIZE + 1` (e.g., 4097), `kaddr + 4097` points one byte past the page and `4096UL - 4097` wraps to `2^64 - 1` in unsigned arithmetic, so memset performs a huge write past the page end — CWE-787 OOB write with CWE-190 unsigned-underflow length as root cause. Guards on the path (lines 9, 28, 31) execute before this sink and admit the witness; no statement bounds i_lenAlloc above.

Sink line: length = `iinfo->i_lenAlloc` (unbounded above by any shown check; line 9 admits all nonzero values) is used as the memcpy size into the PAGE_SIZE-capacity page at kaddr. For iinfo->i_lenAlloc = PAGE_SIZE + 1 the page receives 4097 bytes, exceeding the 4096-byte page object by at least one byte and by arbitrarily more for larger admitted values — CWE-787 OOB write. The source offset `iinfo->i_data + iinfo->i_lenEAttr` has no visible capacity, so the read side is not independently confirmed and is recorded in limitations.

assumptions: The page allocated by find_or_create_page at line 27 and mapped by kmap_atomic at line 32 is a PAGE_SIZE object; the fragment itself uses `PAGE_SIZE` as its capacity operand in the line 33-34 memset arithmetic.

iinfo->i_lenAlloc is a non-negative length field derived from on-disk UDF in-ICB metadata; its declaration/capacity is not visible in the fragment, so it keeps its full value domain subject only to the shown constraints; 4097 (= PAGE_SIZE + 1 on 4 KiB pages) is within that domain and nonzero, satisfying line 9's check.
A freshly created page from find_or_create_page is not PageUptodate, so the branch at line 31 executes on the first expansion path, making lines 33-36 the normal outcome.

The line 60 restore memcpy (`memcpy(iinfo->i_data + iinfo->i_lenEAttr, kaddr, inode->i_size)`) can read past the PAGE_SIZE source page when `inode->i_size > PAGE_SIZE`, but it is gated on a filemap_fdatawrite failure (line 55) and its destination capacity is not shown, so it is left as an environment-dependent, unanchored candidate.

No loops exist in the shown code, so loop termination/iteration-bound analysis is not applicable.

The correctness of the line 34 underflow relies on standard unsigned-wrap semantics of `PAGE_SIZE` (unsigned long) minus a smaller-width positive integer, which is well-defined C behavior; the exact field width of i_lenAlloc is not visible but the witness 4097 is representable in any width that passes the line 9 nonzero check.

verdict.summary: clone_private_mount(const struct path *path) unconditionally dereferences the caller-supplied path parameter at line 3 via real_mount(path->mnt); no NULL validity check protects this deref (lines 3, 6, 9 are the only statements touching path and contain no check). path retains its full declared pointer domain including NULL, and a NULL path (or path->mnt == NULL) faults at the line-3 deref into a kernel NULL/invalid-pointer dereference (CWE-476), yielding a kernel oops/panic (local DoS). The guard at line 6 executes after the line-3 deref and only excludes unbindable mounts, so it cannot protect the deref; CWE-476 is thus confirmed.

evidence.reason: Primary sink (CWE-476): the entry parameter` path` (see line 1 declaration) arrives with residual range = full declared `struct path *` domain, including NULL, since no shown statement constrains it before use; line 3 dereferences the field path->mnt unconditionally (the only guard ahead of it on the path is line 6, which runs AFTER line 3 per quoted order 3 < 6 and tests flag IS_MNT_UNBINDABLE on old_mnt, not path validity; line-6's most-protective reading cannot prevent the line-3 fault). Simulated witness: entry with path == NULL → line 3 executes the load, fault at address 0 (equally with path->mnt == NULL: real_mount(container_of) computes a near-zero address and deref faults at line 6 read). NULL is in the admitted set (no guard before this sink rejects it). Impact: kernel invalid-pointer deref → oops/panic, local DoS; primary CWE-476 (parameter dereferenced with no NULL check).

Same taint reaches a second deref/chained-argument sink for CWE-476: `path->dentry` (declared struct dentry pointer; domain incl. NULL; no valuation/null check visible in the whole function) is passed as the dentry argument consumed (dereferenced) by clone_mnt on the fall-through of the line-6 guard. Witness: path valid with path->dentry == NULL: line 6 admitted (old_mnt not unbindable), line 9 passes NULL into clone_mnt's dentry, deref faults in the callee; guard line 6 precedes line-9 (quoted 6 < 9) but excludes only unbindable mounts, never a NULL dentry. Same primary CWE-476 mechanism as the line-3 deref; reported as a distinct sink statement per evidence rules.

assumptions: real_mount() is the standard container_of-style conversion of struct vfsmount * to struct mount *; with a NULL vfsmount it yields an address just below 0 and faults on any deref of that container.

clone_mnt(old_mnt, path->dentry, CL_PRIVATE) returns success pointers or error pointers (ERR_PTR) per its standard kernel contract, so the IS_ERR(mut) check at lines 10-11 fully protects the derefs of new_mnt at lines 14 and 16 for the admitted (non-error) set.
IS_MNT_UNBINDABLE(old_mnt) (line 6) reads the mount flags and admits every mount whose MNT_UNBINDABLE flag is clear; it runs after the line-3 deref and is the only mount-lifecycle guard visible.
MNT_NS_INTERNAL assignment (line 14) is a lifecycle marker for the cloned longterm mount; it is an initialization visible in the fragment but it does not constrain the `path` pointer or its members.
limitations: The NULL for `path`/`path->mnt`/`path->dentry` must be supplied by an unshown caller; per the analysis rules a pointer-typed parameter dereferenced with no shown NULL check is itself the confirmed defect, so caller identity is recorded here only as a transparency note, not as a demotion.

The real Linux kernel callers of clone_private_mount are internal kernel paths that are conventionally guaranteed non-NULL; that invariant is not visible in this fragment and was not used to justify any safety verdict.

If clone_mnt were to return literal NULL instead of an error pointer, IS_ERR(NULL) is false and line 14 would dereference NULL; this contradicts the callee's standard error contract and is a robustness concern, not a confirmed finding.

No other vulnerability classes are present in the fragment: there is no arithmetic, index/size/pointer-arithmetic derivation, format string, injection, crypto/entropy operation, loop, or discarded status that would form another confirmed finding.

verdict.summary: ZRLE reads uninitialized stack palette entries. `PIXEL_T palette[128]` (line 21) is filled only for `i < palSize` (lines 23-25), but the packed-pixel index (line 65, masked to 0..127) and the palette-RLE index (line 116, masked to 0..127) can exceed `palSize-1`. Witness 1: mode=0x03 (palSize=3, bppp=2), packed byte 0xC0 gives index 3 taken at line 66 — palette[3] is indeterminate. Witness 2: mode=0x82 (palSize=2), palette-RLE index byte 0xFF gives index 127 taken at line 118 — palette[127] is indeterminate. Both indeterminate values are committed to the framebuffer (line 125), enabling uninitialized stack-memory disclosure in server-side decode. The `& 127` masks only keep the subscript inside the 128-entry array, so this is CWE-457 (uninitialized use), not CWE-125; the RLE length guards (lines 88, 111) do not constrain the palette index.

evidence.reason: Taint: palSize (attacker mode byte, line 18/20) and packed byte (line 61) flow to index (line 65); index mask admits [0,127] but only entries 0..palSize-1 are initialized by lines 23-25. Witness: palSize=3 -> bppp=2 (lines 49-50); byte=0xC0 -> nbits=6 (line 64), index=(0xC0>>6)&3&127=3 (line 65); line 66 reads uninitialized palette[3] (array capacity 128, line 21). All guards on the path (27: palSize!=1; 34: palSize!=0; 60) admit the witness. The `& 127` mask protects the subscript bound [0,127] but not the initialized prefix, so the primary CWE is 457 (uninitialized use), with the indeterminate value flowing to pb->imageRect (line 125).

Taint: attacker palette-RLE index byte (line 102) is masked to [0,127] (line 116) while palette (line 21) is initialized only for i < palSize (lines 23-25). Witness: mode=0x82 -> rle=true, palSize=2; index byte 0xFF -> index=127 after `index &= 127` (line 116); line 118 reads uninitialized palette[127]. Guard at line 111 (len=1 <= end-ptr) passes; no guard constrains index < palSize. Indeterminate value is stored to buf and consumed by pb->imageRect (line 125); primary CWE-457.

assumptions: PIXEL_T palette[128] (line 21) is not initialized; entries palSize..127 hold indeterminate values (fill loop lines 23-25 writes only i < palSize).
t.area() <= 64*64 = 4096 because t is clamped by __rfbmin (lines 12, 16) and step increments are 64 (lines 10, 14); buf capacity is buf[64*64] (line 8), so no buf overrun is possible.
bppp in the packed path is {1,2,4,8} (lines 49-50); 8 % bppp == 0, so nbits (line 64) never underflows and shifts at line 65 stay in 0..7.
is->readU32() (line 5) returns an unsigned 32-bit value; the store into `int length` is a narrowing/signedness conversion.
limitations: int length = is->readU32() (line 5) can wrap values >= 2^31 to negative (out-of-domain length argument to setUnderlying, line 6), but the concrete failure mode inside ZlibInStream is not visible in the fragment, so impact cannot be demonstrated; recorded without a CWE.

RLE run-length accumulation (len += b, lines 85/108) can overflow int (to negative) with a multi-gigabyte stream; the guards (lines 88/111) then pass with negative len but the copy loops (lines 92/120) execute zero times, so no OOB write is shown; subsequent stall/EOF behavior depends on unshown ZlibInStream semantics.

Uninitialized palette reads (CWE-457) could be exploited for disclosure only in deployments that relay/view the decoded framebuffer across a trust boundary (e.g., server-side decode); in a purely local viewer the effect is incorrect pixels, which caps confidence at 0.62.

The `& 127` masks (lines 65, 116) and RLE bounds checks (lines 88, 111) are confirmed protective statements for the array-subscript and run-length overflows respectively; they do not cover the initialized-prefix invariant that the confirmed finding violates.

No other sinks exist in the fragment (no size/index/length flows into memory operations, no injection/log/command/crypto/file sinks, no loops, no other branches), so no other vulnerability classes apply.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown ins_bs fragment. Each dangerous-looking operation is covered by a visible protective statement executed before the sink: the two `*(ml_get_cursor() - 1)` reads (lines ~205-206, ~241) are gated by `curwin->w_cursor.col > 0` (lines ~204, ~240, short-circuit && guard precedes the deref on every path, admitted set col >= 1, excluded col <= 0); the `ptr[len - 1] = NUL` write (line ~128) is gated by `if (len > 0 ...)` (line ~127, admitted len >= 1, excluded 0, index len-1 in [0, len-1]); the `u_save(curwin->w_cursor.lnum - 2, ...)` call (lines ~86-87) is safe because line ~28 excludes the only dangerous boundary (lnum==1 && col==0) before the col==0 branch (line ~77) is entered, leaving lnum >= 2 so lnum-2 >= 0; and the backspace do-while loop (lines ~275-346) terminates with cursor col never driven below 0 by the col > mincol guard (line ~342) evaluated before the next dec_cursor(). All loops terminate on bounded cursor-column progress; replace-stack loop ~157-161 terminates as each pop consumes a stack entry (name-implied semantics). Demoted non-findings, with no CWE, are recorded in notes.limitations: the static-write count of utfc_ptr2char into `cpc[MAX_MCO]` is callee-internal and not derivable from the shown arithmetic; NULL deref of `inserted_space_p` has no NULL producer on any shown path; `ml_get(Insstart.lnum)` after `--Insstart.lnum` on the revins path needs an unshown `Insstart.lnum == 1` witness; discarded `do_join()` status has no security-relevant consumer here.

assumptions: Line numbers are relative to the fragment as presented, with `ins_bs(` as line 1.

ml_get_cursor() returns a pointer to the current line's text at the cursor column, and STRLEN(ptr) returns the line length in bytes; cursor col/lnum are non-negative on the paths analyzed in the fragment.
colnr_T/linenr_T are signed integer types; the fragment's shown guards (lines ~28, ~204, ~240, ~342) are treated at their strongest protective readings for admitted sets.

replace_pop() returns -1 when the replace stack is exhausted (name-implied), bounding the `while (cc > 0)` loop; `ins_bs_one(&vcol)` dec_cursors (moving the cursor leftward one column per iteration) per name-implied semantics.

verdict.summary: The unsigned long parameters set/clear reach an unguarded narrowing store into the 32-bit int newflags (line 61); any admitted set value with bit 31 or higher set is truncated before being applied to the file via the FS_IOC_SETFLAGS ioctl (lines 62–68, 77–83), so the requested file flags (including root-only immutable/append-only bits) can be silently corrupted and misapplied.

evidence.reason: set/clear are unsigned long parameters whose only shown constraint is the equality check at line 30 (excludes only (0,0)); their residual range therefore includes every value >= 2^31 (and bits 32–63 on LP64). Line 6 declares int newflags/oldflags, so the line-61 assignment narrows the unsigned long expression (min 0, max ULONG_MAX) into a 32-bit int, dropping all bits above bit 31. Witness: set=0x100000010, clear=0, oldflags=0 (written by the successful GETFLAGS ioctl at lines 51–57) yields 0x10, which is then consumed by the ioctl(FS_IOC_SETFLAGS, &newflags) sink at lines 62–68 (and 77–83 on the EPERM retry), applying FS_IMMUTABLE_FL instead of the requested value. Every guard on the path (lines 30, 33, 37/41, 51–57) admits the witness and none constrains the magnitude; primary CWE-197 numeric truncation of a security-relevant flag value.

assumptions: Target environment is Linux (code references FS_IOC_GETFLAGS/EXT2_IOC_GETFLAGS and O_CLOEXEC); int is 32-bit and unsigned long is 64-bit (LP64), so the line-61 narrowing drops bits 32–63 — on 32-bit targets the same finding holds for any set value >= 2^31 since unsigned long there still admits values not representable in int.
GETFLAGS/SETFLAGS ioctls on a valid fd behave in their standard manner, reading/writing a 4-byte flags int that matches the shown int declarations.
The declared type ranges of int and unsigned long (lines 2 and 6) are the visible capacity bounds used for the truncation analysis.
limitations: At line 39, __archive_ensure_cloexec_flag(myfd) is called with open()'s result before the line-41 validity check; when open fails at line 38, -1 is passed, but the helper's standard behavior (fcntl on an invalid fd returning EBADF) is benign and line 41 returns immediately — robustness note, not a finding.

Absence of a demonstrated flaw here is a weaker verdict than one backed by a decisive protective statement; confidence is capped accordingly, relying on the visible guard at lines 9-10 and the visible order of lines 23,25,27-28 relative to 31-32,34.

verdict.summary: Command injection via the environment-controlled EDITOR/VISUAL value: the space check at line 49 only routes space-free editors to execlp; any editor containing a space is concatenated into a shell command string (line 57) and executed by system() (line 58), so an environment value such as 'sh -c id' runs arbitrary commands with the privileges of the Singular process. evidence.reason: CWE-78: editor is entry-point environment input (getenv at lines 19/21) whose residual range is any non-NULL string, with no sanitization visible after the space test at line 49. verdict.summary: Missing upper-bound validation on runtime->oss.buffer_used (line 26 guards only '> 0') and runtime->oss.period_ptr (line 37) admits values above runtime->oss.period_bytes, so the subtractions at lines 30 and 41 underflow/wrap into a huge frame count passed to snd_pcm_format_set_silence (lines 31-33 and 42-44), writing far past runtime->oss.buffer, for which no capacity is visible. For an admitted witness in the residual range with buffer_used > period_bytes (e.g., 1025 vs 1024), the subtraction wraps and size becomes a huge frame count (up to ~2^32/width), so snd_pcm_format_set_silence writes that many silence frames at buffer+1025 with no visible capacity bounding the offset or count — an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787, unvalidated-size flow; the missing upper check is the defect).

verdict.summary: fill_threshold_buffer copies caller-supplied bytes into dest_strip using fully unvalidated int parameters as memcpy lengths: left_width (line 9), src_width repeated up to num_tiles times (lines 12-14), and right_width (line 17). No check constrains any width, offset, or tile count and no capacity for dest_strip is visible. A negative width (e.g., left_width = -1) converts to a ~2^64-1-byte size_t length (C11 6.3.1.3), and any large positive widths with an unconstrained num_tiles make the total write unbounded — an out-of-bounds write past dest_strip plus an out-of-bounds read from src_strip. The single conditional in the fragment (line 21) executes only inside PACIFY_VALGRIND, after every copy, and never admits a positive value on reachable paths, so it provides no protection.

For left_width = -1 (admitted — no guard precedes this line; it executes first after line 5), C11 6.3.1.3 converts -1 to 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, so the copy reads/writes roughly 2^64-1 bytes: an out-of-bounds write past dest_strip (CWE-787) with the signed-to-unsigned conversion as the independently confirmed root cause (CWE-195). Any positive left_width is likewise unvalidated, and src_strip + left_offset indexes the source with an unbounded offset (source-side OOB read folded into this sink). No capacity for dest_strip exists in the fragment; the missing bound is the defect.

Sink in the tile loop: src_width (full int domain, unconstrained) is passed as the size_t length, and the loop bound at line 12 (`ii < num_tiles`) admits 0..INT_MAX-1 iterations with num_tiles itself unconstrained. ptr_out_temp is advanced by src_width per iteration (line 14) with no capacity bound on dest_strip, so a single negative src_width yields a huge size_t length and any large positive width yields an unbounded cumulative write (CWE-787, CWE-195). The loop guard does not protect this sink: it bounds only the iteration count against an unvalidated int and never against a destination size.

Final sink: right_width (full int domain, unconstrained) is passed as the size_t length after ptr_out_temp has already advanced past the left part and all tiles (lines 10, 14). A negative right_width converts to a near-SIZE_MAX length (C11 6.3.1.3), and any large positive value overflows the destination; no capacity check on dest_strip and no width validation appear anywhere in the fragment (CWE-787, CWE-195).

assumptions: byte is a 1-byte integer type as named in the shown pointer declarations; memcpy's length parameter is size_t per standard C semantics.

Standard C conversion applies: converting a negative int to size_t (unsigned) is defined by C11 6.3.1.3p2 to yield v + 2^N, i.e., -1 maps to 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF for 64-bit size_t; any wider size_t only enlarges the magnitude.
Line numbers 1-24 correspond to the fragment exactly as quoted.

Line 10 `asprintf(&suffix, backup, idstring)` is the same format-string pattern on `backup`; grouped under the same fix family, not reported as an additional CWE to keep the CWE set to one confirmed primary.
`stat`'s non-zero return silently skips the rename (no error surfaced) — missing-error-report robustness, no security-relevant operation on the failure state, therefore not confirmed as CWE-754.

Single-shot leak on partial `asprintf` failure (`suffix` freed / if second asprintf fails both allocations are replaced by FatalError) is an unchecked-allocation robustness issue not attacker-directable at shown scale.

verdict.summary: raptor_xml_writer_start_element_common contains two confirmed memory-safety bugs reachable from unconstrained element fields (attribute_count, attributes, xml_language contents): (1) heap out-of-bounds write in xml:lang serialization — a buf_length-sized escape region (line 114) exceeds the buf_length+1 allocation (line 106) minus the 10-byte prefix, with unconditional quote/NUL tail writes (lines 115-116) that never check the escape return or remaining space; witness xml_language="&" (lang_len=1, escaped &=5 bytes at indices 10..14 of a 13-byte buffer) overflows the allocation by up to 4 bytes; (2) out-of-bounds read at line 50, where the duplicate-check loop indexes element->attributes[j] with j ranging up to nspace_declarations_count-1 (line 49), which exceeds attribute_count (=2 with the element plus first attribute declared, array indices 0..1) on the last attribute loop iterations — witness attribute_count=2 with out-of-scope element and attribute nspaces passes every guard on the path.

evidence.reason: Sink: unconditional heap OOB write (CWE-787 primary). Lang block guard at line 102 admits any non-NULL element->xml_language; strlen (line 103) yields unaudited lang_len; allocation buf_length+1 (lang_len+12 bytes, line 106) holds prefix (10 bytes at line 110, indices 0..9) plus at most lang_len+2 more bytes, yet the escape at lines 112-114 receives buf_length (lang_len+11) as its region size -- 9 bytes more than available. Its return (advancing p, line 112) is never checked against remaining space, so a witness "&" (lang_len=1) is written as & (5 bytes at indices 10..14 of a 13-byte buffer; indices 13-14 past end), then lines 115-116 write quote at index 15 and NUL at index 16, overflowing by up to 4 bytes on every admitted input whose escaped form exceeds lang_len+1 bytes. No protective statement exists between origin and sink.

evidence.file: Element attributes dereference in dedup loop
evidence.reason: Sink line 50 is an out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125 secondary, independent root cause: loop index variable j misapplied to element->attributes instead of i). element->attribute_count is unconstrained (loops at line 41); the fragment's own indexing (lines 43, 46, 56, 67) fixes element->attributes capacity at attribute_count entries. Dedup bound at line 49 is nspace_declarations_count, which grows to 1 + 2i before iteration i+1's check and beyond attribute_count. Witness: attribute_count=2, element name nspace out of scope (count becomes 1 at line 36), attributes[0] nspace out of scope and != name nspace (guard lines 45-46 admits), count reaches 3 after attribute 0's declaration (line 62: write then count++) and value (lines 66-71); at i=1 line 49 admits j in 0..2, and j=2 reads element->attributes[2] past capacity 2 (valid indices 0..1). No clamp of j against attribute_count exists on any path to this sink.

assumptions: element->attributes capacity equals attribute_count entries, established only by the fragment's own repeated indexing element->attributes[i] for i<attribute_count at lines 43, 46, 56, 67 in the shown code.

nspace_declarations capacity (lines 14-20) exactly covers worst-case writes: 2*attribute_count + name nspace (1, lines 29-36) + declared nspaces (<= size, lines 89-97) + xml_language (1, lines 102-121), so no OOB write into nspace_declarations itself is possible from the shown arithmetic.

raptor_xml_escape_string follows its name-implied standard semantics of a bounded XML escaper (writing the escaped form into the given size and returning the bytes written), sufficient for the finite overflow witness and weaker than any behavior needed for a range claim.
limitations: NULL-dereference of element->name->nspace (line 26), xml_writer->iostr/nstack (lines 5-6, 112) and of individual element->attributes[i] pointers (line 43) is possible only via framework-internal NULLs not derived anywhere in the shown code -- robustness concern CWE-476 candidate, not attacker-directed in the fragment, no NULL producer shown.

raptor_xml_escape_string's exact return contract is assumed name-implied; the shown-code arithmetic (lines 106, 110, 114-116) already proves the size argument exceeds the remaining region, capping the primary finding's confidence at ~0.72 as a range-independent overflow once escaped length > lang_len+1.

int overflow in attribute_count*2 (line 14) needs count near 2^30, unattainable with input sizes visible in the fragments; the wrapped-negative capacity routes through a failing RAPTOR_CALLOC to return 1 (lines 22-25), so no exploitable write path materializes.

Element-attribute dedup mis-indexing also compares against the wrong attribute when in bounds (line 50 uses attributes[j] for all j), a correctness/logic defect whose security consequence is already captured as the line-50 OOB read finding; not counted as an independent CWE.
64-bit-to-32-bit cast of raptor_sequence_size at line 80 can truncate only sizes > 4G-elements declared_nspaces sequences, which no shown bound admits realistically.
Unchecked buffer malloc at line 106 before memcpy at line 110 is an environment-failure robustness issue; the failure is not attacker-directed at the shown scale.
xml_language entry stores length=buf_length (line 119) while the escaped content is shorter, causing counted output to read NUL padding inside the allocation -- in-bounds, informational only.

verdict.summary: NULL pointer dereference: the second platform_get_resource call (line 33) for IORESOURCE_MEM stores its result in res with no NULL check, mirroring the IRQ resource check missing here. If the device lacks a MEM resource, res is NULL and is passed unvalidated to devm_ioremap_resource (line 34, which consumes res->start/res->end) and then dereferenced at lines 40-41 (ndev->mem_start = res->start / ndev->mem_end = res->end), crashing the kernel during probe (CWE-476, DoS via kernel NULL deref).

evidence.reason: res is assigned the unvalidated return of platform_get_resource(ofdev, IORESOURCE_MEM, 0) on line 33 with no NULL check afterwards; its residual range includes NULL (the IRQ call's NULL outcome is explicitly handled at lines 25-29, but the MEM call is not). Passing NULL to devm_ioremap_resource is out-of-domain for the resource-pointer argument, which the callee dereferences to compute size, yielding a kernel NULL-deref kernel oops on devices probing without a MEM resource (primary CWE-476).

Unconditional dereference of res->start with res still the unconstrained line-33 return value whose residual range includes NULL; the only prior NULL guard (lines 25-29) guarded the previous IRQ-resource value, and line 35's IS_ERR check tests lp->base_addr after the fact rather than res, so the NULL witness passes every guard on the path (CWE-476 NULL pointer dereference).

Same unvalidated res (line 33 residual range includes NULL) dereferenced as res->end on the same path covered by evidence item line 40; no statement between line 33 and line 41 constrains res, confirming the missing-NULL-check NULL-pointer-dereference (CWE-476 DoS).

assumptions: Line numbers are counted from the first line of the fragment (static int xemaclite_of_probe(...) = line 1).

devm_ioremap_resource consumes the passed resource pointer (reading res->start/res->end to compute the mapping size), so NULL is outside its argument domain; this is the standard, name-implied semantics of the devm API.
limitations: xemaclite_mdio_setup(lp, &ofdev->dev) at line 63 may consume the unchecked lp->phy_node from line 62, but its body is not shown, so any NULL-deref there is unconfirmable and carries no CWE.
Single-shot allocations (alloc_etherdev) do not compound with attacker-controlled volume and are not findings.

No integer-wraparound, injection, format-string, crypto, or loop-related sinks exist in the shown fragment; the remaining checked returns (rc from of_get_mac_address and register_netdev) are handled correctly and were not reported.

verdict.summary: User-controlled format string misuse: fname is passed directly as the format argument to asprintf at line 7 (and backup at line 17) with no escaping, so an attacker who controls fname can supply %n/%s conversion specifiers to perform arbitrary memory writes/reads or crash the process (CWE-134). The header comment itself states the format string is user-controlled; no protective statement exists between the parameters and the asprintf calls.

evidence.reason: CWE-134 primary: the sink is a printf-family asprintf whose format argument is the unconstrained const char* parameter fname (declared at line 1). No shown statement constrains fname's content — lines 5-6 only warn that the format string is user-controlled; the format argument reaches the varargs machinery with the single supplied argument idstring. A value from fname's full declared domain, e.g. fname="%n", causes asprintf at line 7 to write the conversion count into *(( int*)idstring (arbitrary write at an attacker-derived address, per the shown call's own argument passing) or to consume varargs out of range with excess %s specifiers; no guard exists before the sink on any path (clause A witness needs no precondition, so the environment-dependent guard at line 13 cannot degrade this one), giving an attacker-controlled format string that can corrupt memory; the cap-generating alternative would be a literal format ("%s") which is absent.

Same CWE-134 class at a distinct sink: backup is the second user-supplied format string (line 1) used as the format argument of asprintf at line 17. The only preceding guard, `backup && *backup` (line 10), admits every non-empty string (e.g. backup="%n") and excludes only NULL/empty values, and `stat(logFileName, &buf) && S_ISREG(buf.st_mode)` (line 17 preceding it in path order, quoted line 13) constrains logFileName rather than backup's format content, so dangerous format specifiers survive the path; by the same mechanism as the line 7 sink, %n writes through the pointer supplied by idstring or out-of-range varargs reads occur. Reachability of this specific sink additionally depends on stat succeeding on a regular file (environment state outside the fragment), capping confidence accordingly; verdict confidence is driven by the unconditional line 7 primary.

assumptions: asprintf success returns a freshly allocated NUL-terminated string of the length the format expansion requires (the shown call derives the size for the target buffer inside the function), and asprintf failure (return of -1, checked at lines 7, 8, 17-19) terminates execution via FatalError before those values are consumed at lines 13, 23, 31 and the return at line 36; logFileName's non-NULL use after line 7 relies on that contract visible in the shown code's own checks; those checks fully handle the failure branch.
FatalError is treated as process-exiting, matching both the 'Allocate'/'move/remove' error paths, so no NULL logFileName flows past line 8 for later dereference.

verdict.summary: In readconf_main, when CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_NODE or CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_EUID is compiled in, the suffix pointer (L16) points to the end of a config-list item inside big_buffer (capacity big_buffer_size passed at L10), and sprintf writes at L25/L30/L41 to that pointer with no remaining-space check. A list item of length big_buffer_size-1 leaves 1 byte, while even the smallest write (".0\0" = 3 bytes at L41) overflows big_buffer by 2+ bytes; the combined format at L25 can write up to 279 bytes. This is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) during privileged configuration parsing.

evidence.reason: CWE-787 OOB write. suffix (L16: suffix = filename + Ustrlen(filename)) is an input-derived offset into big_buffer, whose capacity big_buffer_size is passed at L10; the item length L has residual range [0, big_buffer_size-1] because the fragment shows no smaller cap on config_main_filelist items. For L = big_buffer_size-1, only 1 byte (R = big_buffer_size - L) remains at suffix, yet this sprintf writes '.', >=1 digit of original_euid, and NUL (>=3 bytes), so indices big_buffer_size and big_buffer_size+1 are written out of bounds. The guards on the path (L10 filename != NULL; L39 config_file == NULL) admit this witness, and no check between L16 and L41 bounds the write.

Same CWE-787 mechanism as the primary finding. With L = big_buffer_size-1 (item admitted by L10 with no length guard), suffix leaves 1 byte of big_buffer; sprintf writes '.' plus the NUL-terminated nodename (>=2 bytes, up to 258 via %.256s), so the write lands at least 1 byte past big_buffer. uname() success (L22) is the only preceding guard and does not constrain the remaining capacity.

Same CWE-787 mechanism, largest write. For L = big_buffer_size-1 the available space at suffix is 1 byte; the format emits at least '.', 1 euid digit, '.', 1 nodename char, NUL (5 bytes) and at most 1+20+1+256+1 = 279 bytes, overflowing big_buffer by up to 278 bytes. Only the L22 uname() gate precedes the sink; it bounds neither the item length nor the total write.

assumptions: big_buffer_size, passed at L10 as the destination capacity of big_buffer, is the size of big_buffer in bytes.
string_nextinlist (L10) writes a NUL-terminated item into big_buffer, so an item's maximum representable length is big_buffer_size-1; the fragment shows no smaller length cap.
The CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_NODE / CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_EUID code paths (L15-L52) are compiled configurations; the fragment contains these branches.
original_euid is a long int; any long value formats via %ld to at least one digit.
limitations: If neither CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_NODE nor CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_EUID is defined, the vulnerable sprints are excluded at compile time (L53-L58) and no overflow exists in that build.

Ustrtol(s, &end, 0) at L390 is reached without checking s == NULL after expand_string(host_number_string) at L389; NULL would require an expansion failure, which is neither attacker-directed nor deterministically produced by a shown input, so it is a robustness concern, not a confirmed finding.

Log-injection potential through config_main_filelist/filename bytes in log_write (L78-L82) is not reported: attacker control of those globals is not established by the shown code, and the memory-safety finding dominates.
read_named_list and readconf_handle_option bodies are not shown; MAX_NAMED_LIST capacity and internal bounds are not visible, so no finding is asserted at those call sites.
host_number is only upper-bounded (L395); no security-relevant consumer of host_number is shown, so the missing lower-bound check is not a confirmed finding.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the fragment alone. The only input-derived value reaching a memory-construction sink is the option argument (jas_optarg) flowed into addopt at lines 116 and 126 together with the bound constant OPTSMAX, whose value and the declared capacity of inoptsbuf/outoptsbuf are not visible in the fragment — no overflow witness can be derived from shown arithmetic (a witness would require assuming an unshown capacity, which is expressly disallowed), and the callee's write bound contract is outside the shown code in either direction of the verdict, so the candidate is demoted into limitations, not confirmed. The initializations at lines 66 and 71 fix inoptsbuf/outoptsbuf to empty NUL-terminated strings before the loop at line 84, excluding uninitialized-length reads in any byte-measuring helper. The remaining sinks are safe on shown arithmetic: the fprintf at lines 152-154 uses a literal format string with a %s whose index is guarded by the strict comparison jas_optind < argc at line 151 (admitted indices 0..argc-1 vs array cardinality argc, check order 151 before access 154); atoi/strtoull results at lines 107/130/136 have no security-relevant consumer in the fragment; all malloc/NULL and option-code error paths are properly checked at lines 57-60 and 144-146. Ledger-wise the verdict is capped at 0.6 because the fragment shows no single statement whose admitted/excluded bound fully rules out byte overflow inside the unshown addopt() callee beyond the OPTSMAX bound argument, and that residual uncertainty is recorded in notes.limitations.

assumptions: argc/argv pairing provides exactly argc valid entries at indices 0..argc-1; the fragment's own guard at line 151 (jas_optind < argc before the argv[jas_optind] access at 154) proves every admitted access index is in 0..argc-1 and within that bound by strict inequality.

cmdopts->inoptsbuf and cmdopts->outoptsbuf are first bytes initialized at lines 66 and 71 to '\0' BEFORE the parse loop at line 84, and before every addopt call at lines 116/126 (path order 66,71 -> 84 -> 116/126), so any strlen-based measurement of these buffers sees length 0 at the start.

OPTSMAX is passed as the bound argument of addopt at lines 116 and 126; the constant's numeric value and the declared capacity of inoptsbuf/outoptsbuf are not shown in the fragment, so neither capacity equality can be imported in either direction.

jas_getopt at line 84 consumes at least one argv entry per call and returns EOF when the finite argv vector is exhausted, so loop termination is bounded; the warning loop 151-155 increments jas_optind each iteration and terminates.
limitations: OOB write candidate demoted (no CWE): jas_optarg of unrestricted length flows to addopt at lines 116 and 126 with only the OPTSMAX bound visible; the destination capacity of inoptsbuf/outoptsbuf is not declared in the fragment, so any overflow witness would have to assume an unshown capacity smaller than OPTSMAX — the OOB standard rejects exactly such an assumed capacity. The fragment cannot prove the write safe beyond the callee name-contract, and cannot prove failure on shown arithmetic, in either verdict direction.

OOB read of uninitialized buffer length inside addopt demoted with the protective statements named: lines 66 and 71 fix inoptsbuf[0] = '\0' and outoptsbuf[0] = '\0', admitted set for measured start length {0}, excluded set all longer/uninitialized starts; these executions precede the loop at line 84 on every path to lines 116/126, so the uninitialized-length hazard class is absorbed by shown code; no CWE attached.

NULL-deref of jas_optarg demoted (CWE-476 candidate unconfirmable): at lines 107/110/113/116/123/126/130/136/139 no NULL check precedes use of jas_optarg, but NULL production requires jas_getopt to return a JAS_OPT_HASARG option code paired with a NULL argument — a framework invariant not visible in the fragment; no shown producer exists, so NULL cannot be derived on a shown path and is therefore not a finding per standard (a deref whose NULL can only arise from an environment/library behavior invisible in the fragment is not a confirmed flaw).

atoi/strtoull errno and wrap handling demoted (CWE-190/391 candidates): strtoull(jas_optarg, 0, NULL, 10) at line 136 and atoi at lines 107/130 ignore the error path, but the stored values (debug, cmptno, max_mem) have no security-relevant consumer anywhere in the fragment; a wrap is provably inconsequential within the shown scope; recorded as a limitation, not confirmed.

Negative jas_optind low-side index demoted to limitations: line 151 bounds the index above by argc before the argv[jas_optind] access at 154 (strict inequality admits exactly 0..argc-1 against cardinality argc, excluding the upper-failure boundary), but a negative side only arises from unshown jas_getopt internals; no shown statement derives it, so no witness exists in the fragment.

Log-injection class at the stderr fprintf (lines 152-154) demoted: attacker-supplied CLI argument text (including embedded newlines) is written unsanitized via a literal %s format (no CWE-134: the format itself is a constant and matches arguments 1:1); the write targets console stderr with no shown structured-log integrity consumer, so the security mechanism is not established; low-impact, no CWE attached.

The fragment is self-consistent as the patched counterpart for the length-measurement hazard (initializations at 66/71 are precisely the small local protective statements of the kind the fix takes); the only residual doubt is the unshown destination capacity for the addopt byte-overflow class, which is why the not-vulnerable confidence is capped at the rubric maximum for a safe verdict lacking a decisive statement for the principal hazard, rather than ambiguity in any confirmed candidate.

verdict.summary: fiber_switch passes the unconstrained argument count `len` (mrb_int, internal-helper parameter, residual range [15, MRB_INT_MAX] on this path) as the element count into mrb_ary_new_from_values(mrb, len, a) at line 40, reading `len` mrb_values from the argument pointer `a` for which no capacity or bound is declared anywhere in the fragment. The `len >= 15` guard (line 38) is a lower bound that admits exactly the unbounded-large side, and `len = 15` (line 41) executes after the read, so it cannot protect it. Same unvalidated-size flow reaches the copy loop at lines 47-49 (elements from `a`) and fiber_result(mrb, a, len) at line 56 on the non-created path. Confirmed mechanism: out-of-bounds read from an unvalidated, input-derived size (missing bound), primary CWE-125.

evidence.reason: CWE-125: `len` is an internal-helper parameter (line 1) whose only in-fragment constraint, `if (len >= 15)` (line 38), admits every value in [15, MRB_INT_MAX]; the guard is a lower bound, so it cannot bound the read. `len` flows unchanged as the element count into mrb_ary_new_from_values(mrb, len, a), which reads `len` contiguous mrb_values from `a`. No statement in the fragment declares a capacity for the array behind `a` or ties `len` to it, and `len = 15` (line 41) executes after this sink, so the out-of-domain read is confirmed by the shown arithmetic as a missing-bound/unvalidated-size flow: any admitted `len >= 15` over-reads whenever the backing array has fewer elements.

CWE-125 (same flow): on the else path of `if (len >= 15)` (line 38), `len` in [0,14] is used as the loop count `e = b + len` (line 46), so `while (b<e)` copies `len` elements read from `a` (line 49). The write side is provisioned by `mrb_stack_extend(mrb, len+2)` (line 44), but the read side consumes `len` elements from `a` with no visible bound on `a`, making this a second sink of the same unvalidated-size read flow.

CWE-125 (same flow): on the non-created path (status != MRB_FIBER_CREATED, admitted via the switch default at lines 23-24), `len` retains its full declared mrb_int domain — no guard constrains it at all — and is passed as the argument count alongside the argument pointer `a` to fiber_result, which by its name and use consumes `len` elements of `a`. No capacity for `a` is shown, so this is a third sink of the unvalidated-size read flow.

assumptions: mrb_int is a signed integer with full domain [MRB_INT_MIN, MRB_INT_MAX].
mrb_ary_new_from_values(mrb_state*, mrb_int n, const mrb_value* vals) reads exactly n contiguous mrb_value elements from vals (standard name-implied semantics).
fiber_result(mrb, a, len) consumes len elements of a (by its name and by the (pointer, length) argument pairing).

mrb_stack_extend(mrb, room) ensures at least room usable slots for the current frame's stack (name-implied standard semantics); under that reading the fiber-stack writes (lines 44-49, 39-40, 52) are in-domain for the counts actually written.
MRB_FIBER_CREATED is admitted by the status switch via `default: break` (lines 23-24); the raises at lines 13/18/21 reject only TRANSFERRED+resume, RUNNING, RESUMED, TERMINATED.
limitations: The OOB read at line 40 is a range claim ([15, MRB_INT_MAX]), not a single demonstrated magnitude: the backing capacity of `a` is not declared in the fragment, so the exact excess cannot be computed; the confirmed mechanism is the missing bound (unvalidated-size flow).

Negative `len` (INT_MIN..-1) is admitted by the else path of line 38 and stored into `c->cibase->n` at line 51 with no sign validation, but the downstream VM handling of a negative frame arg count is not shown, so the impact cannot be substantiated; demoted.

`c->ci--` (line 36) and `c->ci[1].stack[0] = value` (line 57) are gated only by `vmexec`; the callinfo arena capacity (ciend) is never shown and the indices are constants rather than input-derived sizes, so no capacity can be exceeded by shown arithmetic; demoted.

Real-world callers of fiber_switch (fiber_resume/fiber_transfer) may always pass a consistent (len, a) pair; that caller contract is not visible in the fragment and per the analysis rules cannot be used to make the read in-domain.
The value written into `c->stbase[1]`/`stbase[0]`/`c->cibase->n` is trusted framework state; no defect is claimed about it beyond the reads of `a` noted above.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown fragment: every dangerous-looking byte walk and downward stack write the code contains (MULTIBYTECODE len<2 safety check, RE_MARK pos NULL/lnum<=0 guard, backpos ga_data re-fetch after ga_grow, regstack.ga_len += sizeof(regstar_T)/sizeof(regbehind_T) reservations, rex.lnum==0 and rex.line==NULL guards in RS_STAR_LONG / RS_BEHIND2, and fast_breakcheck/got_int/p_mmp caps on repetition loops) contains a concrete protective statement with a named admitted/excluded bound. No sink statement is reachable through a guard-admitted value with the shown arithmetic, so no CWE is confirmed. Confidence capped at 0.6 because the safe conclusion rests on a thorough candidate-by-candidate exclusion rather than a single decisive protective statement for the function as a whole.

assumptions: rex.input/rex.line are NUL-terminated strings: visible in the fragment through *rex.input == NUL checks, c == NUL branches, and the for (i = 0; rex.input[i] != NUL; i += utf_ptr2len(rex.input + i)) loop.

reg_getline(rex.lnum) is valid for the current line: maintained by the shown reg_nextline() guard (rex.lnum <= rex.reg_maxline) before line advance and the shown rex.lnum == 0 guard before --rex.lnum.

regstack/backpos grow arrays: all writes at visible indexes are preceded by ga_grow and the re-derived ga_data pointer (bp = (backpos_T *)backpos.ga_data after ga_grow) or by explicit byte reservations (regstack.ga_len += sizeof(regstar_T)/sizeof(regbehind_T)) mirrored by the -= on pop.
Pattern operand opnd in MULTIBYTECODE is NUL-terminated and the compare loop stops at the first byte mismatch, so reads terminate before the terminator.
Repetition bounds are enforced by the shown fast_breakcheck(), got_int handling, and the regstack.ga_len>>10 >= p_mmp memory cap on the STAR/PLUS and BEHIND growth paths.
limitations: MULTIBYTECODE byte walk: the safety check if ((len = (*mb_ptr2len)(opnd)) < 2) { status = RA_NOMATCH; break; } excludes len < 2 and admits len in [2, encoding-max-char-bytes]; an overrun would require reading past the NUL terminator, which the fragment's own NUL-termination loops exclude. Encoding-change scenarios where the operand string is shorter than the current mb_ptr2len length are not demonstrated in-fragment (no visible capacity of the operand area is exceeded on a shown path).

RE_MARK reg_getline(pos->lnum - rex.reg_firstlnum): the NULL branch of getmark_buf is guarded (pos == NULL || pos->lnum <= 0 → RA_NOMATCH) and on the MAXCOL path the index equals rex.lnum; a positive-but-out-of-range mark line is not derivable from the shown statements.

RS_BEHIND2 multi-line reg_getline(--pos.lnum) and single-line MB_PTR_BACK: the shown guards stop the walk before invalid lines / line start; underflow to -1 yields reg_getline() == NULL → no = FAIL, which is handled.

RS_STAR_LONG backup uses rex.line = reg_getline(--rex.lnum) guarded by rex.lnum == 0 before the decrement and rex.line == NULL break; no OOB/NULL deref on the shown paths; regrepeat() miscount is explicitly mitigated.

RS_BEHIND2 col decrement (*mb_head_off)(line, line + col - 1) + 1 executes only in the col > 0 branch with line from a valid saved position; head_off ≤ col-1, so col cannot underflow, and line == NULL is not produced by the shown guards.
ReDoS through large brace/star counts is bounded by the shown fast_breakcheck()/got_int and the regstack p_mmp memory cap; no unbounded loop on the shown paths.

Composing-character scan (for (i = 0; rex.input[i] != NUL; i += utf_ptr2len(...))) reads a bounded prefix and stops at NUL; 4-byte reads at the line terminus beyond the terminator would require an unshown capacity, so it is not confirmed.

verdict.summary: Unvalidated-size flow into a stack buffer: line 43 assigns attacker-supplied cf->len (u8, residual [0,255] — the only pre-copy guard can_dropped_invalid_skb at line 14 is a call whose enforced bound is not visible in the fragment) to usb_msg.dlc, and line 45 uses it directly as the memcpy length into usb_msg.data (stack object declared line 10) with no shown capacity or bound on the destination. An admitted length >8 writes out of bounds past usb_msg.data (CWE-787) and reads out of bounds from cf->data; no shown statement absorbs the boundary.

No overflow/cap guard exists before this allocation-size sink, so the derived size is out-of-domain for the buffer that line 34 consumes (missing-bound/unvalidated-size flow; CWE-190 root cause corrupting the capacity used at CWE-787 sink).

verdict.summary: bgp_capability_msg_parse performs memcpy of sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) bytes from pnt+3 (line 51) after only checking that pnt + hdr->length + 3 <= end (line 43). The check never requires hdr->length >= sizeof(struct capability_mp_data), so a network-supplied capability with a length byte of 0, 1, or 2 passes both guards and the fixed-size memcpy reads past the end boundary of the message buffer, an attacker-triggerable out-of-bounds heap read.

evidence.reason: The memcpy source size is the fixed constant sizeof(struct capability_mp_data), which is at least 3 bytes because the fragment consumes mpc.afi via ntohs() (16-bit, line 56) and mpc.safi as a byte (line 57). The only visible bound on the source region is the line 43 guard `(pnt + hdr->length + 3) > end`, which enforces hdr->length <= (end - pnt) - 3 but imposes NO lower bound on hdr->length. hdr->length is an attacker-supplied byte of the network message (read at pnt+2 via hdr = (struct capability_header *)(pnt + 1)), with residual range 0..255, and the value 0 is always admitted whenever the header-presence guard at line 18 passes (r = end - pnt >= 3). Witness: a 3-byte message [action=SET, code=MP, length=0] gives r = 3; line 18 passes (pnt+3 == end is not > end) and line 43 passes (pnt + 0 + 3 == end is not > end), yet the memcpy at line 51 then reads sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) >= 3 bytes starting at pnt+3 == end, i.e. entirely beyond the message region [pnt, end) defined at line 13 (end = pnt + length). This is a confirmed heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) that a remote peer can trigger on every iteration of the loop: no shown statement establishes any minimum for hdr->length, so the missing `hdr->length >= sizeof(struct capability_mp_data)` check is the defect.

assumptions: The message byte region being parsed is bounded by `end = pnt + length` (line 13), which the parser itself treats as the buffer boundary via its length-error checks (lines 18 and 43).

`sizeof(struct capability_mp_data)` is at least 3 bytes, derived from the fragment's own consumption of mpc.afi as a 16-bit network-order value (ntohs at line 56) plus mpc.safi as an 8-bit value (line 57); its exact numeric value is not visible in the fragment, but the over-read occurs for any value >= 1.

`hdr->length` is a single byte of the capability message (field of the header pointed to by pnt+1), i.e. entry-point input; values 0, 1, and 2 are within its declared domain and are not excluded by any shown constraint.
limitations: Potential NULL dereference of `peer` (lines 19, 30, 40, 44, 60, 70, 80, 88, 104) is not reported: `peer` is a framework session object whose non-NULL invariant is not modeled by the fragment, and no attacker-derived NULL producer is shown.

limitations: The out-of-bounds read witness relies on an unshown decoder (decodearr) being able to return a success count greater than 8; the shown code neither supplies nor validates that magnitude, so the finding is a residual-range claim capped at confidence 0.55 rather than a pinned single value.

A potential log-injection via the default-case fprintf(stderr, "...%s=%s, fmt %d\n", name, value, fmt) was not confirmed because the fragment does not show varfmt()'s return mapping that would demonstrate reachability of the default branch for attacker-controlled names.

verdict.summary: The callback parses libcurl HTTP response headers as unbounded strings: `size_t bytes = size * nmemb;` (line 4) derives the delivered length but it is never applied as a bound, so `snprintf(url->errormsg, sizeof(url->errormsg), "%s", (char*)ptr+22)` (line 22) scans attacker-chosen header bytes until a NUL with no in-region NUL guarantee, reading up to `sizeof(url->errormsg)`-1 bytes past the delivered frame and copying adjacent memory into `url->errormsg` (OOB read, CWE-125). The same missing length bound also lets the `%u` scan at line 16 read past the delivered end on a crafted digit run. The destination write at line 22 is bounded by `sizeof(url->errormsg)`; only the source scan is unbounded.

evidence.reason: `ptr` (entry-point HTTP header bytes, no NUL-termination guarantee in the shown code) reaches the `%s` source read at line 22; guard 19 admits any header whose first 22 bytes equal "icecast-auth-message: ", which forces a delivered length of at least 22. The fragment's only derived length, `size_t bytes = size * nmemb;` (line 4), is returned at line 31 but is never used to bound the parse. A delivered frame such as "icecast-auth-message: " + 8 non-NUL bytes with no NUL inside the region passes guard 19 (line 19 precedes line 22), then `%s` scans past the delivered end up to sizeof(url->errormsg)-1 bytes and copies adjacent memory into `url->errormsg`. `snprintf`'s `sizeof(url->errormsg)` bound protects only the destination write, not the source scan — missing length bound on an input-derived string read, OOB read (CWE-125).

Same root cause at a second sink: `ptr` entry-point bytes reach the `%u` scan at line 16, guarded only by the prefix match at line 13 (line 13 precedes line 16) which admits arbitrary suffixes including non-NUL digit runs; `bytes` from line 4 is never used to cap the scan. A delivered frame like "timelimit: 99999999999999999999" ending inside the digit run makes `%u` read ~20 bytes past the delivered end (unsigned-int conversion bound) — missing length bound on input-derived scan (CWE-125).

assumptions: `size * nmemb` (line 4) is the delivered header length for the callback frame; on the admitting paths of guards 13 and 19 the delivered length is at least `timelimit_header_len` / 22 respectively (the prefix must match).
`sizeof(url->errormsg)` (line 22) bounds the destination write; its exact value is not shown, and it does not bound the `%s` source scan.
`url->timelimit_header_len` and `url->auth_header_len` are config-derived sizes with no shown cap; they are not attacker-scaled here.
limitations: NULL-deref candidates at lines 5, 9, 10, 17 (`auth_user`, `client->auth`, `auth->state`, `client->con`) are dereferenced without checks, but no shown statement can produce NULL for them and they are framework-populated — robustness, not a confirmed finding.

`sscanf` return at line 16 is discarded; on non-digit content `limit` stays 0 (line 15) making `client->con->discon_time = time(NULL)` (line 17) an immediate disconnect — error-handling/DoS concern whose security-relevant consumer (`discon_time`) is unshown.

`size_t bytes = size * nmemb;` (line 4) could theoretically wrap `size_t`, but the operands' magnitudes are not shown and `bytes` is only returned (line 31), so no security-consumed wraparound is demonstrable.
`time(NULL)` failure sentinel and `time(NULL) + limit` arithmetic at line 17 cannot wrap in the shown 64-bit `time_t`; no downstream use shown.
Empty configured header (`auth_header_len == 0) would make line 11 return 0 unconditionally (auth-acceptance logic), contingent on unshown config semantics.
The line-16 witness magnitude (~20 bytes excess) depends on the unshown backing capacity of `ptr`; the line-22 witness is the primary (bounded by the destination buffer size `sizeof(url->errormsg)`).

verdict.summary: mobi_buffer_move performs memmove with the unvalidated `len` parameter on the negative-offset path: the only guard (line 12: `if (buf->offset < aoffset)`) checks the source start but never bounds `buf->offset + len` against `buf->maxlen`, so any `len > buf->maxlen - buf->offset` writes past the end of the buffer (excess = `buf->offset + len - buf->maxlen`). When `offset`/`len` derive from input data this is a heap out-of-bounds write enabling memory corruption.

evidence.reason: CWE-787 heap out-of-bounds write. `len` (size_t, full [0, 2^64-1] domain) is unconstrained on the negative-offset path: the guard at line 12 (`if (buf->offset < aoffset)`) only rejects offsets whose magnitude exceeds `buf->offset`, protecting the source start, and no statement between line 12 and this sink bounds `buf->offset + len` against `buf->maxlen` (the buffer capacity used at line 5). Witness: offset=-1 -> aoffset=1 (line 2); buf->offset=1 passes line 12 (1 < 1 false, no early return at line 15); len=buf->maxlen; memmove copies `buf->maxlen` bytes into `buf->data + 1`, spanning [1, maxlen+1) over a `maxlen`-byte object — 1 byte out of bounds, and the excess grows with `len`. The line-5 guard is unreachable on this path (line 4 routes `offset >= 0` to the other branch).

assumptions: buf->maxlen is the total capacity of the object at buf->data, matching the capacity semantics of the line 5 comparison.
buf->offset and buf->maxlen are non-negative size fields used as an index and a capacity in the shown code (lines 3, 5, 12, 19).
Line 5 arithmetic on size_t values is unsigned, so the sum can wrap for `len` near 2^64.
limitations: Positive-offset path: `buf->offset + aoffset + len` (line 5) can wrap in size_t for `len` around 2^64 - (buf->offset + aoffset), admitting a huge `len` that reaches the same memmove sink (line 19) — a range claim (CWE-190 root), not a single demonstrated boundary value; same sink as the primary finding, not counted separately.
abs(INT_MIN) at line 2 is undefined behavior; the resulting huge `aoffset` is rejected by line 12 (returns error), so no memory impact is demonstrated.

buf is dereferenced at lines 3/5/12/19 with no NULL check; for an internal helper whose contract requires a valid buffer this is treated as a robustness/internal-contract concern, not a separate confirmed CWE.

`buf->offset += len` (line 20) can advance past `buf->maxlen` after the negative-path move; it shares the same missing destination-capacity bound as the primary finding, not an independent root cause.
If an unshown caller enforced `len <= buf->maxlen - buf->offset`, the negative path would be safe — no such invariant is visible in the fragment and it cannot be assumed.

verdict.summary: Unsigned wraparound of `pcs->status.write_pos - pcs->status.read_pos` (line 4) when the entry state has write_pos < read_pos yields a near-UINT_MAX length; `min()` admits it, so the memcpy at line 7 reads `count` bytes from `buffer + read_pos` starting beyond the valid region [0, write_pos) with no visible capacity or ordering bound, producing a heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) driven by the corrupted length (CWE-190).

evidence.reason: `count` is derived at lines 3-4 as min(max_data, write_pos - read_pos) in unsigned `uint` arithmetic. No shown statement constrains `read_pos <= write_pos` before the sink; on the wrap path (e.g., read_pos=1, write_pos=0, max_data>=1), the subtraction wraps to a huge value and `min()` admits count = max_data >= 1, which passes the `if (count)` guard at line 6. The read at line 7 then dereferences `buffer + read_pos` (offset 1, beyond the fragment's own validity bound write_pos) for `count` bytes with no visible buffer-capacity or ordering check, giving an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125); the unsigned wraparound of the length operand is the independent root cause (CWE-190).

assumptions: `uint` is an unsigned 32-bit integer subject to defined wraparound on underflow.
`data` is a caller-provided buffer of `max_data` bytes; the write side is provably safe because `count <= max_data` is enforced by the `min()` at lines 3-4.
The only visible validity bound for the status buffer used by the fragment is `write_pos` (lines 4 and 9); the buffer allocation size itself is not shown.
limitations: The witness requires an entry state with `write_pos < read_pos`; no shown statement creates that state (the fragment only advances read_pos up to write_pos and resets when equal). If the external status subsystem always maintains the ordering, the path is unreachable; that invariant is not visible in the fragment and cannot be used to exonerate, which caps confidence.

The chosen `max_data` magnitude is an example; the demonstrated claim is a range claim (any max_data >= 1 on the wrap path produces the out-of-domain read), so confidence is calibrated below the exact-witness band.
NULL `data` / `pcs` / `buffer` dereferences were considered and demoted: no shown statement can produce a NULL for these pointers.

Use-after-free / double-free around the `gs_free_object` at line 10 was considered and demoted: the state reset at line 11 and count=0 on the subsequent call keep the buffer unreferenced within the shown code.
A destination heap overflow from memcpy is NOT present: `count <= max_data` at lines 3-4 bounds the write to the caller's buffer.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The fragment is the fixed push_pipe(): every security-relevant operation is covered by a shown protective statement — pipe-ring indices are masked to [0, ring_size-1] (lines 6, 23, 26, 30), the fill loop is bounded by pipe_full (line 29), each fresh buffer gets a default-ops page with offset explicitly zeroed (lines 35–37), each stored length is capped by min_t(..., PAGE_SIZE) (line 38), the alloc_page result is NULL-checked (lines 32–33), and size is clamped and zero-filtered (lines 11–14).

assumptions: pipe_full(head, tail, limit) has its name-implied pipe-ring semantics: true when head-tail occupancy has reached the limit argument (line 29).
pipe->bufs has ring_size entries (capacity-by-name); the shown mask bound iter_head & (ring_size-1) to [0, ring_size-1] is derived entirely inside the fragment.
struct pipe_buffer fields (ops/page/offset/len) hold at most one page of data per buffer, consistent with the one-page alloc_page at line 31 and the min cap at line 38.
